loop:0.t: The R L Loop. Learning by doing: try something, see what happens, adjust.

loop:1.t: Meet Pip. This is Pip, a mouse in a small maze. In the top corner sits a piece of cheese. Close by sleeps a cat. Two rocks block the middle. Pip has never been here. Nobody gives it a map or tells it what to do. Whatever it learns, it must find out by trying things. That is reinforcement learning.

loop:2.t: Two sides: agent and environment. Every R L problem splits the world in two. The agent is the one that makes choices: here, Pip. The environment is everything else: the walls, the rocks, the cheese, the cat, and the rules for what happens next. Pip controls only its own choices. It cannot move a rock or wake the cat.

loop:3.t: State: where things stand. The state describes the situation now. Here the cheese, the cat and the rocks never move, so the state is just Pip’s cell. We number the cells 1 to 20; Pip starts in cell 16. What the agent senses is its observation. Pip always knows its cell, so here the two are the same. A robot with a camera sees only part of a room; then they differ, and the agent must act on what it observes.

loop:4.t: Actions: four moves. In every state Pip picks an action: up, right, down or left. That is the whole menu. The environment decides what an action does. A move goes one cell over, but if a wall or a rock is in the way, Pip bumps into it and stays where it is. From cell 16, down and left both bump.

loop:5.t: Reward: one number per step. After every action the environment hands Pip a reward, a single number. The rule: stepping onto the cheese pays plus 1, stepping onto the cat pays minus 1, and every other step pays 0, bumps included. Cheese or cat ends the walk. The task’s designer chose these numbers. Pip cannot change them and does not know them in advance. The one thing built into Pip is that more reward is better.

loop:6.t: One turn of the loop. Put it together. The agent looks at the state and picks an action. The environment applies its rules and answers with two things: the next state and a reward. Then the same thing happens again from the new state. That cycle is the R L loop. Every method in this course runs on it.

loop:7.t: Counting time. We count time: t equals 0, 1, 2, and so on. At time t, Pip is in state S t and picks action A t. The answer comes one tick later, so it carries the next number: R tplus 1 is the reward for action A t. A walk reads S0, A0, R1, S1, A1, R2, and on. So the third move is A2, it pays R3, and a walk of 14 moves ends at t equals 14.

loop:8.t: Pip’s first move. Pip knows nothing yet, so it picks each action at random, as if rolling a four-sided die. It has no memory either, so it may repeat a bump. Its first roll, at t equals 0: right. The environment moves Pip from cell 16 to cell 17 and pays 0. In symbols: S0 equals 16, A0 equals right, R1 equals 0, S1 equals 17.

loop:9.t: A bump. Pip’s third move, at t equals 2: it is in cell 18 and rolls down. There is a wall below. The environment’s rule says Pip stays put, so S3 equals 18 again, and R3 equals 0. Pip’s wishes don’t matter here: the environment decides what an action does. A wasted move still uses up a time step.

loop:10.t: Round and round. The loop keeps turning: state, action, reward, next state. Pip bumps the wall again, steps back and forth, and walks into a rock. Every one of these moves pays 0. After 13 moves, Pip has collected no reward at all. Each log line shows t, the cell, the action, where Pip lands and the reward.

loop:11.t: The walk ends. On its 14th move, at t equals 13, Pip steps up onto the cheese: R14 equals plus 1. Cheese and cat are terminal states: when Pip reaches one, the walk stops, here at t equals 14. One walk from the start to a terminal state is called an episode. Afterwards Pip is put back in cell 16, and a fresh episode begins.

loop:12.t: Episode after episode. Let random Pip walk episode after episode. Here is a chart to keep score. Each bar is one episode: the further right, the later it was walked. Its height is how many steps it took. Teal means it ended at the cheese, rose means the cat. The first ten: 14 steps to the cheese, 13 to the cat, 67 to the cat, and so on. Only 3 of these 10 reach the cheese.

loop:13.t: What blind wandering gets. After 100 episodes only 26 reached the cheese. One clear reason: the cat can be entered from four open cells, the cheese from only two, and the cat sits on the way to the cheese. Episodes are long, 63 steps on average; we counted about 4 moves in 10 being bumps. Some bars are too tall to draw, so a small arrow marks them; those episodes still ran to the cheese or cat.

loop:14.t: No answer key. Notice what Pip is never told. Nobody says “up was the right move in cell 10”. It only gets rewards, and in episode 1, 13 steps paid 0 before one paid plus 1. Which of those steps earned the cheese? Pip must work that out itself. This is the big difference from supervised learning, where every example comes with the correct answer.

loop:15.t: The goal. So what is Pip trying to do? Collect as much reward as it can in total over an episode, not just on the next step. Here every move but the last pays 0, so the next reward alone says almost nothing. A rule for choosing actions is called a policy. Rolling the die is one, the random policy, and it averages minus 0.48 per episode. Later reels find much better ones.

loop:16.t: Your turn: be the agent. Now you are the agent. Tap an arrow to pick an action. The environment answers with the next state and the reward, and the log records each turn. Try bumping into a rock, then reach the cheese. When the episode ends, tap anywhere to start a new one.

loop:17.t: The same loop, everywhere. The loop is the same in far bigger problems. DeepMind’s Atari player D Q N, in 2015, saw the screen pixels, chose joystick moves, and was rewarded by the change in game score. AlphaGo, in 2016, got its reward only at the end of a game: win or lose. Chat assistants are tuned with R L from human feedback, R L H F: often the whole reply counts as one action, scored once by a model of which answers people prefer.

loop:18.t: Recap. The agent picks actions; the environment answers each one with a reward and the next state. That loop repeats until a terminal state ends the episode. Nobody tells the agent the right move. Its goal is the most reward in total. Adding rewards up sounds simple, but the next reel finds a catch.

returns:0.t: Rewards  and  Returns. Why the agent cares about the total, not just the next snack.

returns:1.t: One number per step. Back in Pip’s maze, with the same rules: cheese plus 1, cat minus 1, every other step 0. In the last reel Pip walked at random, and its first episode took 14 steps. Here are its rewards, one per step: thirteen zeros, then plus 1. How good was that episode as a whole?

returns:2.t: Add them up: the return. Add up all the rewards from a moment until the episode ends. That sum is called the return. For episode 1, counted from the start: thirteen zeros plus one, so the return is 1. The return is the score for a whole stretch of the walk, not for one step.

returns:3.t: Writing it down. The return from time t is written G t. It adds every reward that comes after time t: R tplus 1, plus R tplus 2, and so on, up to R T, where T is the time the episode ends, its number of moves. It starts at tplus 1 because the reward for the action at time t arrives one tick later. After the end nothing is left: G T equals 0. Episode 1: T equals 14, G0 equals 1.

returns:4.t: Why the total counts. Why not judge a move by its own reward? From cell 16, going up pays 0, going right pays 0, and bumping into the wall pays 0. The next reward cannot tell them apart. What differs is what comes later. The return looks at the whole rest of the episode. One walk’s return credits every move in it, good or bad alike; averaging over many walks sorts them out, as later reels show.

returns:5.t: Same return, very different walks. Now compare three random episodes that all ended at the cheese: episode 10 took 10 steps, episode 1 took 14, and episode 5 took 147. Each one’s return is exactly 1. With these rewards, the return ignores how long Pip wandered. A detour of a hundred steps costs nothing, so Pip has no reason to hurry.

returns:6.t: A step cost. A common fix is a step cost: the designer changes the rules so every step that does not land on the cheese or the cat pays minus 0.1, bumps included. Cheese plus 1 and cat minus 1 stay, and both still end the walk. This is a new reward rule, and every number from here on uses it. Why 0.1? It is just a small choice; we will see that the size matters.

returns:7.t: Shorter walks win now. Recount with the step cost. A cheese walk of n steps has n minus 1 ordinary steps, so its return is 1 minus 0.1 times (n minus 1). A cat walk scores minus 1 minus 0.1 times (n minus 1). The shortest possible walk, 7 steps, scores 0.4. Episode 10 scores 0.1, episode 1 scores minus 0.3, and episode 5 scores minus 13.6. The total now prefers short walks.

returns:8.t: A picture of all 100. Here are the 100 random episodes. Across: steps taken. Up and down: the return, with the step cost. Most returns are negative, so the zero line sits near the top; 8 long episodes fall off the right edge. Teal ended at the cheese, rose at the cat. Each dot sits on one of two lines, the cat line 2 below: every extra step costs 0.1, so on each line shorter is better.

returns:9.t: A return from every step. A return can be counted from any time, not just the start. Take the shortest walk. From cell 10, the last cell before the cheese, only the plus 1 is left: G6 equals 1. One step earlier: minus 0.1 plus 1 equals 0.9. So each return is the next reward plus the return after it. Working backward gives 1, 0.9, 0.8, and so on, down to 0.4 at the start. Later reels average returns like these into a value.

returns:10.t: The return is a gamble. From the same start cell, random Pip’s returns are all over the place: the best of the 100 episodes scored 0.3, the worst minus 30.2. The return depends on every random move along the way, so it is a random number. Its average here is minus 6.7. The average over many episodes from this cell, with this way of choosing moves, is what a later reel calls a value; choose moves differently and it changes.

returns:11.t: Careful: the cost changes the goal. The size matters. With a cost of 1.5 per step, the shortest cheese walk scores 1 minus 1.5 times 6 equals minus 8, but running into the cat, 5 steps, scores minus 1 minus 1.5 times 4 equals minus 7. Now rushing to the cat has the highest return, so an agent that maximises it would do that. It chases the return you wrote down, not the one you meant.

returns:12.t: Reward what you want. This happens with real agents. In 2016, OpenAI trained an agent on the boat racing game CoastRunners, where points come from hitting targets along the course. The agent found a lagoon where three targets kept reappearing. It kept circling there, crashing and catching fire, never finishing the race, and still scored more than finishing would. The reward said points, not winning.

returns:13.t: Tasks that never end. Pip’s walks always end. Many tasks don’t: a thermostat or a trading program just keeps going. These are continuing tasks, and their sum has no last term. If such an agent earned plus 1 every step, its return would be 1, 2, 3, and grow forever. Two very different agents could both have an infinite return, and we could not compare them. The next reel fixes this.

returns:14.t: Your turn. Drag the step cost and watch three walks: the shortest way to the cheese, the 14-step episode 1, and the quickest way into the cat. The bars show each walk’s return. At 0 the two cheese walks tie. Small costs reward hurrying. Push the cost up: just above 0.2 the quick cat walk overtakes episode 1, and above 1 it beats even the shortest cheese walk.

returns:15.t: The big bet. R L rests on one idea, often called the reward hypothesis: any goal can be written as getting the largest expected return, the total reward averaged over the agent’s own random choices and the environment’s. Richard Sutton, a founder of the field, put it this way. It is a working assumption, not a theorem, and still debated. In practice it has carried R L far, when rewards are designed with care.

returns:16.t: Recap. A reward scores one step. The return adds up all the rewards from a step until the episode ends, and that total is what an agent tries to make large. How you set the rewards decides what “good” means: a step cost makes short walks win, and too big a cost can make the cat win.

discount:0.t: The Discount Factor gamma. A reward tomorrow is worth a bit less than a reward today.

discount:1.t: Two loose ends. The last reel left two problems. With plain rewards, a 10-step and a 147-step walk to the cheese both return 1; a step cost fixed that, but too big a cost made the cat the best plan. And a never-ending task’s sum can grow forever. Discounting helps with both. Its knob must be chosen too, but it can never make the cat look good.

discount:2.t: Sooner is better. Would you take 100 rupees today or 100 rupees in a year? Most people take it today. You can use it now, and who knows what happens in a year. So a reward far in the future should count for a little less than the same reward now. R L builds this in with one number.

discount:3.t: The discount factor gamma. That number is the discount factor, written gamma (gamma), from 0 to 1. The first reward after now counts fully. A reward one step after it is multiplied by gamma; two steps after, by gamma times gamma, written gamma squared; k steps after, by gamma to the power k. The bars show gamma equals 0.9: 1, 0.9, 0.81, 0.73, and on. gamma equals 1 means no discount; gamma equals 0 means only the first reward counts.

discount:4.t: The discounted return. Now redefine the return. The first reward counts fully, the next is multiplied by gamma, the one after by gamma squared, and so on. G t equals R tplus 1 plus gamma R tplus 2 plus gamma squared R tplus 3 plus ... With gamma equals 1 this is the plain sum from the last reel. With gamma below 1, every reward still counts, just less the later it comes.

discount:5.t: Back in the maze. Drop the step cost: cheese plus 1, cat minus 1, other steps 0 again, and take gamma equals 0.9. On the shortest walk, the plus 1 is the seventh reward, six steps after the first. So it counts 0.9 to the sixth: 0.9 times 0.9 times 0.9 times 0.9 times 0.9 times 0.9 equals 0.53. The discounted return of the shortest walk is 0.53.

discount:6.t: Long walks lose, cats stay bad. Now the same three random episodes. Episode 10, 10 steps: 0.9 to the ninth, 0.39. Episode 1, 14 steps: 0.25. Episode 5, 147 steps: about 0.0000002, practically nothing. Shorter walks win, with no step cost at all. And a discounted cheese is always above 0 while a discounted cat is always below 0, so the cat can never become the best plan. Wandering forever earns 0: better than the cat, worse than any cheese.

discount:7.t: Counting backward again. As before, count from every step of the shortest walk. From the last cell before the cheese, the return is 1. One step earlier, the plus 1 comes one step later: 0.9. Then 0.81, 0.73, and so on, down to 0.53 at the start. The rule: G t equals R tplus 1 plus gamma times G tplus 1. A later reel builds on this rule; it is the seed of what is called the Bellman equation.

discount:8.t: Reason 1: the future may not come. Why multiply by gamma? Here is one honest reason. Suppose that after every step there is a 1 in 10 chance the walk is simply cut short: the lights go out, or Pip is called home, and nothing more is earned, good or bad. We sent Pip along the shortest walk 10,000 times like that. It reached the cheese 5,302 times: 53.0 percent, close to 0.9 to the sixth, 0.53.

discount:9.t: gamma as a survival chance. So gamma equals 0.9 behaves like a 9 in 10 chance, at every step, that the world keeps going. A reward six steps away survives six such chances: 0.9 to the sixth. On average over the cut-offs, the plain return in such a fragile world equals the discounted return, exactly. That is reason one: the far future is less certain. It is a way to read gamma; in practice gamma is a setting the designer picks.

discount:10.t: Reason 2: sums stay finite. Back to the never-ending task that pays plus 1 every step. The plain sum grows forever. Discounted with gamma equals 0.9: 1 plus 0.9 plus 0.81 plus ... reaches 6.5 after 10 steps, 8.8 after 20, 9.9 after 50. It never passes 10: by the geometric series from algebra, the sum of gamma to the k is 1 divided by (1 minus gamma). Every agent now has a finite return to compare.

discount:11.t: How far ahead does it look?. That same number, 1 divided by (1 minus gamma), is a handy rule of thumb for how far ahead an agent effectively looks. With gamma equals 0.9 it is 10 steps; with gamma equals 0.99 it is 100. Why that number? In the fragile-world reading, a world that ends with chance 1 in 10 per step lasts 10 steps on average. It is not a hard cut-off: at that distance a reward still counts about 0.35.

discount:12.t: A crumb or the cheese?. Now gamma changes which plan is best. Put a crumb worth plus 0.3 in cell 6, two steps up. Eating it also ends the walk. The cheese, plus 1, is seven steps away along the bottom. Crumb plan: 0.3 times gamma. Cheese plan: gamma to the sixth. With gamma equals 0.5 the crumb wins, 0.15 against 0.016. With gamma equals 0.9 the cheese wins, 0.53 against 0.27. They swap at gamma about 0.79.

discount:13.t: Your turn. Drag gamma. Pip does not know the maze, but we do, so for each setting we compute the best plan, counting rewards with the discount, and let Pip walk it. Later reels show how Pip can learn this. Bars: each plan’s worth from the start. Below about 0.79, the crumb wins: the cheese is too far away to matter. Above it, Pip is patient enough to walk to the cheese.

discount:14.t: The price of patience. Why not always use gamma close to 1? The more the far future counts, the more its luck counts too. Here are random Pip’s 100 discounted returns for three values of gamma. With gamma equals 0.5 they all squash to almost 0: steady, but they barely tell the cheese from the cat. With gamma equals 0.99 they spread almost from minus 1 to plus 1, so judging the start from a few walks would depend heavily on which walks you happened to see.

discount:15.t: Where you meet gamma. Discounting is old: economists discount future money the same way, through interest rates. In R L, gamma is part of the problem setup, picked by the designer. DeepMind’s Atari player D Q N used gamma equals 0.99. Games that always end, like Go, can use gamma equals 1, with no discount at all. And people? Studies suggest we care much more about today versus tomorrow than about day 100 versus day 101, unlike a constant gamma.

discount:16.t: Recap. The discount factor gamma makes a reward k steps after the first count gamma to the k. Later rewards count less because the future is uncertain and sooner is better, and the sum stays finite even in never-ending tasks. Small gamma is impatient, gamma near 1 is patient but its returns vary more. The agent looks roughly 1 divided by (1 minus gamma) steps ahead.

mdp:0.t: Markov Decision Process. The board game that almost every R L problem is written as.

mdp:1.t: Writing the world down. Pip the mouse is back in its maze. Every step, Pip notes which cell it is in, its state, picks a move, its action, and gets a reward. This reel writes the maze’s rules down so precisely that a computer could run them. That rulebook is called a Markov Decision Process, or M D P.

mdp:2.t: Ingredient one: states. First, list every situation Pip can be in. Here a state is simply Pip’s cell. We keep the numbers from the first reel, 1 to 20. Cells 7 and 13 are rocks, so there are 18 states. Two of them are special: landing on the cheese or the cat ends the walk. These are called terminal states. That leaves 16 cells where Pip still has to choose a move.

mdp:3.t: Ingredient two: actions. Next, list the moves. Pip has the same four actions in every cell: up, right, down and left. One convention matters: if a move points into the outer wall or a rock, Pip bumps and stays put. That still counts as a step.

mdp:4.t: Ingredient three: rewards. Then the rewards. The reward is paid for the step that lands on a cell: plus 1 for landing on the cheese, minus 1 for landing on the cat, and the walk ends there. Every other step pays 0, bumps included. In general a reward may depend on the cell, the move and where Pip lands, written R(s, a, s prime). In this maze only the landing cell matters.

mdp:5.t: A wet floor. Now a twist: someone mopped the floor. When Pip tries a move, it goes that way 8 times in 10. The other 2 times it slides sideways, relative to the direction it tried: 1 in 10 to its left, 1 in 10 to its right. It never slides backwards. So the same action can lead to different cells. The world has become random.

mdp:6.t: Try it at the start. Pip stands at the start and tries right, again and again. Right leads on to the next cell. A slide up lands one cell higher. A slide down hits the outer wall, so Pip stays put. The bars count where each try ended, one bar per outcome. In the first 10 tries: 9 moved right and 1 slid up.

mdp:7.t: A thousand tries. Keep going to 1000 tries. The bars settle: 795 moved right, 102 slid up and 103 stayed put. That is 0.795, 0.102 and 0.103 of the tries, close to the 0.8, 0.1 and 0.1 built into the floor. Each single try is a surprise, but the chances behind them are fixed. The dashed lines mark 800 and 100.

mdp:8.t: Transition probabilities. These chances are written P(s prime given s, a), read “P of s prime given s and a”: the probability that Pip lands in cell s prime, the next state, when it is in state s and takes action a. If Pip bumps and stays put, s prime is simply s. For every cell and move, the chances over all landing cells add up to 1. Sixteen cells times four moves: 64 little lists like this one.

mdp:9.t: The whole rulebook. Put the pieces together: states, actions, transition probabilities, rewards, and gamma (gamma), the discount, here 0.9. Like the rewards, gamma is chosen by the designer: it says what we want, not how the floor behaves. That list is an M D P. Pip does not get to read this rulebook; it learns by trying, like those 1000 tries. When a reel computes the best plan from the rulebook itself, as the discount reel did, that is called planning.

mdp:10.t: Why “Markov”?. Here is the key assumption. The chances of what happens next depend only on the current state and action, not on the path that led there. This is the Markov property. Pip can reach this cell straight from the start, or after a detour along the bottom row. Either way, trying right gives the same 0.8, 0.1 and 0.1.

mdp:11.t: Checking it in data. Pip wanders at random for 2000 walks. Every time it tries right in this cell, we note where it came from and where it lands. Bumps in place are left out. From below: 0.799, 0.093, 0.108. From the right or above: nearly the same. In a world whose rules you cannot read, this is the test: rows further apart than luck allows would mean the cell is not enough. Our maze was built Markov, so here it passes.

mdp:12.t: When the cell is not enough. Imagine a new rule: the cat wakes after Pip’s 10th step, and an awake cat pounces if Pip is next to it. Beside the cat, step 4 is safe and step 12 is not. The cell alone no longer says what comes next: not Markov. Adding “is the cat awake?” is not enough: a sleeping cat might wake on the next step. The state must hold the clock: the cell plus the steps taken so far.

mdp:13.t: Cells, not paths. Why does Markov matter so much? Because of it, anything Pip works out about what to do or what to expect can be stored per cell, and only 16 cells need it. If the past mattered, Pip would need an entry for every path instead. Counting paths from the start, with a bump counting as a step: 3 after one step, 37 after three, and 202,435 after ten.

mdp:14.t: Every visit counts. In those 2000 random walks, Pip stood on this cell 16,047 times. 13,887 of those arrivals came by a path it had never walked before. Filed by path, almost every page of Pip’s notebook would hold one lonely visit. Filed by cell, all 16,047 land on one page. That pooling is allowed only because of Markov: what happens next does not depend on how Pip got here.

mdp:15.t: Your turn. Pip memorises one shortest route as a fixed list: up three times, then right four times. The slip chance is the total chance of sliding sideways; so far it was 0.2. Drag it, and Pip runs the list 1000 times. Bars count runs ending on the cheese, the cat, or nowhere. At 0.2, only 229 reach the cheese: a list cannot react to a slip. A rule for every cell can. That is a policy, coming next.

mdp:16.t: Where MDPs are used. The name honours Andrey Markov, who studied chains of random events in the early 1900s. Richard Bellman studied Markov decision processes in the 1950s, for planning under uncertainty. Robot navigation, stock and inventory planning, and board games are often written as MDPs. When one snapshot is not Markov, people widen the state: DeepMind’s Atari player fed in the last four screen images, so a ball’s motion was visible.

mdp:17.t: Recap. An M D P writes a world down as states, actions, transition probabilities, rewards and gamma. The same action can lead to different cells, but the chances are fixed. The Markov property says the next step depends only on the current state and action. That is what lets everything Pip gathers be filed per cell instead of per path.

policy:0.t: Policies. The agent’s rulebook: in this situation, do that.

policy:1.t: The list that broke. In the last reel, Pip memorised the shortest route as a list of seven moves. On the wet floor, only 229 of 1000 runs reached the cheese. Here is why. On move 2, Pip slid right into a new cell. The list still said “up” and then “right”, which here point into rocks. In this run, Pip bumped five times, and the list ran out.

policy:2.t: A rule for every cell. So Pip writes a rule card instead: for every cell, one move. This is a policy, written pi (pi). pi of s is the action the policy picks in state s. Why is the cell enough? The maze is Markov: the cell tells Pip everything about what can happen next. So what Pip must find, per cell, is a move. This card follows shortest routes; at the start, where up and right tie, it picks up. Call it policy A.

policy:3.t: Slip, then recover. Watch policy A on the wet floor. On move 2, Pip slides right instead of going up. No problem: the new cell has its own arrow, pointing back to the route. Pip reaches the cheese in 9 steps instead of 7. A policy keeps working after surprises, because it never assumes where Pip will be. It only asks: where am I now?

policy:4.t: How many rule cards?. How many different policies are there? Each of the 16 cells can hold any of 4 arrows, so 4 times 4 times ... sixteen times: about 4.3 billion. Most of them are silly: arrows into walls, or arrows that send Pip in circles. Scoring one card fairly takes thousands of walks, so trying them all is hopeless. Finding a good one without trying everything is what the rest of reinforcement learning is about.

policy:5.t: Two candidates. Here is a second card, policy B. It is a copy of A with a single arrow changed: in cell 8, just left of the cat, B points down, into a rock. Pip only lands in cell 8 after slipping down from the top row, so B looks just as good most of the time. Is it really worse? Pip does not know the maze’s rules, so it has to find out by walking.

policy:6.t: Scoring a walk. To compare policies, score each walk by its return: the rewards added up, each discounted by gamma (gamma) equals 0.9 per step of delay. Here the only reward comes at the end, so the return is 0.9 to the power of steps minus one, plus for the cheese, minus for the cat. Seven steps: 0.9 to the sixth, 0.53. A walk still going after 100 steps is stopped and scores 0, as no reward has come; with A and B it never happens.

policy:7.t: Walk 1: a tie. Pip walks once with each card. To be fair, both walks use the same dice: the same slips at the same moments. Then any difference comes from the arrows, not from luck. Walk 1: twice Pip slides into the outer wall and stays put, but both walks follow the same arrows to the cheese in 9 steps. Return 0.43 each. This walk tells Pip nothing about the difference.

policy:8.t: Walk 2: the trap. Walk 2. On the top row, Pip slips down into the changed cell. With A, the arrow points up: Pip climbs back and reaches the cheese in 10 steps, return 0.39. With B, the arrow points into the rock. Pip bumps, then a slip throws it right into the cat: minus 0.48. Not just bad luck: from cell 8, B can only bump, slip into the other rock, or slip into the cat. Once there, B always ends on the cat.

policy:9.t: Five thousand walks. Up the side: the average return of all walks so far. Along the bottom: the number of walks. Early on the lines jump; then they flatten. After 5000: A 0.331, B 0.288, each give or take about 0.005 of leftover luck, so the gap is real. B ends on the cat 1,030 times, A 641. Judge a policy by its average return. Measured from every cell, that average is its value: next reel.

policy:10.t: Rolling dice on purpose. So far each cell held one fixed move: a deterministic policy. A policy can also hold chances: a stochastic policy. We write pi(a given s), read “pi of a given s”: the probability of picking action a in state s. The random Pip from the first reel was one too: a quarter for each move. Careful, there are now two kinds of chance. The wet floor is the world’s randomness. These dice are Pip’s own choice.

policy:11.t: Why roll dice?. Two good reasons. A learner must explore: slips carry Pip into new cells, but if it always picks its arrow, it never finds out what the other moves would do. And against an opponent, being predictable gets punished: in rock, paper, scissors, play each one third of the time. A fixed maze has no opponent. In each cell, some move is at least as good as the others, so putting all the chance on it cannot hurt: the best policy needs no dice.

policy:12.t: Dial in randomness. Drag epsilon (epsilon): on each move, with chance epsilon, Pip ignores its arrow and picks one of the four moves at random. Otherwise it follows policy A. At 0, plain policy A: 0.331. At 0.2, the 0.85 and 0.05 card from two steps back: 0.233. At 1, Pip ignores its card: minus 0.031. That is close to 0, not clearly negative, because discounting shrinks the late endings of long random walks.

policy:13.t: Your turn: write a card. Tap any cell to turn its arrow a quarter turn clockwise. After each change, Pip walks your card 5000 times from the start, with the same dice as before. Policy A scores 0.331. Can you beat it? Barely. Worked out exactly from the rulebook, the best card is worth 0.3345 from the start, and A 0.3339. The best card differs from A in one cell; on these walks it scores 0.332. Or break A, and see which cells matter.

policy:14.t: Where policies live. A thermostat runs a tiny deterministic policy: too cold, heat on; warm enough, heat off. A robot’s controller maps sensor readings to motor commands. AlphaGo, which beat Lee Sedol at Go in 2016, used a policy network: given a board, it output a probability for every legal move, a stochastic policy learned first from millions of human moves, then improved by playing against itself.

policy:15.t: Recap. A policy pi is a rule from state to action: an arrow in every cell, so it keeps working after any slip. It can be deterministic, or stochastic with pi(a given s). To compare policies, run each many times and average the returns. One walk is luck. That average, from every cell, is next: the value of a policy.

values:0.t: Value Functions. How good is it to be here? How good is this move?

values:1.t: Back in the maze. Pip is back in its maze. Stepping onto the cheese pays plus 1, onto the cat minus 1, and either one ends the walk. Other steps pay 0. The return adds up the rewards, each step later multiplied by one more gamma (gamma), here 0.9. One change: the floor is dry again, so every move goes where Pip intends. All randomness now comes from Pip’s own habit, so the numbers differ from the policy reel’s on purpose.

values:2.t: Pip’s policy. Pip uses policy A from the policy reel, the rule card with an arrow in every cell, with the epsilon (epsilon) dial at 0.2: one move in five, Pip picks one of the four directions at random. So the arrow wins 85 times in 100, and each other move 5 times. Bumping into a wall or a rock leaves Pip where it is, and that still counts as a step.

values:3.t: One walk. How good is it to start in the bottom-left corner with this policy? Let’s try. Walk 1: Pip follows the arrows up and along the top and reaches the cheese in 7 steps. The first step’s reward counts fully, and each later one is multiplied by one more 0.9. The plus 1 came on step 7, so the return is 0.9 multiplied 6 times: 0.53.

values:4.t: Same start, different walks. Walk 2: Pip gets distracted twice. Once it steps back down, once it bumps into the top wall. Cheese on step 10, return 0.39. Walk 3: right beside the cheese, a random move points down, onto the cat. Return minus 0.48 after 8 steps. Walk 4 has one random move, at the very start, but it happens to pick up, the arrow’s own direction, so nothing changes: 0.53. Same cell, same policy, different returns.

values:5.t: Keeping score. Let’s put the returns on a chart. Across is the walk number, up is the return, from minus 1 to plus 1. Each dot is one walk: gold means the walk reached the cheese, rose means the cat. The dark line is the average of all returns so far. After four walks: (0.53 plus 0.39 minus 0.48 plus 0.53) divided by 4 equals 0.24.

values:6.t: Many walks. Pip keeps walking. Early on the average jumps around: after 10 walks it is 0.28, after 100 walks 0.44. Each new walk moves the average less and less. After 1000 walks it has settled at 0.40, give or take about 0.015 of leftover wobble. That settled number is what we were after.

values:7.t: The value of a cell. The average return of many walks that start in a cell and follow the policy is that cell’s value. In probability terms it is the expected discounted return: the number the average closes in on as walks pile up. We write it V of s, said “V of s”, where s is the state, here a cell. So V(start) is about 0.40.

values:8.t: A whole notebook. Now do the same from every cell: 1000 walks each, and write the average in the cell’s corner. That is Pip’s notebook of values for this policy. Stronger gold shading means a higher value. The cheese and cat cells get no walks. Standing on them, the walk is already over, so their value is 0 and they stay blank.

values:9.t: Reading the notebook. Beside the cheese the value is 0.87, not 1. The arrow points at the cheese, but one move in five is random, and one in twenty goes down, onto the cat. Two cells three steps from the cheese: on the top row 0.68, beside the cat only 0.60. From there, a random move to the right lands on the cat.

values:10.t: A different policy. Meet the Wanderer: a policy with no arrows at all. Every single move is random. Same maze, same rewards, same way of computing returns. The Wanderer’s first walk from the start wanders back and forth and does find the cheese, but only on step 35. By then the plus 1 has shrunk to a return of 0.03.

values:11.t: The Wanderer’s notebook. 1000 Wanderer walks from every cell give a new notebook. Every value is negative: the start is worth minus 0.03, the cell left of the cat minus 0.53. Why? A random walker usually meets the cat first: from the start, 77 walks in 100 end there, about three in four. The cat can be entered from four cells, the cheese from only two. And long walks shrink any reward to almost nothing.

values:12.t: Values belong to a policy. Same maze, same cell, two numbers: the start is worth 0.40 under the arrows and minus 0.03 under the Wanderer. A value only means something for a given policy, so we may write V with a small pi (pi). Here the arrows win in every single cell, so they are the better policy wherever Pip starts. If each policy won in some cells, neither would be better everywhere: the answer would depend on where Pip starts.

values:13.t: How good is a move?. The notebook says how good a cell is. To choose a move, Pip wants to know how good each move is. The action value, written Q of s, a, said “Q of s and a”, is the average return when Pip takes move a first, then follows the policy as usual. It is measured the same way: many walks, each forced to start with that move.

values:14.t: The four moves beside the cheese. Right pays plus 1 at once: Q equals 1. Down is the cat: minus 1. Left gives 0.69, and up bumps the wall and wastes a step: 0.80. The best move has the biggest Q. The value mixes these with the policy’s chances, pi(a given s): the arrow 85 times in 100, 80 by habit and 5 by chance, each other move 5 times. 0.85 times 1 plus 0.05 times (0.80 minus 1 plus 0.69) equals 0.87, the notebook value.

values:15.t: Why values are worth having. V answers “how good is it to be here?”: compare cells, and policies cell by cell. Q answers “how good is this move?”: the biggest Q is the best next move if Pip follows the policy afterwards. And if a move has a bigger Q than the policy’s habit, switching to it can only help: on every visit to that cell Pip now does better, and those gains add up. Much of R L builds on this.

values:16.t: The catch. Measuring by walking is slow. This notebook took 16,000 walks and 76,481 steps. The Wanderer’s took 601,861 steps. And every number is still a little noisy. Yet neighbouring numbers are clearly linked: 0.87 beside the cheese, 0.76 one step back, a little less than 0.9 times as much. The next reel turns that link into a shortcut, the Bellman equation.

values:17.t: Your turn. Drag the slider to change how often Pip moves at random; the notebook is remeasured with 1000 walks per cell. With no randomness every walk from a cell is identical, so one walk gives the value. At “always”, Pip is the Wanderer. Tap a cell to send Pip on one walk from there and compare its return with the notebook.

values:18.t: Where values show up. AlphaGo, in 2016, had a value network: shown a Go position, it estimated the expected result of the game for the player to move, with plus 1 for a win and minus 1 for a loss. Chess programs score positions in a similar spirit. And many modern learners, including those used to fine-tune chatbots, train a value estimate called a critic to judge how well things are going.

values:19.t: Recap. A cell’s value is the expected discounted return when Pip starts there and follows its policy: the average over many walks. Change the policy and the values change. Q scores a move: take it first, then follow the policy. Pick the move with the biggest Q.

bellman:0.t: The Bellman Equation. Value of here equals reward now plus discounted value of next.

bellman:1.t: A shortcut?. Here is Pip’s notebook from the last reel: for each cell, the average return of 1000 walks that start there and follow policy A with one move in five random, on the dry floor. Measuring it took 76,481 steps of walking. Neighbouring numbers look related. If the value of a cell could be worked out from its neighbours, Pip could skip most of that walking.

bellman:2.t: Split a walk in two. Take one walk from the start: cheese on step 7, return 0.53. Now cut it after the first step. The rest is a walk of its own, starting from the cell above, with return 0.9 multiplied 5 times: 0.59. Seen from the start, everything after step 1 counts 0.9 times less, the rule from the discount reel. So: return equals first reward plus 0.9 times return of the rest equals 0 plus 0.9 times 0.59 equals 0.53.

bellman:3.t: Average both sides. The split holds for every walk, so it holds on average. The rest is a fresh walk from the landing cell: Pip’s rule looks only at the cell, and how Pip got there does not matter (the Markov property). Check: 876 walks went up first (about 850 expected; chance). Their rests averaged 0.45, close to that cell’s value, 0.46. So value here equals average of [ reward plus 0.9 times value where Pip lands ]: the Bellman equation.

bellman:4.t: What exactly is averaged?. Two kinds of chance, as in the policy reel. Pip’s own: which move it picks, pi(a given s): 0.85 for the arrow, 0.05 for each other move. The floor’s: where the move lands, P(s prime given s, a). On today’s dry floor each move lands in one known cell. On the mdp reel’s wet floor, a move lands ahead 8 times in 10 and to each side once in 10, and the rule averages over that too.

bellman:5.t: Where can Pip land?. Take the cell beside the cheese. The arrow says right: that move happens 85 times in 100, 80 by habit and 5 by chance. Each other move happens 5 times in 100. Right lands on the cheese: plus 1, and the walk ends, so the next value is 0. Down lands on the cat: minus 1, also 0 after. Up bumps the wall: Pip stays, reward 0. Left leads to the next cell back, reward 0.

bellman:6.t: Check it with real numbers. For each move: its reward plus 0.9 times the notebook value where it lands. On a dry floor that is exactly the move’s Q. Up stays here, worth 0.87; left lands on 0.76. The last reel measured up and left by forced walks as 0.80 and 0.69: the same two Q values, both estimates carry a little noise. Weighted by how often each move happens: 0.87. The notebook says 0.87. To two decimals, the rule holds.

bellman:7.t: Another cell. The start: up happens 85 times in 100 and lands on 0.46. Right lands on 0.45. Down and left both bump, so Pip stays on 0.40. Every reward here is 0, so the rule is just 0.9 times the average landing value. The rule gives 0.41, the walks gave 0.40. Close, but not equal: even 1000 walks leave a little noise. The true values obey the rule exactly, and soon we compute them.

bellman:8.t: A recipe with no walking. Turn the rule around and use it to compute values. Start with a blank notebook: every number 0. Then apply the rule to every cell, using the current numbers for the landing cells, and write the results into a fresh notebook. One pass over all cells is a sweep. Repeat until the numbers stop changing; we will see why they do. Pip never takes a step.

bellman:9.t: Sweep 1. From all zeros, only cells next to the cheese or the cat change. Beside the cheese: 0.85 times 1 for the cheese, 0.05 times minus 1 for the cat, the rest are 0: 0.80. The cell below the cheese gets the same, 0.80. The two other cells beside the cat get minus 0.05: a 5 in 100 chance of stepping onto it. Everything else stays 0.

bellman:10.t: The news spreads. Each sweep, the good news moves one cell further from the cheese. After 3 sweeps, each number counts exactly the discounted rewards Pip can expect in its first 3 steps; after 7 sweeps, in its first 7. That is why the start stays at about 0 until sweep 7: the cheese is 7 steps away. Then it jumps, and keeps creeping up as walks that need more than 7 steps add their smaller rewards.

bellman:11.t: Until nothing changes. This chart shows the start cell’s number after each sweep: across is the sweep number, up is the value. The dashed line is where it settles. By sweep 13 every number in the notebook has its final two decimals; by sweep 16 no number moves by more than 0.001. Why does it settle? The rule multiplies every landing value by 0.9, so each sweep keeps at most 0.9 times the old numbers’ biggest error. Here it shrinks even faster.

bellman:12.t: Walks versus sweeps. Left: 1000 walks per cell. Right: 16 sweeps. They agree to within 0.014, and the sweeps have no noise. From here on, the notebook shows the swept values. The walks took 76,481 steps. The sweeps did 16 passes over 16 cells with 4 moves each: 1,024 small sums, each about as cheap as one step. On a wet floor, with three landings per move, the sums would triple.

bellman:13.t: The catch. Sweeps need the rules of the maze: for every move in every cell, where Pip can land, how likely each landing is, and what it pays. That description is called a model: here it means the world’s rulebook, not a neural network. The walks needed none of it. Often nobody hands you a model. Later reels keep the Bellman rule but replace the known probabilities with real experience, one step at a time: that is T D learning.

bellman:14.t: The best Pip could do. What is the best any policy could do? Pip would pick the best move in every cell, and keep picking the best afterwards. So: value here equals the biggest, over moves, of reward plus 0.9 times value where that move lands. That is the Bellman optimality equation. Its solution, V star, is the value of the best policy: no policy beats it in any cell. Sweeping it settles after 7 sweeps.

bellman:15.t: Reading the best map. In each cell, the best move has the biggest reward plus 0.9 times V star where it lands: the biggest Q. Those arrows lead straight to the cheese. Where two moves score the same, like the cell between the rocks, either is best. The best policy needs no random moves: the start is worth 0.53, against 0.40 for Pip’s habit. On the wet floor, each move’s score would first average over where it lands, then the max picks the best.

bellman:16.t: Your turn. Drag the slider to run more sweeps of Pip’s policy, starting from all zeros, and watch the news spread from the cheese and the cat. Tap any cell to see the rule at work there: its four moves, how likely each is, and the numbers from the sweep before.

bellman:17.t: Where it shows up. Richard Bellman described this idea in the 1950s as dynamic programming: link each state to the states one step later. Sweeping the rule is how planners solve problems with a known model. Without a model, T D learning nudges its numbers toward reward plus gamma times value of the next state. Q-learning and the Atari-playing D Q N of 2015 aim at reward plus gamma times the biggest Q in the next cell, the value of the best next move.

bellman:18.t: Recap. A walk’s return is its first reward plus gamma times the return of the rest. Averaging gives the Bellman equation: value here equals expected reward for the next step plus gamma times expected value of where you land. Sweep it over every cell until nothing changes and you get the values without walking, if you know the model. Put a max over moves inside, and you get the best possible values.

explore:0.t: Exploration versus Exploitation. Order your favourite dish, or try something new?

explore:1.t: Tonight’s dinner. Meet Pip, a mouse with a favourite café: The Usual. The food there is always good. Last week a New Place opened down the road. It might be wonderful. It might be awful. Pip can only eat in one place tonight. Which one?

explore:2.t: Two ways to choose. Going back to The Usual is exploiting: using what you already know works. Trying the New Place is exploring: taking a choice you know less about, to learn something. Exploring might cost Pip a good dinner tonight. It might also find a better café for every night after.

explore:3.t: It depends on what’s ahead. If Pip leaves town tomorrow, tonight is the last dinner. A great discovery would have no later dinners to improve, so The Usual is the safe bet. If Pip just moved here, a great find pays off for hundreds of dinners. Exploring is an investment: you pay now, and the reward comes later, from better choices.

explore:4.t: The cheese arcade. To study this, Pip visits an arcade with four cheese machines, A, B, C and D. Each pull of a lever either drops one cheese crumb, worth 1, or nothing, worth 0. Each machine has its own hidden chance of dropping a crumb. Pip gets 1000 pulls tonight and wants as many crumbs as possible. Unlike the maze, nothing moves: after every pull the same four machines wait.

explore:5.t: A peek at the secret. We will peek inside the machines, so we can judge Pip’s choices. Pip cannot see this. A drops a crumb 30 percent of the time, B 55 percent, C 70 percent, and D only 15 percent. So C is the best machine. Pip has to find that out by pulling.

explore:6.t: Pip the exploiter. First Pip tries each machine once. A drops a crumb. B, C and D drop nothing. Then Pip follows a simple rule: always pull the machine that has paid best so far. That is A, with 1 crumb in 1 pull. This rule is called greedy.

explore:7.t: Stuck. After 1000 pulls, Pip pulled A 997 times and collected 308 crumbs. It never went back to C. Why? B, C and D still show 0 crumbs from their single try, and A’s average never drops to 0. One unlucky pull of C, the best machine, decided the whole evening.

explore:8.t: Pip the explorer. Same visit, same luck: each machine drops its crumbs in the same order as before, so C’s first pull is a miss again. This time Pip always explores: every pull goes to a machine picked at random. Pip learns a lot: its averages end close to the secret chances. But it collects only 398 crumbs, because three pulls in four go to machines worse than C.

explore:9.t: Each pull has a hidden cost. To compare the two, imagine someone who knew the secrets. They would pull C every time and expect 70 crumbs per 100 pulls. Every pull of another machine gives up some of that. A pull of B gives up 0.70 minus 0.55, which is 0.15 of a crumb. A gives up 0.40, D gives up 0.55, and C gives up nothing.

explore:10.t: Regret. Add up those costs over the evening and you get Pip’s regret: the price of not knowing. The exploiter’s regret is 399.5. The explorer’s is 279.3. Regret counts chances, not luck: a pull of A costs 0.40 whether or not this pull happened to drop a crumb. So regret measures the choices, not the dice.

explore:11.t: One visit is not enough. That was one visit. With different luck, the exploiter might have found C. So let’s run 2000 visits of 1000 pulls each and average. Here is the chart. Left to right: pulls during the evening. Upward: total regret so far, averaged over all visits. Lower is better. A line that goes flat has stopped losing.

explore:12.t: Explore always, or never?. Gold, always explore: straight and steep, ending at 275. Red, always exploit: only 78. A twist: in the one visit we watched, the exploiter lost more than the explorer. That was its bad luck. On average it does far better. But red never goes flat. In 1299 of the 2000 visits, greedy settled on C, meaning C was the machine it pulled most. In the other 701, it stuck to B, A or D and kept losing.

explore:13.t: A little of both. Now a mixed Pip: one pull in ten goes to a random machine, any of the four, the rest to the best so far. Its teal line ends at 42, lower than both. The random pulls rescue it from an unlucky start: C gets more tries, and its true quality shows. Yet it keeps paying for random pulls forever. How much to explore, and smarter ways to do it, come in the next reels.

explore:14.t: Your turn. Tap a machine to pull its lever. You get 20 pulls. Pull the ones you believe in, but don’t forget the ones you haven’t tested enough. After your last pull, the secret chances and your regret appear. Tap again to start over.

explore:15.t: Where you meet this. A music app plays songs you love, but also slips in new ones to learn your taste. A website shows its usual page to most visitors and a new design to some, to see which works better. Some medical trials also adapt as results come in, sending more patients to the treatment that is doing better. Each is the arcade in disguise.

explore:16.t: Recap. Exploit what you know, or explore to learn more: every choice under uncertainty faces this. Never exploring can lock you onto a worse option after one unlucky try. Always exploring wastes most of your pulls. Regret measures the price of not knowing. The next reels show smarter ways to keep it small.

bandits:0.t: Multi-Armed Bandits. R L with one room and a row of slot machines.

bandits:1.t: One-armed bandits. Old slot machines had a single lever, an arm, and they slowly took your money. People called them one-armed bandits. Pip’s cheese arcade has four machines, so it is a multi-armed bandit: a row of options, each paying out by its own hidden rule. It is the simplest puzzle in reinforcement learning, and one of the most useful.

bandits:2.t: The pieces. Each machine is an arm. Each turn Pip pulls one arm: that is its action. The reward is a crumb, worth 1, or nothing, worth 0. Each arm has its own reward distribution, the hidden rule for what it pays. Here the rule is simple: a crumb with some fixed chance. So an arm’s true average reward per pull equals that chance. Pip never sees it.

bandits:3.t: No map to plan over. In Pip’s maze, every move changed where Pip stood, and the next choice depended on it. In the arcade nothing changes: after any pull, the same four machines wait, with the same chances. There is no situation, or state, to keep track of. One visit of 1000 pulls plays the part of an episode, and its return is simply the total crumbs, with no discounting. The only question, every turn, is which arm to pull.

bandits:4.t: Estimate by averaging. Pip can’t see B’s chance, but it can estimate it. Pip pulls B five times: crumb, nothing, crumb, nothing, crumb. Its estimate of B is the average reward so far: 3 crumbs in 5 pulls, so 0.6. The true chance is 0.55. Close, but five pulls can’t pin it down exactly.

bandits:5.t: Update as you go. Pip doesn’t need to keep a list of every reward. After each pull of a machine it updates one number: new estimate equals old plus (reward minus old) divided by n, where n counts the pulls of that machine so far. Here are B’s five pulls again. Each line gives exactly the average so far. Why? The new average is (old times (n minus 1) plus reward) divided by n, which rearranges to the same rule.

bandits:6.t: Why divide by n?. The bracket, reward minus old estimate, is the surprise: how far this pull landed from what Pip expected. Dividing by n decides how far to move. The first pull moves the estimate all the way, the tenth a tenth of the way. Every pull ends up counting equally, which suits machines that never change. T D learning uses the same shape with a fixed step instead, because what it averages keeps changing as Pip learns.

bandits:7.t: The greedy player. Now a full visit of 1000 pulls. We picked visit 94 from our numbered, seeded visits. Pip plays greedy: it pulls each machine once, then always the arm with the highest estimate, ties broken at random. Under the machines: crumbs out of pulls so far. The bars are Pip’s estimates, and the yellow box marks the current favourite. After four pulls, B and C each show 1 crumb in 1 pull: a tie.

bandits:8.t: A lucky start for B, an unlucky one for C. Pull 5 goes to B, by the coin flip: nothing, so B drops to 0.5. Pull 6, C: nothing, 0.5. Another tie; pull 7 goes to C: nothing again, 0.33. Now B leads, so pull 8 goes to B: a crumb, 0.67. B’s average never dips below C’s 0.33 again, so C is never pulled again. Two misses in a row hit a 70 percent machine about one time in eleven.

bandits:9.t: Frozen. After 1000 pulls, B got 995 pulls and its estimate settled at 0.54, near its true 0.55. C’s is still 0.33, from three pulls long ago, though its true chance is 0.70. The chart follows both estimates through the visit: solid lines are Pip’s estimates, dashed lines the true chances. B’s line wanders and settles. C’s line never moves again.

bandits:10.t: Why greedy can’t recover. An estimate only changes when its arm is pulled. If an estimate is too high, greedy keeps pulling that arm, and the extra pulls bring it back down. Self-correcting. If an estimate is too low, greedy stops pulling the arm, so the mistake is never corrected. Here A, C and D are all stuck below their true chances. Greedy fixes over-optimism, never pessimism. Over 2000 visits it froze like this in 701, as the explore reel showed.

bandits:11.t: Your turn. A simple fix: try every machine several times before going greedy. Drag to choose how many tries. Too few, and an unlucky start still freezes a good machine out. Too many, and Pip wastes pulls on A and D. The best number depends on the visit length and on how close the machines are, which Pip doesn’t know in advance.

bandits:12.t: Where bandits live. The first paper on this problem, by William Thompson in 1933, asked how to choose between two medical treatments. Herbert Robbins framed the general problem in 1952. Today bandit methods choose which headline, ad or page design to show each visitor. Each click is a reward, and each option is an arm.

bandits:13.t: Recap. A multi-armed bandit: several arms, each with an unknown reward distribution, and no states. Pull one arm per turn, collect as much as you can. Estimate each arm by its average, updated as you go. Pure greedy can freeze out a good arm after an unlucky start, because low estimates never get re-checked. The next reels show smarter ways to explore.

epsgreedy:0.t: epsilon-Greedy. Mostly do the best thing, occasionally roll the dice.

epsgreedy:1.t: Greedy needs a nudge. At the cheese arcade, four machines each drop a crumb with a hidden chance, shown here but not to Pip. Greedy Pip tries each once, then always pulls the best average so far. Visit 266 is not the explore reel’s visit, but it starts just as badly: A paid first, the others didn’t, so greedy pulled A 997 times out of 1000. Its regret, the crumbs it expected to lose against always pulling C, is 399.5.

epsgreedy:2.t: Spin before you pull. The fix is almost silly. Before each pull, Pip spins a little wheel. A small slice says random: pull any machine, chosen at random. The rest says best so far: pull the greedy choice. The size of the random slice is called epsilon, the Greek letter epsilon. This rule is epsilon-greedy.

epsgreedy:3.t: What epsilon equals 0.1 means. With epsilon equals 0.1, nine pulls in ten go to the favourite. One in ten is random. A random pull can land on the favourite too, one time in four. So the favourite gets 92.5 percent of the pulls, and each other machine gets 2.5 percent. Every machine keeps getting a few pulls, however bad it looks. If you saw the policy reel, this is its epsilon-random rule.

epsgreedy:4.t: Visit 266 again. Same visit, same crumbs in every machine, but now Pip spins first. The first four pulls try each machine once, as before: A pays, B, C and D don’t. Then the wheel mostly says best so far, and best so far is A. The top corner shows each spin.

epsgreedy:5.t: Random pulls. Pull 15: the wheel says random, and the random pick happens to be A itself. Pull 19: random again, B, nothing. Pull 25: random, B, a crumb. Between them, the greedy pulls keep going to A. Its average sits near 0.3. C and D still show 0 from their single tries.

epsgreedy:6.t: Pull 32. Pull 32: random, and this time it picks C. A crumb! C now shows 1 crumb in 2 pulls, an average of 0.5. That beats A’s 0.28. So from now on, best so far means C. C pays 6 of its next 8 pulls, and its average climbs. One lucky spin undid one unlucky first try.

epsgreedy:7.t: After 1000 pulls. C got 901 of the 1000 pulls, and its average settled at 0.71, close to the true 0.70. Regret for the visit: 33.9, against 399.5 for greedy. Every estimate keeps getting fresh pulls, so a wrong first impression can always be corrected. That is the whole point of epsilon.

epsgreedy:8.t: 2000 visits. The chart: total regret so far, across 1000 pulls, averaged over 2000 visits. Lower is better. Greedy, in red, ends at 77.6. epsilon-greedy with epsilon equals 0.1, in teal, ends at 42.1. Of the 701 visits where greedy got stuck on a worse machine, epsilon-greedy ended up on C in 598. In the other 103 it was still behind on B. It lost only 5 of the visits greedy got right.

epsgreedy:9.t: The price: exploring forever. Look at the teal line near the end. It never goes flat. Even after Pip is sure C is best, one pull in ten is still random, and three in four of those go to worse machines. Over the last 500 pulls, the teal line still rises by about 0.032 per pull. Greedy’s lucky visits pay nothing at all once C is found, but its unlucky ones pay forever.

epsgreedy:10.t: Exploring blindly. The random pulls ignore everything Pip has learned. In visit 266 the wheel said random 94 times. D, the worst machine, got 16 of those pulls, A got 25, and B, the close runner-up, got 31. The wheel splits them evenly on average, about 23 each, whatever Pip believes; the spread is luck. A smarter explorer would check where it is still unsure, or where a machine might be best. The next reels, U C B and Thompson sampling, do that.

epsgreedy:11.t: Your turn. Drag epsilon to change the size of the random slice. Each line is one epsilon, labelled at its end, averaged over 2000 visits. At 0 Pip is plain greedy and sometimes freezes. Too much epsilon wastes pull after pull on bad machines. In this arcade the lowest line is epsilon equals 0.05, at 36.6, a little better than 0.1.

epsgreedy:12.t: Explore less as you learn. Early on, exploring is cheap and useful. Later it mostly wastes pulls. So let epsilon shrink. Here epsilon equals 10 divided by the pulls so far, capped at 1: random for about the first ten pulls, 1 in 10 after 100, about 1 in 100 by the end. Average regret: 26.6, below 42.1 for a fixed epsilon of 0.1, and about as good as the best try-first number in the bandits reel.

epsgreedy:13.t: But not too fast. Shrink epsilon too quickly and Pip is back to greedy. With epsilon equals 1 divided by the pulls so far, epsilon is already a quarter right after the four first tries, and a whole visit averages only 5.6 random pulls. Average regret: 48.3, and C got over half the pulls in only 75 percent of visits. So epsilon-greedy hands you a knob, or a schedule, to tune. With machines closer in quality, or a longer visit, a different setting would win.

epsgreedy:14.t: Where you’ll see it. epsilon-greedy is everywhere because it is one line of code. Pip already used it in the T D learning reel: one move in five was random, so epsilon was 0.2. DeepMind’s Atari player D Q N, published in 2015, started with epsilon equals 1, fully random, lowered it to 0.1 over its first million frames of play, and kept it there, so it never stopped trying new moves.

epsgreedy:15.t: Recap. epsilon-greedy: with chance epsilon pull a random arm, otherwise the arm with the best average. Every arm keeps being re-checked, so an unlucky start can be undone. It is simple and often good enough. But it explores blindly, spending as many random pulls on hopeless arms as on promising ones, and epsilon has to be tuned. Shrinking epsilon over time helps.

ucb:0.t: Upper Confidence Bound. Be optimistic about what you haven’t tried much.

ucb:1.t: Back at the arcade. Pip is back at the cheese arcade: four machines, A to D. Each pull drops one crumb or nothing, and each machine has its own hidden chance of a crumb. Pip keeps an estimate for each machine: crumbs divided by pulls. Greedy can get stuck. epsilon-greedy unsticks it with random pulls. This reel shows a smarter way to explore.

ucb:2.t: Random pulls are blind. With epsilon equals 0.1, every tenth pull goes to a machine picked at random, even one Pip already knows is bad. Over 1000 pulls, averaged over 2000 visits, D gets 27 pulls, and almost all of them are dice rolls. The dice never stop. Pip pays for them on pull 10 and on pull 10,000 alike. Fair warning: in the first 1000 pulls, U C B will check D just as often. The difference is what happens after that.

ucb:3.t: Two kinds of “looks bad”. Picture two machines. One gave nothing in its only pull. The other gave 6 crumbs in 40 pulls. Both look poor. But one pull says almost nothing: that machine might still be great. Forty pulls say a lot. A smart explorer should spend its tries where it is unsure, not spread them evenly.

ucb:4.t: How much does an average wobble?. Take machine B, true chance 55 percent, and 30 different visits. Each dot is the average of B’s first 3 pulls in one visit. With 3 pulls only four averages are possible, and the dots use all of them, from 0 to 1. Now the average of the first 30 pulls: from 0.37 to 0.8. More pulls, less wobble. Roughly, 4 times the pulls halves the wobble.

ucb:5.t: The benefit of the doubt. U C B gives each machine a hopeful score: its estimate plus a bonus. The bonus is big when Pip has pulled the machine only a few times and small when it knows the machine well. Then Pip pulls the machine with the highest score. A machine can win because it is good, or because Pip barely knows it. This is optimism in the face of uncertainty.

ucb:6.t: Upper Confidence Bound. Think of the bonus as stretching each estimate up to the top of the range the true chance could plausibly reach. Few pulls, wide range, tall cap. That top is called an upper confidence bound, which gives U C B its name. If a machine is truly worse than C, pulling it shrinks its cap until its top drops below C’s top. After that, Pip checks it only rarely.

ucb:7.t: The bonus, in words. U C B uses bonus equals c times square root of (2 times log t divided by n). c is a bonus scale; the classic version, UCB1, sets c equals 1. n is how often this machine was pulled: 4 times the pulls, half the bonus, just like the wobble. t is the total pulls so far. Its natural logarithm, log t, grows forever but slowly: 4.6 at 100 pulls, 6.9 at 1000. So an ignored machine’s bonus creeps up: it always gets another look, but rarely.

ucb:8.t: Pull 5: the first scores. We follow one visit, number 24. As before, Pip first pulls each machine once. A, C and D give nothing; B gives a crumb. Now t equals 4 and every n equals 1, so every bonus is the same: 1.67. Scores: A 1.67, B 2.67, C 1.67, D 1.67. B wins. A score above 1 is fine: it is a hopeful score, not a chance.

ucb:9.t: C gets a second look. Pulls 5 to 8 go to B twice, then A, then D. On pull 9, C has still been pulled only once, so its bonus is the biggest. Scores: A 1.94, B 1.84, C 2.04, D 1.44. Pip pulls C... and gets nothing again: 0 of 2. Plain greedy, in this same visit 24 with the same dice, never went back to C. It pulled B 997 times out of 1000.

ucb:10.t: Patience pays. C now has 0 crumbs from 2 pulls. But every pull of another machine raises t, so C’s bonus slowly grows. On pull 20 its score is on top again (1.72). This time the crumbs come. By pull 40, C has 10 of 14. The gold caps shrink as machines are pulled, and C’s bar rises toward its true 70 percent.

ucb:11.t: Where the checks go. After 1000 pulls in this visit: A 58, B 242, C 671, D 29 pulls. Look at the scores: all four tops sit at about the same height, 0.83. U C B always pulls the highest top, which pushes the tops level. D’s estimate is far below C’s, so it can keep a tall cap: few pulls. B is close to C, so its cap must be thin: many pulls. Promising machines get checked more, hopeless ones less.

ucb:12.t: Keeping score. Is U C B better than epsilon-greedy? Recall regret: every pull of C adds 0, B adds 0.15, A 0.40 and D 0.55, the crumbs given up compared with always pulling C. The chart: left to right, pulls; upward, total regret so far, averaged over 2000 visits. First, epsilon-greedy with epsilon equals 0.1, the teal line: 42 after 1000 pulls.

ucb:13.t: A surprise. Now UCB1, in gold. After 1000 pulls its regret is 61: worse than epsilon-greedy! Its early bonuses are big, so it checks B a lot: 169 pulls on average, against 104 for epsilon-greedy. Both lines are still climbing. But epsilon-greedy can never stop paying: one pull in ten is a dice roll, forever. U C B’s checks get rarer as its caps shrink, so its climb keeps slowing.

ucb:14.t: The long game. So play longer: 10,000 pulls, averaged over 500 visits. UCB1 overtakes epsilon-greedy at about pull 2,800 and finishes far lower: 141 against 294. From pull 5000 to 10,000, epsilon-greedy’s regret grows by 138, UCB1’s by only 26. The card shows why: after pull 1000, epsilon-greedy pulls the hopeless D about 225 more times, UCB1 only about 23.

ucb:15.t: A fair comparison. The earlier reels found strong rules for this arcade too. Shrinking epsilon, with epsilon equals 10 divided by t, ended 1000 pulls at 27; trying each machine 10 times first, at 25. Both beat UCB1’s 61. Even at 10,000 pulls, shrinking epsilon wins: 80 against 141. So what does U C B buy? No schedule to pick: the 10s in those rules were chosen for this arcade. A proven guarantee for any arcade. And a tuned bonus, c equals 0.25, beats them all.

ucb:16.t: Your turn. Drag c, the bonus scale, to replay the 2000 visits. At c equals 0 there is no bonus: U C B becomes plain greedy, and in 701 of the 2000 visits it settles on the wrong machine. Too big, and Pip keeps re-checking machines it already knows. Here c equals 0.25 does best, ending at 14. But that value is tuned to this one arcade; with c equals 0.1, C gets under half the pulls in 533 visits.

ucb:17.t: The fine print. UCB1’s guarantee: in any arcade with rewards between 0 and 1, regret grows at most like the logarithm of the pulls, so each doubling adds about the same amount. Here: 25 from pull 2500 to 5000, 26 from 5000 to 10,000. The proof relies on the bonus being at least this big. It also assumes the chances never change. If C, pulled hundreds of times, suddenly got worse, its thin cap would make Pip slow to notice.

ucb:18.t: Where it is used. The optimism idea goes back to Lai and Robbins in 1985. The simple UCB1 rule and its guarantee were published by Auer, Cesa-Bianchi and Fischer in 2002. A game program tries out moves in its head before playing: each candidate move is like an arm. In 2006, Kocsis and Szepesvári used the U C B score at every such choice, an algorithm called UCT. It powered strong Go programs, and AlphaGo’s search used a related rule to choose which moves to explore.

ucb:19.t: Recap. U C B scores each machine as its estimate plus a bonus for uncertainty, and pulls the top score. The bonus shrinks as a machine is pulled and creeps up while it is ignored. So U C B spends its checks on machines that could still turn out best, and its regret keeps flattening while epsilon-greedy’s grows at a steady rate.

thompson:0.t: Thompson Sampling. Act on a random guess drawn from your beliefs.

thompson:1.t: Pip’s hunch. Back at the cheese arcade: machines A to D, each dropping a crumb or nothing, each with a hidden chance. Pip could keep one estimate per machine. But “1 crumb from 1 pull” and “50 crumbs from 100 pulls” are very different evidence, even though the first estimate looks better. This reel tracks that difference with a belief, and lets the belief do the exploring.

thompson:2.t: A curve of hunches. Here is how Pip pictures one machine, B, before pulling it. Left to right: every chance of a crumb the machine could have, from 0 to 1. Height: how plausible Pip finds that chance. Pip knows nothing yet, so every chance is equally plausible: a flat line. The tallest point always marks the most plausible chance.

thompson:3.t: One crumb. B’s first pull drops a crumb. Which chances fit that? Chance 0.9 would drop a crumb 9 times in 10, chance 0.1 only once. So after one crumb, 0.9 is nine times as plausible as 0.1, and chance 0 is ruled out. Height at each chance equals how likely that chance makes what Pip saw. The flat line tilts into a ramp.

thompson:4.t: Then nothing. The second pull drops nothing. Now a chance of 1 is ruled out too: such a machine never fails. Multiply the old heights by how likely each chance makes “nothing”, and the ramp bends into a hill around 0.5. Then rescale, so the tallest point is full height again. This way of updating a belief with evidence is called Bayes’ rule.

thompson:5.t: More pulls, narrower hill. Keep pulling B. After 10 pulls with 5 crumbs, the hill narrows around 0.5. After 100 pulls with 54 crumbs, it is a thin spike near 0.54, close to B’s true 0.55. This family of curves has a name: the Beta distribution. With w crumbs and l nothings, Pip’s belief is Beta(1 plus w, 1 plus l). Its peak sits at the estimate, crumbs divided by pulls; its width shows how unsure Pip is.

thompson:6.t: The rule: one draw each. Thompson sampling uses the curves like this. Every turn, Pip draws one random chance from each machine’s curve: draws land more often where the curve is tall. Then it pulls the machine whose draw came out highest, and updates that one curve. At the start all four curves are flat, so the four draws are just random numbers.

thompson:7.t: The first pulls. We follow one visit. Pull 1: A’s draw, 0.86, is highest. A drops nothing, so its curve tilts toward low chances. Pull 2: A’s draw is now just 0.09, and C wins with 0.30. Nothing again. Watch the draws on each pull: one dot per machine, and the highest one decides. B’s draws happen not to win at first, so it stays untried for a while.

thompson:8.t: B gets lucky. B drops crumbs on 8 of its first 9 pulls. Its hill moves high, so its draws usually win, and Pip pulls B again and again. C, meanwhile, has 0 crumbs from 2 pulls. Its curve leans low but is still wide: by its curve, the chance that C is better than 0.5 is still 1 in 8. That width keeps C in the game.

thompson:9.t: C’s comeback. On pull 22, C’s wide curve throws a lucky draw, 0.66, just above B’s 0.65. C drops a crumb. More chances follow: by pull 60, C has 5 crumbs from 7 pulls, and its hill has caught up with B’s. Nobody told Pip to explore. The width of C’s curve did it.

thompson:10.t: Picked as often as it might be best. Back at pull 40: how often would each machine win the draw? In 4000 draws from these curves, B wins 83 percent, C 8 percent, D 8 percent, A 1 percent. That is Thompson sampling’s secret: it pulls each machine as often as Pip believes it could be the best one. A machine loses its share only as Pip grows sure it is worse: D, at 1 crumb of 3, is still unsure, so it still wins 8 percent.

thompson:11.t: Narrowing down. Fast-forward to pull 1000 in this visit. C’s curve has become a spike near 0.70, from 872 pulls. A and D were pulled only 6 and 7 times, so their curves stay wide. That is fine: Pip never needs to know exactly how bad D is, only that it is very unlikely to beat C.

thompson:12.t: Keeping score. Compare with the others by regret: each pull gives up 0.70 minus the chance of the machine pulled. The chart shows total regret over 1000 pulls, averaged over 2000 visits; lower is better. epsilon-greedy with epsilon equals 0.1 ends at 42, UCB1 at 61, Thompson sampling, in purple, at 18. It also beats shrinking epsilon from the epsilon-greedy reel (27). Only U C B with a bonus tuned for this arcade, c equals 0.25, does slightly better: 14.

thompson:13.t: Your turn. Pull the machines yourself: tap a machine to pull it once, and watch its curve change. Or tap the button to let Thompson sampling choose: you will see its four draws first. Try pulling one machine many times, and see how thin its curve gets.

thompson:14.t: The fine print. Thompson sampling needs a starting belief. Here it was flat: every chance equally plausible. A strong wrong start can slow it down. The neat Beta curves fit crumb-or-nothing rewards. Other rewards need other belief shapes, often only approximate. And it is random. That helps when many choices are made before results come back: a rule without dice, like U C B, would send every waiting visitor to the same machine, while Thompson’s draws spread them out.

thompson:15.t: Where it is used. William Thompson proposed the idea in 1933, to choose between two medical treatments. It was then largely forgotten. Around 2010 it came back: engineers at Microsoft used a version for ad placement in Bing, and Chapelle and Li at Yahoo found in 2011 that it worked very well for ads and news recommendations. Proofs followed in 2012 that its regret, like UCB1’s, grows only like the logarithm of the pulls. Today it is a common choice for website tests.

thompson:16.t: Recap. Keep a belief curve for each machine: how plausible each chance is, given the crumbs so far. Every turn, draw one chance from each curve and pull the highest. Wide curves sometimes draw high, so unsure machines get explored; narrow low curves almost never win, so bad machines get dropped. No epsilon schedule or bonus to tune, only a starting belief.

valueiter:0.t: Value Iteration. Know the rules? Spread value outward from the goal, step by step.

valueiter:1.t: Planning at a desk. Pip’s maze again. Stepping onto the cheese pays plus 1, onto the cat minus 1, and either one ends the walk. Other steps pay 0, a bump into a wall or rock leaves Pip in place, and gamma (gamma) is 0.9. This time we hold the maze’s rulebook, its model: for every cell and move, where Pip lands and what the step pays. With it we can plan at a desk, while Pip waits.

valueiter:2.t: The best-move rule. In the Bellman reel we swept the rule for Pip’s distracted habit until the numbers settled. At the end we swapped the average over moves for the best move, giving the best possible values, V star (V star): value here equals the best, over the four moves, of reward plus 0.9 times value where that move lands. Sweeping that rule over every cell, from all zeros, is value iteration. Let us watch the best arrows appear.

valueiter:3.t: One cell, four scores. Take the cell beside the cheese in sweep 1, while every number is still 0. Right lands on the cheese: plus 1, and the walk ends, so nothing is added. Up bumps the wall: 0 plus 0.9 times 0. Down is the cat: minus 1. Left: 0 plus 0.9 times 0. The best score is 1. So the cell’s new number is 1, and its arrow points right, at the move that won.

valueiter:4.t: Sweep 1. Do that for all 16 cells, each using the numbers from before the sweep. Only the two cells beside the cheese reach 1. Next to the cat, the best score is 0: simply do not step on it. Where three or four moves tie for best, there is no arrow yet, only a question mark. After one sweep, most cells are like that: every move still scores 0.

valueiter:5.t: The news spreads. Each sweep, the good news moves one cell further: 0.90 two steps from the cheese, 0.81 three steps away, and so on. A cell gets its arrow as soon as one move beats the others. At sweep 7 the news reaches the start: 0.53. Where two routes are equally short, two moves tie for best and both arrows stay, as at the start.

valueiter:6.t: When to stop. Sweep 8 changes nothing, so we stop: these are V star. On a dry floor a number is final the moment it appears: three steps from the cheese, 0.9 times 0.9 equals 0.81, and no longer route can beat that. The arrows form a policy: in each cell, take the best-scoring move. It is the best policy. Following it, Pip reaches the cheese in 7 steps. Work: 8 times 16 cells times 4 moves equals 512 scores.

valueiter:7.t: A wet floor. Now someone mops the floor, as in the M D P reel. When Pip tries a move, it goes that way 8 times in 10. It slides sideways 1 time in 10 to each side, and never backwards. A slide into a wall or rock means staying put. Rewards and gamma stay the same, so every change in the numbers comes from the slipping alone. The rulebook now lists, for each move, every landing and its chance.

valueiter:8.t: A move’s score is an average. A move’s score now averages over its landings: chance times (reward plus 0.9 times value there). It is that move’s Q, as in the values reel. The cell takes the best Q: Pip chooses the move, not where it lands. Beside the cheese, in sweep 1: right reaches the cheese 8 times in 10 but slides onto the cat 1 in 10: 0.8 minus 0.1 equals 0.7. Pushing up into the wall scores 0.1, from a lucky slide onto the cheese.
