valueiter:9.t: Sweeping the wet floor. The numbers grow out from the cheese again, but no longer stop after 7 sweeps. The start gets nothing until sweep 7, then 0.12, 0.20, 0.26, 0.30, and is still creeping at sweep 14. After 7 sweeps, each number is the best Pip could expect if every walk were cut off after 7 steps. Each sweep allows one step more. Slides make walks long, so extra steps keep adding a little, less each time because of gamma.

valueiter:10.t: When to stop, now. The chart shows, for each sweep, the biggest change in any cell. Across: sweep number. Up: that change; each line is ten times smaller. Grey dots are sweeps we no longer need. Stop once it is below 0.001: sweep 16. Each later change is at most 0.9 times the one before, so all of them together add at most 0.001 times (0.9 plus 0.81 plus ...) equals 9 times 0.001. Checked against 400 sweeps, the real gap is under 0.001.

valueiter:11.t: The arrows settle first. Watch the arrows during those sweeps. They stop changing at sweep 10, while the numbers keep creeping until sweep 16. The start points right in sweeps 7 to 9, then flips to up for good. Which move is best often becomes clear before its exact value does. From inside the sweeps you cannot tell the arrows are final, so the stopping rule watches the numbers. The next reel, policy iteration, works with the arrows directly.

valueiter:12.t: Dry arrows, wet arrows. Left, the best arrows on the dry floor; right, on the wet floor. The clearest change is right below the cat: on the dry floor the best move was right, on the wet floor it is down, away from the cat. Where the dry floor had two equally short routes, the slipping makes one of them better by a hair, so the ties disappear. At the start, up beats right only in the third decimal.

valueiter:13.t: Why go down?. Below the cat, going right risks a slide up, onto the cat, 1 time in 10. Going down risks nothing: its slides either bump into the rock and stay, or land one cell to the right. The detour costs two extra steps, yet the averages favour it: 0.45 for down against 0.41 for right.

valueiter:14.t: Does it matter?. Send Pip from below the cat 1000 times. First keep the dry floor’s arrow there, right; only this one cell differs. 207 walks end on the cat. With the new arrow, down, only 114, although the walks get longer. Why not zero? Both cells next to the cheese are also next to the cat, so the last step always risks a slide onto it. The policy cannot remove that risk; it just stops adding more.

valueiter:15.t: Your turn. Drag the slip chance, the total chance of sliding sideways; so far 0.2. Value iteration reruns from zeros. More slipping makes walks longer, so the numbers creep for more sweeps, and the arrows bend away from the cat. At 0.3 the start takes the bottom route. At 0.4 the cells beside the cheese push into the wall, waiting for a lucky slide. Tap a cell to send Pip from there.

valueiter:16.t: The catch. Value iteration needs the whole rulebook, and every sweep visits every cell, every move and every landing. Here that is 16 cells. The board game Go has so many legal positions that writing their number takes 171 digits: no table could hold them. And often nobody hands you a rulebook at all. Later reels learn values from experience instead, and replace the table by a network.

valueiter:17.t: Where it shows up. Richard Bellman introduced this kind of step-by-step computation in the 1950s, under the name dynamic programming. Value iteration is still a standard solver when the rules are known and small enough to list: inventory planning, maintenance schedules, robot routes on a known map. Q-learning aims at a similar target, reward plus gamma times the best Q of the next cell, but estimates it from experience instead.

valueiter:18.t: Recap. With the rulebook in hand, value iteration sweeps one rule over every cell, from all zeros: value here equals the best Q, the best over moves of the average of reward plus gamma times value where it lands. It closes in on V star. Stop when the biggest change is tiny; the best arrows are the best policy. On a slippery floor it bends away from danger, because the averages count the slides.

policyiter:0.t: Policy Iteration. Judge your plan, fix it, repeat, until nothing changes.

policyiter:1.t: Another way to plan. Pip’s maze, with the wet floor: a tried move goes that way 8 times in 10 and slides 1 time in 10 to each side. A bump into a wall or rock leaves Pip in place. Stepping onto the cheese pays plus 1, onto the cat minus 1, both end the walk, other steps pay 0, and gamma (gamma) is 0.9. We hold the rulebook, the model, so we plan at a desk, improving a whole plan round after round.

policyiter:2.t: A bad first plan. A plan, or policy, puts one arrow in every cell, and Pip always tries that move. Any randomness now comes from the floor alone. Start with a plan that is clearly bad: every arrow points up. From the start, Pip walks up to the top corner and then pushes against the wall, moving on only when it happens to slide.

policyiter:3.t: Round 1: evaluate. First, measure how good this plan is: compute its notebook as in the Bellman reel, now averaging over the floor’s landings. Each cell gets the average of reward plus 0.9 times value there, using only the plan’s move. Sweep that rule from zeros until no number moves by more than 0.001: 24 sweeps, more than value iteration needed, because this plan’s walks are long and the news travels slowly. The start is worth only 0.01.

policyiter:4.t: Reading the bad notebook. Below the cheese the plan is already right: up reaches the cheese, worth 0.77. Beside the cheese it pushes into the wall and only a slide gets the cheese: 0.40. Below the cat, up walks straight into the cat: minus 0.83, and the bottom-row cells to its lower left drift into it too. Left of the cat shows 0.00: a slide onto the cat loses about what moving up gains.

policyiter:5.t: Round 1: improve. Now fix the plan. In each cell, score the four moves using this notebook: average over landings of reward plus 0.9 times value there. That score is the move’s Q from the values reel: take it once, then follow the plan. Point the arrow at the best Q, keeping the old arrow on a tie so ties cannot flip back and forth. Beside the cheese: up has Q 0.40, right 0.8 times 1 minus 0.1 plus 0.1 times 0.9 times 0.40 equals 0.74. Switch.

policyiter:6.t: Ten arrows change. Do it in every cell: 10 of the 16 arrows change. The top row now runs right, and below the cat the arrow turns away from it. Some new arrows look odd. Left of the cat it now pushes into the rock: up gains little and risks a slide onto the cat, while the rock is safe. Two bottom-row cells point left. These are best only by the bad plan’s notebook; the next round judges them again.

policyiter:7.t: Round 2. Evaluate the new plan, starting its sweeps from the last notebook: 23 sweeps (from zeros it would take 24). The start jumps from 0.01 to 0.32. Improve again with the new numbers: only 3 arrows change. Left of the cat it points up again, below the cat it now goes down, around the cat, and one bottom-row cell turns right.

policyiter:8.t: Rounds 3 and 4. Round 3: 10 sweeps, start 0.32, and just 1 arrow changes, in the bottom row. Round 4: 4 sweeps, start 0.33, and no arrow changes at all. When improving changes nothing, we stop. This is exactly the plan that value iteration, the previous reel, found on the same floor, including the detour below the cat.

policyiter:9.t: Round by round. Here are the four rounds in a table. Each row is one round’s plan: how many sweeps its evaluation took, what that plan makes the start worth, and how many arrows its improvement changed. Round 1’s fix shows up in row 2: the start jumps from 0.01 to 0.32. After that, rounds only fine-tune: 10, 3, 1, 0 arrows changed.

policyiter:10.t: Why it never gets worse. Take the cell beside the cheese. The old plan, up, is worth 0.40 there. Right once, then the old plan, is worth its Q, 0.74: that is why right was picked. Wherever Pip lands next, the new arrow also passed that test, so using it twice is at least as good, then three times, and so on. The new plan, always: 0.77. Over the whole maze, 15, 7, 4 numbers went up per round, and none went down.

policyiter:11.t: Why it stops at the best. A switch only happens where some Q is strictly higher, so that cell really gains: each changing round is strictly better, no plan comes back, and among 4,294,967,296 plans the rounds must end. At the end every arrow has the best Q in its cell. Beside the cheese: right 0.77, up 0.71, left 0.44, down minus 0.64. Any other plan’s move, used once and then ours, is no better; used twice, still no better; and so on. No plan beats ours.

policyiter:12.t: Rounds versus sweeps. Policy iteration needed 4 rounds; value iteration needed 16 sweeps. But each round hides a whole evaluation: 61 sweeps in total. Those sweeps are cheaper, one move per cell instead of four. Counting move scores: 1,232 here against 1,024 for value iteration, about the same. Value iteration is the extreme case: its max picks the best arrow and does one evaluation sweep at once.

policyiter:13.t: Your turn. Pick a different first plan and watch the rounds play out. Starting all right takes 3 rounds; all down or all left take 7 each, because they reach the cheese only by sliding, so their early notebooks are mostly zeros and the news spreads slowly. Every start ends at the same plan. Tap a cell to see its four Q values in the round on screen.

policyiter:14.t: The big template. Evaluate a plan, then improve it using what you learned: this loop is everywhere in reinforcement learning. Loosened, it is called generalised policy iteration: evaluate with only a few sweeps, or improve only some cells, or shift the plan only a little, and repeat. Later reels, such as actor-critic, follow it with learning instead of a rulebook: a critic estimates values from experience, and an actor nudges the plan toward moves the critic rates higher.

policyiter:15.t: Where it shows up. Ronald Howard described policy iteration in 1960, in his book on dynamic programming and Markov processes. It remains a standard way to solve planning problems whose rules are known, like stock and maintenance decisions. Its biggest legacy is the loop itself: judge the current behaviour, then nudge it toward what the judgement says is better.

policyiter:16.t: Recap. Policy iteration starts from any plan and repeats two halves: evaluate the plan’s notebook, then point each arrow at its best-scoring move. Each round is at least as good as the last, in every cell. When no arrow changes, the plan is the best one. Few rounds, but each holds a full evaluation.

mc:0.t: Monte Carlo Learning. Play to the end, then learn from what really happened.

mc:1.t: Back in the maze. Pip is back in its maze, and the floor is dry again: every move goes where Pip intends. Stepping onto the cheese pays plus 1, onto the cat minus 1, and either one ends the walk; other steps pay 0. A bump leaves Pip in place but counts as a step. gamma (gamma) is 0.9. Pip follows its habit from the values reel: the arrow, except that one move in five goes in a random direction.

mc:2.t: No rulebook. Pip has no rulebook: nobody told it where moves lead or what they pay, so it can’t work values out on paper. It can only walk. In the values reel, Pip was placed in every cell for 1000 walks each: that averaging was already Monte Carlo, the wasteful kind. Real Pip always starts in the corner. Monte Carlo learning learns from the complete walks it actually takes. The name comes from the famous casino.

mc:3.t: One walk, seven returns. Walk 1, as in the values reel: cheese in 7 steps. Once the walk is over, Pip writes a return into every cell it passed, not just the start. A cell’s return counts the rewards from the step that leaves it until the walk ends. Beside the cheese that is 1. Each cell further back waited one step longer, one more times 0.9, down to 0.53 at the start.

mc:4.t: A notebook of averages. For every cell the notebook keeps two things: how many returns it has, n, and their average. A new return nudges the average: new equals old plus (return minus old) divided by n. The hundredth return moves it only a hundredth of the way. Some versions nudge by a fixed fraction instead, so old walks fade: useful when the habit keeps changing.

mc:5.t: Walk 2: twice in one cell. On walk 2 Pip steps back down once and bumps the top wall once, so it passes three cells twice. Which return counts? Here, only the one from the first visit in each walk. Counting every visit also works: after 1000 walks the two notebooks differ by at most 0.04. The start averages (0.53 plus 0.39) divided by 2 equals 0.46. Beside the cheese: (1 plus 0.9) divided by 2 equals 0.95.

mc:6.t: Walk 3: same path, opposite lesson. Walk 3 starts along the same path. Halfway, Pip can’t write anything: whether these cells lead to cheese or cat is still unknown. Then, right beside the cheese, a random move points down, onto the cat. Every return on the path is negative. The start’s average drops to 0.15, beside the cheese to 0.30. A single walk can swing the notebook a lot.

mc:7.t: Many walks. Pip keeps walking from the start. After 10 walks the start reads 0.28, after 100 walks 0.44, after 1000 walks 0.40: exactly the values reel’s number, because these are the same 1000 walks. But now every cell on the route got its own returns from those walks too, at least 964 each, with no extra walking.

mc:8.t: Where Pip rarely goes. Compare with the values reel, which started 1000 walks in every cell. Along Pip’s usual route the two notebooks agree within 0.01. Off the route, cells got only 33 to 59 returns, mostly from the same few walks, and are off by about 0.1: the cell below the cheese reads 0.73 against 0.87. Below the cat: only 3 returns, minus 0.33 against 0.59. Monte Carlo only learns where Pip actually goes.

mc:9.t: How much one return varies. Here are all 1000 returns from the start. Across is the return of one walk, from minus 1 to plus 1. Each bar counts how many walks gave that return: gold walks reached the cheese, rose ones the cat. They spread from minus 0.53 to 0.53, because every random move until the end of the walk changes the return. Only the average of many walks settles, near 0.40.

mc:10.t: Your turn. Drag the slider to choose how many of Pip’s walks the notebook has seen. Tap any cell to see every return it has collected, as dots on a line from minus 1 to plus 1, with its average. Try the start, then a cell in the bottom right. With few walks, see how far one return can pull an average.

mc:11.t: From judging to improving. So far the arrows came from someone else; the notebook only judged them. To improve, a cell’s value isn’t enough: without a rulebook, Pip can’t tell where each move leads. So Pip keeps an average per move: Q(cell, move), said “Q of cell and move”: the average return after taking that move there, first visit per walk. Picking moves by Q changes the habit: policy iteration’s evaluate-then-improve loop, done a little after every walk.

mc:12.t: A habit built from averages. Pip drops the arrows and starts from scratch: every Q is 0. In each cell it takes the move with the biggest Q, ties broken at random. One move in five is random anyway, so moves that look bad still get tried. Walk 1 wanders for 51 steps and ends on the cat. Every move it used now has a negative average, so next time an untried move, still at 0, looks better.

mc:13.t: The catch: wait for the end. Walk 4 takes 493 steps. In the top-left corner, “up” has the least bad average, minus 0.006, because the walks that tried it were so long that the cat’s minus 1 had shrunk to almost nothing. So Pip bumps that wall 151 times. Its averages can’t change until the walk is over, and a walk that never ended would teach nothing. T D learning, in a coming reel, updates after every step.

mc:14.t: How Pip got out. After walk 4, up and down in the corner both averaged just below 0, the best there, so long walks went on. The way out: a walk that reaches the cheese gives every move it used a positive return. On walk 8 Pip left the corner to the right, and that walk reached the cheese. “Right” got the corner’s only positive average, 0.02, so Pip now turns right there.

mc:15.t: 200 walks later. One bar per walk: height equals steps (up to 100, faint line at 10); teal cheese, rose cat. After about 19 walks most take 7 to 10 steps. The biggest-Q arrows lead Pip to the cheese in 7 steps, the shortest route. In 40 more runs with different luck, 35 found it; 5 kept a 9-step detour: the shorter way, tried mostly by random moves, still looked worse. With 1000 walks, 4 of the 5 find 7.

mc:16.t: Where you’ve seen this. The name dates from the 1940s, when Stanislaw Ulam and John von Neumann used random sampling for physics calculations at Los Alamos. A classic R L example is blackjack: the value of holding 18 is estimated by playing many hands to the end and averaging the results. AlphaGo, in 2016, also judged Go positions partly by playing fast games to the end and averaging who won.

mc:17.t: Recap. Monte Carlo learning needs no rulebook. After each complete walk, every cell passed gets its return, and its average moves toward it. The returns are real outcomes, but they vary a lot, and cells Pip rarely visits stay rough. Averages per move, Q, let Pip improve its own habit. The price: nothing is learned until the walk ends.

td:0.t: Temporal-Difference Learning. Learn a guess from a slightly better guess, every single step.

td:1.t: Back in the maze. Same maze and rules as in the values and Bellman reels. The floor is dry: every move goes where Pip points. Stepping onto the cheese pays plus 1, onto the cat minus 1, and either ends the walk. gamma (gamma) is 0.9. Pip keeps its usual habit: follow the arrows, but one move in five goes in a random direction. The sweeps worked out this habit’s notebook: 0.87 in the cell left of the cheese, 0.40 at the start.

td:2.t: No rulebook, no waiting. The sweeps needed the rulebook: where every move leads and what it pays. Monte Carlo learning, from the Monte Carlo reel, needs no rulebook: it averages the returns of whole walks. But a return is only known when the walk ends. Now Pip gets neither help. Its notebook starts blank, every guess 0, and it must learn the habit’s numbers while it walks, from what it actually sees.

td:3.t: Learn now, not later. Think of driving home. You guess 30 minutes. Ten minutes in, you hit a traffic jam, so you revise: 40 minutes. You learned before you got home. Your new guess was what you had seen so far plus a guess for the rest. That idea is temporal-difference learning, or T D learning, and Pip’s target will have exactly this shape.

td:4.t: The Bellman rule, one real step. The Bellman rule: value here equals the average, over all moves, of reward plus 0.9 times value where the move lands. That average needs the rulebook. After each step Pip has one real example: the reward it got and where it landed. Its target, reward plus 0.9 times its guess for that cell, is the Bellman rule with one real step in place of the average. Over many steps these targets average out to the Bellman sum, if the guesses are right.

td:5.t: Walk 1: no news yet. Pip walks its habit. After each step it updates the guess of the cell it just left. Step 1: reward 0, and the cell it landed on has guess 0, so the target is 0 plus 0.9 times 0 equals 0. The old guess was 0 too: nothing changes. The same happens on each of the first 6 steps. Pip has not met a reward yet, so there is no news to learn from.

td:6.t: Cheese!. On step 7, Pip steps from the cell left of the cheese onto it: reward plus 1, and the walk ends, so there is no landing cell to add. The target is simply 1. The old guess was 0. The gap, target minus old guess, is the T D error: how surprised Pip is. Here the surprise is 1.

td:7.t: A fifth of the way. Pip does not jump straight to 1. It moves its guess a fifth of the way: 0 plus 0.2 times 1 equals 0.20. That 0.2 is alpha (alpha), the learning rate. It has nothing to do with the one random move in five; the numbers just happen to match. Why so cautious? The next walk might end on the cat. Small steps let many walks average out.

td:8.t: The news travels back. Walk 2. Pip steps into the cell left of the cheese, worth 0.20. Target: 0 plus 0.9 times 0.20 equals 0.18, so the cell Pip left moves a fifth of the way, to 0.036. Learning a guess from another guess is bootstrapping, the heart of T D. Then a random move bumps Pip into the wall: target 0.9 times 0.20 equals 0.18, a bit below its guess, which dips to 0.196. The cheese then lifts it to 0.36.

td:9.t: How surprised is Pip?. Each time Pip steps onto the cheese, split the plus 1 in two: what it expected, its guess for the cell left of the cheese, and the surprise, the T D error. Walk 1: expected 0, surprise 1. Walk 2: expected 0.20, surprise 0.80. On walk 3, in that cell, one of Pip’s random moves points down, into the cat: T D error minus 1.36, and the guess drops to 0.085. So on walk 4 the cheese surprises Pip again: 0.91. Walk 7 brings another cat.

td:10.t: 200 walks. Now let Pip walk 200 times. The chart shows the guess for the cell left of the cheese after each walk, from walk 1 on the left to walk 200 on the right. The dashed line is the true value from the sweeps, 0.87. Rose ticks mark walks that ended on the cat. The guess climbs fast, then hovers around the dashed line, dropping after each cat scare. After 50 walks the start already reads 0.35; its true value is 0.40.

td:11.t: Close, but never still. After walk 200, left of the cheese, T D says 0.98, the sweeps 0.87. Why higher? Since the last cat scare, on walk 185, 15 good walks each pulled the guess toward 1. Cat scares are rare but knock it far down: a cluster once dragged it to 0.27. Averaged over the last 100 walks it is 0.85. So with a fixed alpha, guesses keep wobbling around the true values instead of settling. The right half of the grid is far off too; that has a different cause, coming up.

td:12.t: Monte Carlo, same walks. The Monte Carlo reel’s walks began with these same 200. Averaging their real returns ends up closer almost everywhere: on Pip’s usual route within 0.01 of the sweeps, against 0.10 for T D; in the rarely visited cells 0.06 off on average, against 0.38. In this small maze every walk ends after a few steps, so waiting costs little and Monte Carlo wins. T D pays off when walks are very long or never end.

td:13.t: Why T D lags off the route. Not for lack of visits: right of the start, Monte Carlo had 8 returns and T D 9 updates. But every T D target there leaned on the next cell’s guess, never above 0.003: the news from the cheese had not crawled back that far. Plug in the true values for the landing cells, and the same 9 updates give 0.40. Bootstrapping is fast where Pip walks often, slow where news must pass through rarely visited cells. The small numbers count visits in 200 walks.

td:14.t: A smaller step. Same 200 walks with alpha equals 0.05; the habit ignores the notebook, so only alpha differs. The blue line wobbles less: over the last 100 walks 0.66 to 0.99, against 0.27 to 1.00. But after 100 walks the start reads only 0.08, against 0.42. Monte Carlo’s running average shrinks its step as 1 divided by n. For T D that shrinks too fast here: early targets leaned on zeros and keep their weight, so after 200 walks the start reads only 0.10. It gets there in the long run, but slowly.

td:15.t: Your turn. Drag alpha to rerun the same 200 walks with a different learning rate. The gold line is the guess left of the cheese, the teal line the start; dashed lines are their true values. Watch two things: how wildly the lines jump around the dashed ones, and how long the teal line takes to climb toward its dashed line. Big alpha learns fast but nervously; small alpha is calm but slow.

td:16.t: Where you’ve seen this. Pip’s surprise at the cheese shrinks, with jumps after cat scares. And it moves earlier: on walk 2, a T D error of 0.18 came one step before the cheese, on entering a promising cell. In the 1990s, Wolfram Schultz found dopamine neurons in monkeys firing at unexpected juice. Once a light reliably came first, they fired at the light instead, and dipped when promised juice did not come. T D also powered the backgammon program T D-Gammon (1992).

td:17.t: What T D cannot do yet. T D filled Pip’s notebook with how good each cell is under its habit, using nothing but experience. But it never changed the habit. To pick a better move from these numbers, Pip would need to know where each move leads and what it pays: the rulebook again. The fix, as in the Monte Carlo reel, is a number for each move. Q-learning, next, learns those numbers with T D’s one-step update.

td:18.t: Recap. T D learning estimates the values of the habit Pip follows, from experience alone, and updates after every step instead of waiting for the walk to end. Its target is the Bellman rule with one real step in place of the average over moves. A fixed alpha makes the guesses hover around the true values; a smaller alpha wobbles less but learns slower.

qlearning:0.t: Q-Learning. Learn the value of every move, even while acting randomly.

qlearning:1.t: Where T D left off. In the T D reel, Pip followed a fixed habit: the arrows, with one move in five random. T D learning worked out, from experience, how good each cell is under that habit. Here is that notebook, with the true values of the habit, which T D’s guesses head toward. Now Pip wants to do better than its habit. Can the notebook tell it which move is best?

qlearning:2.t: A notebook is not enough. Say Pip stands in the bottom row, in the middle. The cell to its right is worth 0.59, the cell to its left 0.45. Going right looks better, but only if Pip knows that “right” leads to the right-hand cell. Pip does not know the rules of the maze. It knows its cell; only after a move does it see the reward and where it landed. It could learn the rules as well, a later topic. Q-learning skips them and learns a value for each move directly.

qlearning:3.t: A number for each move. Instead of one number per cell, Pip keeps four: one for each move. Each cell is split into four triangles; the one pointing up holds the number for “up”, and so on. Gold is positive, rose negative. Each number is an action value, Q of s, a. In the values reel it meant: make move a, then follow the habit. Q-learning aims at a different one: make move a, then act as well as possible. That is the Q of the best policy, Q star, said “Q star”. All start at 0.

qlearning:4.t: Choosing needs no map. To move, Pip looks only at its own cell and takes the move with the biggest number. Ties are broken at random. Bumping into a wall is a move too, with its own number. One move in five is still random, any of the four directions, so that every move gets tried. This habit is called epsilon-greedy, with epsilon (epsilon) equals 0.2: greedy means taking the biggest number.

qlearning:5.t: The update, in words. After each move, Pip looks back at the number for the move it just made. The target: the reward for that move, plus 0.9 times the biggest of the four numbers in the cell where it landed. Then it nudges the old number a fifth of the way toward the target. That fifth is alpha (alpha), the learning rate, as in T D learning. If Pip landed on the cheese or the cat, the walk is over and nothing is added.

qlearning:6.t: In symbols. Written out, with s the cell Pip left, a the move it made, r the reward, and s prime, said “s prime”, the cell where it landed: Q of s, a becomes Q of s, a plus alpha times (r plus gamma times max Q(s prime,  times ) minus Q of s, a). “max Q(s prime,  times )” is the biggest of the four numbers in s prime. gamma (gamma) equals 0.9 and alpha equals 0.2, the same two knobs as in T D learning.

qlearning:7.t: Walk 1. All numbers are 0, so every choice is a tie, a coin toss. For 23 steps every update says “0 stays 0”. On step 24, from the cell below the cheese, one of the one-in-five random moves points up, onto the cheese: reward plus 1, walk over. Target 1, so that one number, “up” in that cell, goes from 0 to 0.2. Nothing else changes.

qlearning:8.t: The news travels back. Walk 2 ends by stepping right onto the cheese, so “right” beside the cheese becomes 0.2 too. In walk 3, Pip steps right into that cell. The biggest of its four numbers is 0.2. Target equals 0 plus 0.9 times 0.2 equals 0.18, and the number for “right” in the cell Pip left becomes 0 plus 0.2 times 0.18 equals 0.036. A guess learned from the next guess, as in T D learning, but stored on a move.

qlearning:9.t: The max ignores what comes next. Walk 7. Pip steps right into the cell beside the cheese and updates at once, before choosing its next move. The biggest number there is 0.672, for “right”: target 0.9 times 0.672 equals 0.605, and the old 0.236 becomes 0.31. The target asks: what if Pip makes the best move from here? Whatever Pip actually does next plays no part.

qlearning:10.t: Bad news stays with the bad move. Then Pip picks its next move, and it is one of the random ones: down, onto the cat. Reward minus 1, walk over. Only the “down” number of that cell changes, from 0 to minus 0.2. “Right” keeps its 0.672. With one number per cell, as in the T D reel, this minus 1 would have pulled down the value of the whole cell. Four numbers keep a bad move apart from a good one.

qlearning:11.t: Walk by walk. This chart follows two of the four numbers beside the cheese. Across is the walk number, 1 to 20; up is the number after that walk. Gold is “right”, onto the cheese; rose is “down”, onto the cat. “Right” climbs: 0.2, 0.36, 0.49 ... 0.96 after 20 walks. Cat scares only push “down” lower. “Right” never drops: it lands on the cheese, so its target is always exactly 1.

qlearning:12.t: 300 walks later. Repeat for 300 walks. The bars show the steps each walk took; teal means cheese, rose means the cat. Early walks wander: 24, 20, 28, 31 steps. Over the last 100, the average is 8.9. The arrows show Pip’s best guess at the best move. The small numbers count visits. Cells off the usual route were rarely visited, so their guesses can be wrong: the two left arrows in the bottom row are not best moves. A ? means all four numbers are still equal.

qlearning:13.t: The best route’s numbers. Read the biggest number in each cell along the arrows: 1 beside the cheese, then 0.9, 0.81, and so on, down to 0.53 at the start. These are the perfect values of always taking the shortest route: the V star of the Bellman reel, learned here from walks alone. Under Pip’s old habit, that cell beside the cheese is worth 0.87: the value of distracted walking. Q-learning learned 1, though Pip still moved at random one time in five. The max makes every target assume the best next move.

qlearning:14.t: Why they sit still. In the T D reel, a fixed alpha of 0.2 kept the guesses wobbling. Here they settle exactly. Why? The floor is dry, and the max ignores Pip’s random next move. So once the numbers in the next cell have settled, every target for a move is the very same number, walk after walk. Nothing is left to wobble. T D’s targets kept changing because the habit’s random moves changed where Pip went next.

qlearning:15.t: But Pip still stumbles. Those numbers describe a Pip that never makes a random move. The real Pip still moves at random one time in five. Each dot below is one of its last 100 walks, placed at the return it got: gold reached the cheese, rose met the cat. 6 met the cat, and the average is 0.39, not 0.53. Q-learning learns about the best way to act, not about how Pip acts while learning. The next reel learns numbers for the Pip that really walks.

qlearning:16.t: Your turn. Drag epsilon, how often Pip moves at random, and all 300 walks are rerun. At every setting the start’s number reaches 0.53. The more Pip moves at random, the more cells it visits: at 1, all 16 arrows are best moves, at 0.2 only 11. But a more random Pip earns less along the way. Tap a cell to drop Pip there and follow the arrows.

qlearning:17.t: Where it came from. Chris Watkins introduced Q-learning in his 1989 PhD thesis. With Peter Dayan he proved in 1992 that the table version reaches the best values, if every move in every cell keeps being tried and the steps shrink suitably over time. Our run broke both rules and still found the route, but its rarely tried cells stayed wrong. In 2015, DeepMind’s D Q N replaced the table with a neural network that read the screen of Atari games and output one Q value per joystick move.

qlearning:18.t: Recap. Without a map, keep a number for every move: Q of s, a. Pick the biggest, explore now and then. After each move, nudge its number toward the reward plus gamma times the best number where you landed. Because of that max, the numbers head for the best way to act, even while Pip acts at random.

sarsa:0.t: SARSA. Learn the value of what you’ll actually do next.

sarsa:1.t: A new room. Pip has a new room to learn: six cells wide, four tall, no rocks. It starts bottom left, the cheese sits bottom right, and between them, along the bottom row, four cats are asleep. The rules are the old ones: the floor is dry, stepping onto the cheese pays plus 1, onto a cat minus 1, either one ends the walk, gamma (gamma) is 0.9, and bumping into a wall leaves Pip where it is.

sarsa:2.t: Two ways across. The short way runs right along the cats: up one cell, five steps right, down onto the cheese. Seven steps, a return of 0.9 multiplied six times, 0.53. One row higher takes nine steps: 0.43. For a mouse that never moves at random, the short way wins. But Pip moves at random one time in five, and on the row above the cats, one move in twenty points down, at a cat.

sarsa:3.t: What Q-learning learns. First, Q-learning, exactly as in the last reel: 500 walks, one move in five random. Its arrows take the short way, right along the cats. That fits what Q-learning measures. Every target assumes the best next move, so its numbers describe a Pip that never moves at random. In the top rows, which Pip rarely visits, the arrows are rough guesses.

sarsa:4.t: SARSA’s one change. SARSA changes one thing. When Pip lands, it first picks its next move, with the same habit: the biggest number, or one time in five a random move. Then it updates using the number of that move, the one it will really make, not the biggest one. Then it makes it. Its name lists what one update uses: State, Action, Reward, next State, next Action.

sarsa:5.t: In symbols. With a prime, said “a prime”, the next move Pip has already picked in s prime: Q of s, a becomes Q of s, a plus alpha times (r plus gamma times Q(s prime, a prime) minus Q of s, a). The only difference from Q-learning is inside the target: Q(s prime, a prime) instead of max Q(s prime,  times ). If the walk is over, there is no next move and nothing is added.

sarsa:6.t: One SARSA update. Walk 26 of SARSA’s own run. Pip steps right onto the cell above a cat, and picks its next move: a random one, down, whose number is minus 0.2. So the target is 0 plus 0.9 times minus 0.2 equals minus 0.18, and the old 0.42 drops to 0.3. Q-learning would have used the best number there, 0.73: target 0.66, new 0.47.

sarsa:7.t: Then it really goes down. SARSA commits to the move it picked: Pip steps down onto the cat. Reward minus 1, walk over, so that number becomes minus 0.36. Picking a move in advance is what makes SARSA honest about Pip. Its targets contain the random moves Pip really makes, so cells where a random move is dangerous get lower numbers.

sarsa:8.t: The edge gets a bad name. After 500 walks, compare one cell on the row above the cats, second from the left. Q-learning says “right” is worth 0.66: the perfect value of the short way. SARSA says only 0.15, because walking on along the cats, a random move will sometimes take Pip into a cat. For SARSA, “up”, away from the cats, is the best move here: 0.36.

sarsa:9.t: Two routes. Follow each learner’s arrows from the start. Q-learning goes along the cats. SARSA climbs two rows, keeping an empty row between itself and the cats. In this run, if Pip keeps moving at random one time in five, Q-learning’s arrows are worth 0.15 from the start, SARSA’s 0.25. These are exact values, computed with sweeps over the room’s rules as in the Bellman reel; Pip itself never sees them.

sarsa:10.t: Is this one run a fluke?. To check, run both learners 100 times with different random seeds, 500 walks each. The chart shows what Pip actually earned while learning: each dot is the average return of 25 walks, averaged over the 100 runs. Across is the walk number; up is the return. Orange is Q-learning, teal is SARSA.

sarsa:11.t: SARSA earns more while learning. Averaged over all walks, SARSA earned 0.18 per walk, Q-learning 0.15. SARSA’s route is longer, but only 12 in 100 of its walks ended on a cat, against 22 for Q-learning. Early on, both still wander and earn about the same. Then SARSA’s numbers settle away from the cats, while Q-learning’s route keeps costing it cats. Q-learning settled on the route along the cats in 61 of 100 runs, SARSA in none.

sarsa:12.t: So who is right?. Both, about different Pips. If Pip stopped moving at random, Q-learning’s route would be worth 0.53 and SARSA’s only 0.43. While Pip still explores, SARSA’s is worth more. Q-learning learns the best way to act, whatever Pip does meanwhile. SARSA learns the best way to act given its own habit, random moves included. Rule of thumb: if mistakes while learning cost something real, use SARSA; if only the final route matters, Q-learning.

sarsa:13.t: Your turn. Drag epsilon. Each setting reruns both learners 100 times and draws the route each settled on most often. The more Pip moves at random, the more SARSA avoids the cats. At 0.2 the other SARSA runs take the top row or a mix; in 91 of 100 its arrows never touch a cell above a cat. At 0 the two rules are the same; with little randomness SARSA earns a bit less.

sarsa:14.t: Where it came from. Gavin Rummery and Mahesan Niranjan described the method in 1994 as “modified connectionist Q-learning”; Richard Sutton suggested the name SARSA. A room like this one is the cliff walking example from Sutton and Barto’s textbook. The lesson carries over: when mistakes made while learning are costly, as for a real robot near stairs, learning about the behaviour you actually have can be the safer choice.

sarsa:15.t: Recap. SARSA picks its next move first, then updates toward the reward plus gamma times that move’s number. So its numbers include Pip’s own random moves. Near danger it learns a safer route and earns more while exploring. Q-learning, with its max, learns the best route for a Pip that never moves at random.

onoff:0.t: On-Policy versus Off-Policy. Learn only from your own behaviour, or from anyone’s?

onoff:1.t: Two jobs. In the last two reels, Pip learned four numbers per cell while moving with its epsilon-greedy habit: the biggest number, or one time in five a random move. Any such learner has two rules in play. One picks the moves that create the experience: the behaviour policy. The other is the rule whose values the numbers describe: the target policy. Careful: that is not the update target, the number each update moves toward. A policy is just a rule for picking moves.

onoff:2.t: SARSA: one rule. SARSA’s update target uses the next move that its epsilon-greedy habit really picks, random moves included. So its numbers describe epsilon-greedy: the very rule that is acting. Run in this maze, its biggest number at the start is 0.34, close to what its Pip really earned, 0.37. When the two rules are the same, the learning is on-policy: you learn about exactly what you do.

onoff:3.t: Q-learning: two rules. Q-learning also acts epsilon-greedy, but its update target uses the biggest number: it assumes the best next move every time. Its numbers describe the greedy rule, a Pip that never moves at random. That is why they said 0.53 at the start while Pip really earned 0.39. Learning about one policy while following another is off-policy learning.

onoff:4.t: Why Q-learning can do it. Q of s, a asks: what happens after move a in cell s? The maze answers with a reward and a landing cell, and the answer is the same whoever chose the move. Then the max fills in the best way to carry on. So nothing in Q-learning’s update target depends on who was acting. SARSA’s needs the next move of the walker, so it describes that walker.

onoff:5.t: Someone else’s diary. Remember the Wanderer, the mouse whose every move is random? Pip finds a diary of 100 of its walks from the start: every cell, move, reward and landing, 7,148 steps in all. Only 27 of those walks reached the cheese; 73 ended on the cat. The quickest took 17 steps. Can Pip learn the best route from this, without taking a single step itself?

onoff:6.t: Replaying the diary. Pip reads the diary step by step and applies Q-learning’s update to each step, as if it had made that move itself. It reads the whole diary 10 times. The biggest number at the start: 0.45 after one reading, 0.53 after two, 0.53 after 10. So fast, because one reading is 7,148 updates spread over every cell. Both shortest routes, up the left side or along the bottom, get the perfect numbers, 0.53 up to 1, though the Wanderer never walked either.

onoff:7.t: SARSA, same diary. Replayed with SARSA, the same diary gives the Wanderer’s own values, since its update target uses the Wanderer’s next move. At the start, all four are close to minus 0.03. Why near 0, when 73 walks in 100 met the cat? The walks average 71 steps, and 0.9 multiplied 70 times is 0.0006: late endings barely count. Correct, but useless for Pip.

onoff:8.t: Why off-policy matters. Learning about one rule while following another opens doors. Pip can reuse old experience, replaying it many times instead of walking again. It can learn from other walkers: a random one, a human, an older version of itself. And it can explore as wildly as it likes, while still learning the best way to act. The random diary even got the bottom-row arrows right, which Pip’s own walks did not: 16 of 16 arrows are best moves.

onoff:9.t: Risk: only what the data shows. Another diary, from a careful mouse that follows the habit’s arrows and never moves at random: 100 walks, all the same 7 steps. Q-learning learns that route perfectly, and nothing else. In 9 of 16 cells the four numbers never moved. Drop Pip in one of those cells and it has no clue. Off-policy data can only teach about moves someone actually tried.

onoff:10.t: Risk: a rule that never acted. Off-policy numbers describe a rule that never acted. In the cat room, Q-learning’s numbers were about a greedy Pip; the Pip that really walked was epsilon-greedy, and met more cats than SARSA’s. With large problems a neural network replaces the table, and changing one guess shifts others. A guess chasing a guess can then run away, and off-policy data brings no walk of that rule to correct it. Sutton and Barto call this mix the deadly triad; more in a later topic.

onoff:11.t: Your turn. Pick whose experience Q-learning learns from: Pip’s own epsilon-greedy walks, the Wanderer’s random diary, or the careful mouse’s diary. The diaries are replayed ten times. Tap a cell to drop Pip there and follow the arrows. Where the data never went, Pip has no clue.

onoff:12.t: Where you meet them. Off-policy: Q-learning, and D Q N, which in 2015 kept a memory of past Atari moves and replayed them in random order. sack, a 2018 method for robot control, does the same. Learning purely from logged data is called offline R L. On-policy: SARSA, and P P O (2017), used to fine-tune chatbots. P P O learns a policy directly, without a Q table (a later topic). It gathers fresh experience with its current policy, learns from it briefly, then throws it away.

onoff:13.t: Recap. The behaviour policy acts; the target policy is what the numbers describe. Same rule: on-policy, like SARSA. Different rules: off-policy, like Q-learning. Off-policy learners can reuse old experience and learn from others, but only about moves the data contains, and they are harder to keep stable.

traces:0.t: Eligibility Traces  and  T D(lambda). Give credit to recent steps, fading into the past.

traces:1.t: Two ways to pass the news. Pip follows its habit, the arrows with one move in five random, and learns each cell’s value from its walks. Cheese plus 1 and cat minus 1 are paid on the step onto them; both end the walk. gamma (gamma) is 0.9. T D learning updates every step using the next cell’s guess; Monte Carlo waits for the real return. Can we get the best of both? The same trick also works for Q-values, in SARSA and Q-learning.

traces:2.t: After walk 1. Walk 1 is the familiar 7-step trip to the cheese. With T D, only the cell beside the cheese learns anything: 0 plus 0.2 times 1 equals 0.2. Every other step had nothing to pass on yet. The fixed-fraction version of Monte Carlo, with the same fifth, moves every cell a fifth of the way to its return: 0.2 beside the cheese, down to 0.11 at the start. One walk reached the whole path.

traces:3.t: Who deserves the credit?. Which earlier moves earned the cheese? This is the credit assignment problem. T D hands the credit back about one cell per walk: on this run its guess for the start first moves on walk 7, and after 10 walks it is only 0.0004. Monte Carlo credits every cell at once, but only after the walk ends, and one unlucky ending shakes every cell on the path. Is there a middle ground?

traces:4.t: Looking n steps ahead. T D’s target looks one step ahead; Monte Carlo looks to the end. In between is the n-step target: the next n real rewards, each discounted as in a return (the first, plus 0.9 times the second, plus 0.81 times the third ...), then 0.9 multiplied n times times the guess where Pip is n steps later. If the walk ends sooner, stop at the end. One step is T D, the whole walk is Monte Carlo.

traces:5.t: A fading memory. A smoother trick than waiting n steps: give each cell a mark, its eligibility trace, and set a dial lambda (lambda) between 0 and 1. Each step, in this order: every mark shrinks, times 0.9 times lambda; then the cell Pip just left gets mark 1. With lambda equals 0.8, after step 1 the start has 1; after step 2 the start has 0.72 and the cell above it 1.

traces:6.t: One surprise, many cells. At each step Pip computes the T D error as usual: reward plus 0.9 times next guess minus old guess. Then every cell moves by alpha times T D error times its mark. On walk 1 every T D error is 0 until the cheese, where it is 1. That single surprise updates the whole recent path: 0.2 beside the cheese, then 0.144, 0.104, and so on, down to 0.028 at the start.

traces:7.t: The dial lambda. At lambda equals 0 marks vanish after one step: plain T D. At lambda equals 1 marks shrink by 0.9 per step, like discounting, so on walk 1 each cell gets the cheese’s plus 1 just as its return would: exactly Monte Carlo. Later, guesses shift mid-walk, so it is only close. Values in between act like an average of all the n-step targets, longer ones weighted less. This is T D(lambda).

traces:8.t: A fair race. Pip’s habit never changes, so every lambda can learn from the very same walks. We score each by its error: the average gap between its guesses and the true values on the 7 cells of Pip’s usual route. The true values are the values reel’s notebook: 0.87 beside the cheese, 0.40 at the start. To avoid a lucky draw, the race is repeated on 200 different sets of walks and averaged.

traces:9.t: The first 50 walks. Across: walks 1 to 50. Up: the error, averaged over all the sets of walks. Lower is better. After 10 walks, T D’s error is still 0.40; with lambda equals 0.8 it is 0.17, with lambda equals 1 only 0.09. Spreading each surprise over the recent path makes early learning much faster. But watch the rose line creep back up.

traces:10.t: Fast early, noisy later. The bars show the error after 20 and after 200 walks, on one shared scale. After 20 walks the winner is lambda equals 0.9, in the middle. After 200, plain T D wins: 0.06 against 0.10 for lambda equals 1. Why? Large lambda leans on the real rest of the walk, so one cat ending jolts many cells, as in Monte Carlo. Small lambda leans on neighbours’ guesses, which already average many walks.

traces:11.t: Is one alpha fair?. Every lambda used alpha equals 0.2, but large lambda spreads each surprise over many cells, so it may want smaller steps. Here each lambda gets its best alpha, from 0.05 to 0.5. After 20 walks lambda equals 0.9 still wins, 0.07. After 200 walks small steps help everyone, and now lambda equals 0.5 edges ahead: 0.037, against 0.045 for T D and 0.046 for lambda equals 1. Plain T D’s late win was partly the shared alpha.

traces:12.t: Your turn. Drag lambda. The maze shows this run’s notebook after 10 walks, and the bars show the averaged error after 20 and 200 walks for your setting. At 0, watch the news stay near the cheese; at 1, it reaches the start at once. Which lambda would you pick for 20 walks? For 200?

traces:13.t: The cost. Traces are not free. Every step, every marked cell is updated, not just one. With lambda equals 0.8, a mark stays above 0.01 for 15 steps, so on a long walk Pip updates up to 15 cells per step instead of 1. Smaller marks can simply be dropped. Here a revisited cell’s mark is reset to 1, not added to. And lambda is one more dial to tune, together with alpha.

traces:14.t: Where you’ve seen this. Richard Sutton introduced T D(lambda) in 1988. Gerald Tesauro’s T D-Gammon (1992) used it to learn backgammon by playing itself, coming close to the best human players. The same lambda lives on in G A E (generalised advantage estimation, 2015). It judges how much better a move turned out than the cell’s value, blending short and long lookaheads with lambda; the popular P P O method commonly uses it.

traces:15.t: Recap. An eligibility trace is a fading mark on recently left cells. Each T D error updates every marked cell, in proportion to its mark, so one surprise reaches the whole recent path. lambda sets how slowly marks fade: 0 is T D, 1 is Monte Carlo-like. Large lambda learns fast early but is noisier; in between is often a good compromise.

funcapprox:0.t: Function Approximation. Too many states for a table? Learn a function that generalises.

funcapprox:1.t: Out of the maze. Pip has left the maze. Now it roams an open meadow: no cells, no walls inside. Its position is just two numbers, x from left to right and y from bottom to top, each between 0 and 1. The rules stay the same: plus 1 on the step that lands inside the cheese circle, minus 1 inside the cat’s circle, and either ends the walk. gamma (gamma) is still 0.9.

funcapprox:2.t: Moves on bumpy grass. Pip still has four moves: up, right, down, left. A move carries it 0.15 that way, plus a small random wobble from the uneven grass. Three moves right from the start (0.10, 0.10) landed at (0.25, 0.11), then (0.39, 0.09), then (0.53, 0.08). The fence round the meadow stops Pip at the edge.

funcapprox:3.t: Pip’s habit. Like in the values reel, Pip follows a fixed habit. Below 0.7 high, it goes up. Higher than that, it steps toward the cheese along whichever gap is bigger, sideways or up and down. One move in five goes in a random direction instead. Here is walk 1. It took 10 moves; move 4 was a random one. We want this habit’s values: from each spot, the expected discounted return.

funcapprox:4.t: A notebook for every spot?. In the maze, Pip kept one number per cell, and every cell was visited again and again. Here positions are real numbers and the wobble is random, so every landing spot is new. We let Pip take 10,000 walks, from walk 2 on each starting at a random spot. It stood on 66,674 spots and, apart from being squeezed into a fence corner, never on exactly the same spot twice. A notebook would fill a page per spot and never read it again.

funcapprox:5.t: Chop it into squares?. We could cut the meadow into squares and keep one number per square. With 16 by 16 squares that is 256 numbers, and each learns only from its own visits. Worse, two neighbouring squares are almost the same place, yet what one learns teaches the other nothing. Finer squares mean more numbers and fewer visits each; coarser ones blur everything together.

funcapprox:6.t: Nearby spots, similar values. Here are the habit’s true values, colour by colour: gold for good, rose for bad, stronger for bigger. We worked them out with 100 test walks from the middle of each square, something Pip cannot do. It must learn them. Notice the dark band below the cat: from there the habit climbs straight into it. minus 0.69 at (0.60, 0.30). Mostly, though, spots close together have similar values.

funcapprox:7.t: Four measurements. So instead of naming the spot, Pip describes it with a few measurements, called features: its x, its y, its distance to the cheese and its distance to the cat. At the start these are 0.10, 0.10, 1.06 and 0.71. Spots that are close have similar measurements, so a rule built on them treats them alike. That is generalisation.

funcapprox:8.t: A recipe with five knobs. The simplest rule: multiply each measurement by its own number and add them up, plus a fixed amount b. Those five numbers are weights, the knobs Pip can turn. This kind of rule is called a linear recipe. All five knobs start at 0, so the recipe guesses 0 everywhere. One recipe gives a guess for every spot on the meadow, even spots Pip has never visited.

funcapprox:9.t: Nudging the knobs. Same T D target as before: reward plus 0.9 times the guess where Pip landed, or just the reward if the walk ended. At the end of walk 1, Pip stepped from (0.81, 0.75) into the cheese: target 1, guess 0, error 1. The nudge: each knob moves by step size times error times its measurement (b counts as measurement 1). With step size 0.05, b becomes 0.050. This is a gradient step on the squared error, (target minus guess) squared, if we pretend the target is a fixed number: knobs with bigger measurements sway the guess more, so they move more.

funcapprox:10.t: One nudge moved every spot. That single nudge changed the guess everywhere. The spot Pip left now guesses 0.115. The start, far away, now guesses 0.073, and the spot below the cat 0.093, though nothing happened there. This sharing is the whole point, and its danger: every lesson about one spot spills onto all the others.

funcapprox:11.t: Training the recipe. Now train on all 10,000 walks; the random starts make sure the whole meadow gets visited. Pip nudges after every move, and the step size shrinks from 0.05 to 0.003 by the end, so late walks only fine-tune. The chart shows the average gap between the recipe’s guess and the true value, averaged over the 240 grass squares. It drops from 0.47 to 0.21, mostly in the first few hundred walks, then wobbles as each walk tugs the shared knobs.

funcapprox:12.t: What a straight recipe can’t draw. Left: the true values. Right: the trained recipe. It gets the big picture: good near the cheese, poor far away. But the band below the cat is missing: at (0.60, 0.30) the truth is minus 0.69, the recipe says 0.06. Why? The recipe only adds up measurements. A dip only where Pip is near the cat’s x and below it needs measurements to combine, and adding can’t do “and”.

funcapprox:13.t: A tiny neural network. Pip could hand-make a measurement for that band, but only by knowing the answer already. Instead: a tiny neural network. The four measurements, scaled to between minus 1 and 1, feed 8 hidden units; each adds them up with its own weights and squashes the sum to between minus 1 and 1. The output adds up the hidden units with more weights: the guess. Lines are weights: gold positive, rose negative, thicker for bigger. 49 knobs, all starting small and random. Fed the start’s measurements, the dots light up and it guesses 0.19.

funcapprox:14.t: Same nudge, through the network. Same target rule. Each knob moves by step size times error times how much turning that knob would change this guess. For the recipe, that amount was simply the measurement. In a network it is worked out layer by layer, from the output back: backpropagation. At the end of walk 1, the network guessed 0.175 at that spot beside the cheese, so the error is 1 minus 0.175 equals 0.825. After one nudge with step size 0.1, it guesses 0.366.

funcapprox:15.t: The network learns the shadow. The same 10,000 walks, now nudging the network, step size 0.1 shrinking to 0.005. Blue is its average gap, gold the recipe’s. The network ends at 0.14 against 0.21. The band below the cat appears: at (0.60, 0.30) the network says minus 0.35, the truth minus 0.69. But it is too wide: at (0.41, 0.34), truly worth 0.23, it says minus 0.16.

funcapprox:16.t: The catch: shared knobs. Walk 56 was a single move into the cheese: one nudge at one spot, raising it by 0.064. The start, far away, moved too, by plus 0.014. And T D targets come from the same knobs, so every nudge also moves the targets. Shared knobs, guesses learned from guesses, and data from a different policy together can make learning blow up: Sutton and Barto’s deadly triad. Here the third was missing: Pip learned about the very habit it followed, and learning stayed calm.

funcapprox:17.t: Your turn. Tap a spot on the meadow to teach Pip “this spot is worth 1”: 5 nudges there, step size 0.05, starting from the trained model. Watch which other spots change with it. Slide to switch between the linear recipe and the network. The recipe moves near and far spots about equally. The network moves nearby spots more, but far ones too: never only the spot you tapped.

funcapprox:18.t: Where you’ve seen this. In 1992 Gerald Tesauro’s T D-Gammon learned backgammon with exactly this mix: a neural network for the values of board positions, trained with T D targets from games against itself. Later versions played close to the best human players. Today almost every large R L system uses a network instead of a table. The next reel, D Q N, does it for Q-values and learns Atari games from the screen.

funcapprox:19.t: Recap. When states are too many, or never repeat, a table cannot work. Function approximation describes a state with features and learns a function with a few knobs that gives a guess for any state. Learning nudges the knobs toward T D targets, a gradient step. Because the knobs are shared, every lesson generalises to similar states, and sometimes spills where it should not.

dqn:0.t: Deep Q-Network (D Q N). Q-learning plus a neural network: superhuman Atari from pixels.

dqn:1.t: From values to choices. In the last reel, a tiny network learned the values of Pip’s habit on the meadow. But values of a fixed habit don’t tell Pip how to do better. For that, the maze had Q-learning: a number Q for every spot and move, “how good is this move here, if I play well afterwards”. On the meadow, with no two spots alike, a table of Q-values is as impossible as a table of values.

dqn:2.t: Q-learning, remembered. After each move, Q-learning nudges the number for the move just made toward a target: the reward plus 0.9 times the largest Q at the landing spot, or just the reward if the walk ended. Taking the largest means: assume Pip plays its best from there on. And Pip acts epsilon-greedy (epsilon-greedy): one move in five at random, to keep exploring; otherwise the move with the largest Q.

dqn:3.t: One output per move. The fix is the one from the last reel: a network. This one has four outputs, one Q-value per move: up, right, down, left. Feed in Pip’s four measurements and one pass gives all four Q-values at once. That is a Deep Q-Network, or D Q N. Its 76 knobs start random. At the start spot it says: up minus 0.28, right 0.61, down 0.04, left 0.10. Pure noise, for now.

dqn:4.t: The simple way: learn as you go. First try: after every move, one nudge on the output for the move just made, as in the maze. Move 37 was a step left, chosen because its untrained numbers made left look best, by a hair: 0.113 against 0.111 for right. It went from (0.86, 0.63) into the cat: target minus 1. One nudge took “left” from 0.113 to 0.101. Each nudge moves every knob by only about 0.003, so one bad moment cannot wipe out everything. The other outputs share the knobs, so they moved a little too.

dqn:5.t: It flounders. Pip learns this way for 8,000 moves, walks starting at random spots. Every 250 moves we test it from 30 fixed spots, the black dots, following its largest Q with no random moves. The chart counts walks that reach the cheese. It hardly learns. In 28 of the 32 tests, at most 1 of the 30 walks reaches the cheese. Only the very last test, after 8,000 moves, scores 27: one good test after 31 poor ones is nothing to rely on.

dqn:6.t: Problem 1: a target that runs away. Why? Unlike a table, here the target is computed by the same network being nudged, at a spot only 0.15 away. Nudge the guess up, and the target goes up too. In this run the target moved, on the median, 0.90 times as far as the guess, the same way 84 percent of the time. So a nudge closes only a sliver of the gap: here from 0.025 to 0.024. The target network reel freezes the targets; on this meadow that mostly steadies the numbers. The next problem matters more.

dqn:7.t: Problem 2: one moment at a time. Second problem: the moves arrive in order. The rose dots are 60 moves in a row, early in the run we will see next: a few walks, each hugging one patch or one fence. So the network bends toward one patch and drifts elsewhere, then the next walk bends it somewhere else. Picking old moves at random from a memory, the blue dots, would mix every part of the meadow into each lesson. That is experience replay, with its own reel.

dqn:8.t: D Q N’s two fixes. DeepMind’s D Q N adds two things. A replay memory keeps the last 2000 moves. After every move, Pip draws 32 of them at random, a batch that may include the newest, and makes one nudge using the average of their 32 errors. A target network, a frozen copy, computes the targets; it is refreshed every 100 nudges, so every 100 moves. Each fix gets its own reel. Here we switch both on and run the same meadow again.

dqn:9.t: Now it learns. The same 8,000 moves of experience, the same dice. Blue is D Q N, rose the simple version. D Q N first reaches the cheese in 28 or more of the 30 tests after 4,250 moves, and after 8,000 it gets all 30. Not a fair race in effort, though: each D Q N nudge averages 32 moves, each simple nudge one. The replay reel runs a fair race, and the memory still wins clearly. Over 12 seeds D Q N usually ended near 30, the simple version mostly far lower.

dqn:10.t: What the network learned. Here is the trained network’s best move on a grid of spots, with its largest Q-value as the colour. From the bottom left it heads up the side and along the top; from the right it climbs straight up. Mostly it goes around the cat, but 10 of the 40 grid spots directly below the cat still point up, into it. From the start the teal walk takes 12 moves; over 200 different wobbles it averages 11.9. Five up and five right would take about 10, so it is good but not the best. Nobody told it the rules: it learned from moves and rewards alone.

dqn:11.t: Inside the network. Feed in the start spot. The hidden units light up, and the four outputs read: up 0.39, right 0.32, down 0.31, left 0.34. Pip picks up. These are estimates, and rough ones. The 12-move walk it actually takes is worth 0.9 to the power 11, about 0.31, less than its 0.39. And left, a wasted bump into the fence, scores above right, a good first move. The network ranks the best move correctly here, but its numbers are only roughly right.

dqn:12.t: Your turn. Tap a spot on the meadow to drop Pip there. It walks by its network’s largest Q, with no random moves. Teal ends at the cheese, rose at the cat, grey runs out of moves. Slide to pick how long D Q N had trained. Early networks wander, bump the fence or walk into the cat; later ones take Pip round the cat to the cheese from almost anywhere.

dqn:13.t: Atari, from pixels. D Q N made its name on Atari video games. In 2013 Volodymyr Mnih and colleagues at DeepMind trained it on seven games. In 2015, in the journal Nature, they ran one D Q N, with the same network and settings, on 49 games, learning from the screen pixels and the score alone. Instead of four measurements, the input was the last four frames, so the network could see motion; the outputs were one Q-value per joystick action.

dqn:14.t: What it did, and didn’t. D Q N reached at least three quarters of a professional human tester’s score on 29 of the 49 games, and beat earlier learning methods on most of them. It failed where rewards are rare, like Montezuma’s Revenge, where random moves almost never score. It needed tens of millions of frames per game, far more practice than a person. Later reels show replay, target networks and their successors.

dqn:15.t: Recap. D Q N is Q-learning with a neural network: Pip’s measurements in, one Q-value per move out, epsilon-greedy to act, and nudges toward reward plus 0.9 times the largest Q at the landing spot. Done naively, the targets run away and the lessons come one corner at a time. Replay memory and a target network made it learn, here on the meadow and on 49 Atari games.

replay:0.t: Experience Replay. Store experiences, then learn from random old memories.

replay:1.t: Pip’s network, again. In the D Q N reel, the simple version floundered until two fixes were switched on: a replay memory and a frozen copy for the targets. This reel takes apart the first. To see it alone, the frozen copy stays off: targets come from the network being trained. Same network as before: four measurements in, one Q-value per move out. Walks start at random spots, last at most 60 moves, and one move in five is random.

replay:2.t: Learning on the go. The simplest plan: learn from experience in the order it comes. Each move gives one experience, written here as a card: where Pip stood, the move, the reward, and where it landed or that the walk ended. That is all a target needs. For a fair comparison later, each update learns from 32 cards: the latest 32 moves. Then Pip moves, and the handful slides on by one card, so each card is used in 32 updates in a row.

replay:3.t: Near-duplicates. Now look at the latest 32 cards on the meadow. For a while Pip has stayed in the top-left corner: x from 0.00 to 0.17, y from 0.57 to 1.00. 15 of the 32 moves bumped the fence; when this stretch began, the network’s favourite move at all 32 spots was left, toward it. Experiences that follow one another are alike: they are correlated. The network gets nearly the same lesson 32 times.

replay:4.t: Old lessons get overwritten. Meanwhile watch the spot just below the cheese, ringed. One move up is the cheese, so its true value is about 1; the network said 0.80. Pip never comes near it, yet in 96 moves it falls to 0.29. Every spot shares the same 76 knobs: fitting the corner also moves the numbers by the cheese, and no card reminds the network. Old lessons get overwritten. The moving target is not the main cause: with the frozen copy on, in run 2, the same value slid from 0.96 to 0.40 in 80 moves.

replay:5.t: A shoebox of cards. The fix is experience replay. Every experience card goes into a shoebox, the replay memory, and stays there for a while. This box keeps the latest 2000 cards; when it is full, the oldest card is thrown out. So the box holds moves from many walks, all over the meadow.

replay:6.t: A random handful. Before each update, Pip draws 32 cards from the box at random: a random handful, called a minibatch (the D Q N reel’s 32 picked at random). One gradient step then fits all 32 at once, on average. This handful comes from all over the meadow. On average over the run, two cards in a random handful lie 0.60 apart; two of the latest 32 only 0.31.

replay:7.t: A fair race. Let both versions train, same seeds, 8000 moves each. Each update uses 32 cards and one gradient step of the same size. The only difference is which 32: the latest ones, or a random handful from the box. Every 500 moves we test the network: from 30 fixed test spots, Pip follows its largest Q-value, no random moves. The chart counts the spots from which it reaches the cheese, out of 30.

replay:8.t: The race. Four training runs of each version: thin lines are single runs, thick lines their average. Teal learns from random handfuls; orange from the latest 32. The single runs jump a lot. After 8000 moves, replay reaches the cheese from 25.8 of the 30 spots on average, the latest 32 from 7.8. Replay ended ahead in 3 of the 4 runs, and its average is ahead at every test. Same amount of work; only the choice of cards differs.

replay:9.t: Why the shuffle helps. A random handful is a fair sample of the whole meadow, so each step nudges the numbers everywhere a little, instead of bending them toward one corner. Below the cheese, over the last 4000 moves, the replay run swings by about 0.09; the latest-32 run by 0.27. Both versions use each card about 32 times; replay just spreads those uses over 2000 moves, mixed with other cards, instead of 32 updates in a row.

replay:10.t: Two maps. Here are the two networks of run 1 after 8000 moves, as maps of their largest Q-value: left with replay, right from the latest 32. Gold means a good spot, rose a bad one. From the start, following its largest Q-value, the replay Pip reaches the cheese in 13 moves, along the bottom and up the right side; the route up the left side, as in the D Q N reel, is about as long. The other one reaches the cheese in 45 moves.

replay:11.t: Old cards, old habits. The cards in the box were made by an older Pip, with older Q-values and older habits. For D Q N that is fine: its target asks what the best move from the landing spot is worth, whichever habit made the card, as in Q-learning. Any card gives a fair target. Methods that learn about the habit Pip follows right now, like SARSA, would be learning about a Pip that no longer exists. They cannot simply reuse old cards.

replay:12.t: What about the deadly triad?. The funcapprox reel warned: a network, plus targets built from guesses, plus data from another habit can blow up. Replay has all three: old cards come from older Pips. Nothing guarantees safety, but here it stayed calm. A likely reason: the box holds only the latest 2000 moves, so its cards come from Pips much like today’s. The frozen copy of the next reel adds more safety.

replay:13.t: Your turn. Drag the memory size (four runs each). With 32 cards even a random handful is a near-duplicate; a few hundred already work much better. Keeping all 8000 was worse here (13.8 against 25.8). Every card gives a fair target, but the box decides which spots get lessons. Likely: most cards then come from early walks, in places today’s Pip rarely visits.

replay:14.t: Where it came from. Long-Ji Lin proposed experience replay in 1992. D Q N made it famous in 2015: its memory held the latest one million moves, and each update used a random handful of 32. Without replay, D Q N’s Breakout score dropped from about 317 to about 10. One upgrade, prioritised replay (Schaul and others, 2016), draws the surprising cards, those with a big T D error, more often.

replay:15.t: Recap. Moves that follow each other are near-duplicates, and fitting the latest ones bends the shared knobs toward one corner, overwriting old lessons. Experience replay keeps the latest moves as cards in a memory and learns from random handfuls: varied, fair samples of the whole meadow, each card reused many times.

targetnet:0.t: Target Networks. Stop chasing your own tail: freeze the target for a while.

targetnet:1.t: Where replay left off. The D Q N reel spotted the problem: the target is computed by the same network that is being nudged, so it moves with the guess. Here Pip keeps the replay memory from the last reel, and we look at that chase up close. A card’s target is the reward plus 0.9 times the largest Q-value at the spot where Pip landed. And who supplies that Q-value? The very network being trained.

targetnet:2.t: One card, many steps. To see what that does, try an experiment. Take Pip’s network after 3000 moves of training and one card: from the spot (0.50, 0.20) Pip moved right and landed at (0.65, 0.20), reward 0. The network says this move is worth minus 0.04, and its target is 0 plus 0.9 times the best Q-value at the landing spot equals 0.00. Now take 200 small gradient steps on this one card and watch both numbers.

targetnet:3.t: Chasing your own shadow. Gold is the move’s Q-value, teal the target. Each step pulls gold toward teal, but teal moves too: after 200 steps gold is 0.14 and the target has climbed to 0.15, levelling off. No new information came in: whatever the true value is, this climb came from the chase alone. Why? The landing spot is close by and shares the same 76 knobs. Raising the value here also raises it there, so the target runs ahead, like chasing your own shadow.

targetnet:4.t: Freeze a copy. The fix: keep a second network, a frozen copy of Pip’s network, used only to compute targets. It is called the target network. Training changes the live network; the copy stays as it was. Now the target is reward plus 0.9 times the largest Q-value the copy gives at the landing spot.

targetnet:5.t: The chase stops. Same card, same 200 steps, but the target comes from the frozen copy. Teal stays at 0.00, and gold reaches it, to within 0.01, after 27 steps, then stays there. With the target held still, each update solves an ordinary fitting problem: hit a fixed number.

targetnet:6.t: Refresh every N updates. A copy frozen forever would never learn. So every N updates the live network’s knobs are copied into it. Here N equals 50: the target holds still, gold catches up, then the target jumps. With one card nothing anchors the numbers, so the drift remains, only slower: 0.07 after 200 steps instead of 0.14. The copy slows the loop; it does not remove it. In real training, the other cards bring real information.

targetnet:7.t: Back to real training. Now the real thing: full training, 8000 moves with replay, once with targets from the live network and once with a copy refreshed every 100 updates. Same seeds. The chart follows one number during training: the largest Q-value at Pip’s start spot, bottom left. Across: moves of experience, 0 to 8000. Up: that Q-value. Orange: live targets. Teal: with the copy. At move 0 the number comes from random knobs.

targetnet:8.t: Calmer numbers. Live targets jitter. Measure the jumps: the average size of the change between readings 100 moves apart, over moves 4000 to 8000, four runs each: 0.05 with live targets, 0.02 with the copy. Cheese from 30 test spots after 8000 moves: 25.8 against 28.3. So in this meadow replay did most of the work; the copy mainly steadies the numbers and adds a little.

targetnet:9.t: Your turn. Drag N, the number of updates between refreshes of the copy (four runs each; “none” means live targets). Too often, and the chase is back. Too rarely, and the targets go stale: N equals 1000 gives only 7 refreshes in the run, the calmest numbers (jumps 0.01), but only 16.0 of 30 spots reach the cheese. N equals 100 balances the two here.

targetnet:10.t: Where it’s used. D Q N (2015) used a target network refreshed every 10,000 updates. Without it, still with replay, its Breakout score fell from about 317 to about 241. Many later methods, like D D P G and sack, use soft updates instead: after every update the copy moves a tiny fraction, such as half a percent, toward the live network, so the target drifts smoothly.

targetnet:11.t: Recap. When a network computes its own targets, every update moves the target it chases: the numbers can drift and wobble. A target network, a frozen copy refreshed every N updates, holds the targets still, so each stretch of training is a fixed fitting problem. Refresh too rarely and learning slows.

doubledqn:0.t: Double D Q N. Taking a max over noisy guesses is too optimistic.

doubledqn:1.t: The max in the target. Pip now trains the full D Q N: replay memory, plus the frozen copy refreshed every 100 updates. A card’s target is the reward plus 0.9 times the largest of the copy’s four Q-values at the landing spot. That word “largest” hides a problem. To see it, leave the meadow for a moment and play with plain numbers.

doubledqn:2.t: Four moves worth nothing. Imagine a spot where all four moves are truly worth exactly 0. Pip does not know that; its guesses are 0 plus a bell-shaped random error, typically about 0.1 either way. One round of guesses: plus 0.15, minus 0.10, plus 0.07, plus 0.11. The largest guess is plus 0.15. If the target uses the largest, it says this spot is worth plus 0.15, not 0.

doubledqn:3.t: Roll again. New round, new errors. Each yellow box is that round’s largest guess. A single guess is right on average: over 1000 rounds, the guesses for “up” average 0.00. But the largest guess was above 0 in 945 of 1000 rounds, and it averaged plus 0.10. The max keeps picking the lucky errors. An error that leans the same way every time is a bias: here an overestimation bias.

doubledqn:4.t: It spreads backwards. In Q-learning and D Q N the target is reward plus 0.9 times the largest Q-value at the landing spot. On the meadow those Q-values are noisy guesses: the network is still wrong here and there, and the wobble adds chance. So the target leans high. And it does not stay there. The spot one move earlier learns from that inflated number, the spot before learns from that one, and so on: the optimism travels back along Pip’s routes.

doubledqn:5.t: Two opinions. The fix needs two independent sets of guesses, A and B. Let A choose the move: the one with A’s largest guess. Then let B score that move, with B’s guess for it. B’s error has nothing to do with A’s, so B’s number is just 0 plus a fresh random error: no longer lucky on purpose.

doubledqn:6.t: Back to zero. Over the same 1000 rounds, the largest guess averaged plus 0.10. Choosing with A and scoring with B averaged 0.00: the bias is gone. This trick is called Double Q-learning. Hado van Hasselt proposed it in 2010 for tables of Q-values, keeping two tables and letting each pick moves for the other.

doubledqn:7.t: D Q N already has two. D Q N already keeps two networks: the live one and the frozen copy. Double D Q N (van Hasselt, Guez and Silver, 2015) uses them as A and B: at the landing spot the live network chooses the move, the copy scores it. Nothing else changes. But the copy is the live network from at most 100 updates ago, so their errors are only partly independent. The trick cuts the bias; it need not remove it.

doubledqn:8.t: One real card. A real landing spot: the corner (0.05, 0.05), Double D Q N run, after 7050 moves. The copy’s largest Q-value is “up”, 0.28; the live network prefers “down”, a bump into the fence. So D Q N would use 0.28, Double D Q N the copy’s “down”, 0.16. Who is right? Walking a simple route from here, up the left side and along the top, “up” first is worth about 0.30, “down” first about 0.26. So here D Q N was about right and Double D Q N underestimates: the trick can err low too.

doubledqn:9.t: Estimates against reality. Does it matter in the meadow? Measure it. At each of the 30 test spots, compare the network’s largest Q-value, its estimate, with what Pip really gets: the average discounted return of 5 walks from there following its largest Q-values.
