The chart shows estimate minus reality, averaged over the spots and over 8 runs, so the chance in single walks mostly averages out. Above 0 means too optimistic.

doubledqn:10.t: The bias shrinks. Eight training runs of each, averaged. Orange, D Q N: 0.23 too high after 1000 moves, 0.09 on average over the eight checks. Teal, Double D Q N: 0.11 at first, then near 0, sometimes below: 0.01 on average. The gap is mostly early: by 8000 moves both are 0.03 too high. Counting misses either way, Double D Q N is off by 0.04, D Q N by 0.09. Cheese reached: 26.6 and 25.9 of 30 spots (8 runs here).

doubledqn:11.t: Your turn. Back to the plain numbers. Drag the number of moves, all truly worth 0, and see a thousand rounds. More moves give the max more chances to catch a lucky error: with 2 moves the largest guess averages plus 0.06, with 16 it averages plus 0.18. Choosing with A and scoring with B stays near 0 every time.

doubledqn:12.t: Where it’s used. Van Hasselt, Guez and Silver found that D Q N’s value estimates on several Atari games were far above the scores it really earned. Double D Q N brought them down and played better on many games. The same worry shaped later methods. T D 3 (2018) keeps two critics and trusts the smaller of their two guesses. Rainbow (2017) bundles Double D Q N with other upgrades.

doubledqn:13.t: Recap. The largest of several noisy guesses is too high on average. D Q N’s target takes exactly such a max, so its numbers lean optimistic, and the optimism spreads backwards. Double D Q N lets the live network choose the move and the frozen copy score it. Their errors are only partly shared, so most lucky high guesses stop getting in for free.

pg:0.t: Policy Gradient Methods. Skip the values: directly tweak the policy to win more.

pg:1.t: Two ways to get better. In the Monte Carlo and Q-learning reels, Pip learned a number for every move, Q, and then mostly picked the move with the biggest number, with a few random moves. Values first, choices second. This reel tries the other way round. Pip keeps its choices themselves, as chances, and adjusts them directly: moves that led to good outcomes become more likely. These are policy gradient methods.

pg:2.t: The door room. To see the idea clearly, start with one decision. Pip stands in a room with three doors, A, B and C. It picks one and walks through, and that ends the episode. Behind each door a crumb appears with a hidden chance, worth reward 1; otherwise the reward is 0. Pip does not know the chances. The question marks on the doors stand for them.

pg:3.t: A policy made of chances. Pip’s policy is a chance for each door, drawn as a pie. At first it is a third each: Pip has no idea which door is best, so it tries all of them. This is a stochastic policy from the policies reel, pi of a given s. Here there is only one situation, the room, so the pie is the whole policy.

pg:4.t: Turn scores into chances. Pip keeps one preference number per door, any number, positive or negative. To turn them into chances it raises e, about 2.72, to the power of each preference, then divides each by their total. This recipe is called softmax. All preferences 0: e to the 0 is 1 for each door, the total is 3, so a third each. Raise C’s preference to 1: C gets 2.72, the total is 4.72, and C’s chance becomes 0.58.

pg:5.t: Why preferences?. Pip can push any preference up or down freely, and softmax always returns proper chances: all above 0 and adding up to 1. So no move ever gets chance exactly 0: Pip keeps trying every door now and then, which helps it explore, but it can only approach “always C”, never reach it. Only the differences matter. Add 1 to every preference, from 0, 0, 1 to 1, 1, 2, and the chances stay 0.21, 0.21, 0.58.

pg:6.t: How good is a policy?. Let us peek at the hidden chances: A 0.2, B 0.5, C 0.8. Pip still does not know them; we use them to score Pip’s policy. The expected return of a policy is its average reward per episode: for each door, Pip’s chance of picking it times the crumb chance behind it, added up. With a third each: 0.2 plus 0.5 plus 0.8, divided by 3, gives 0.50. Always picking C would give 0.8.

pg:7.t: Which way is uphill?. Now the key question: which way should Pip nudge each preference to raise the expected return? The answer is the gradient, as in machine learning, but we climb instead of descend. The chart keeps A and B at 0. Along the bottom: C’s preference. Up the side: expected return. At 0 the curve rises with slope 0.10: raise C’s preference a little, and the return goes up about 0.10 times as much. Then the dot steps uphill.

pg:8.t: Every preference at once. The gradient has one entry per preference. For softmax it comes out simple: Pip’s chance of a door times how much that door beats the current expected return. A: 0.33 times (0.2 minus 0.5) equals minus 0.10. B: 0, it matches the average, for now. C: plus 0.10. Why? Raising C’s preference grows C’s chance and takes a little from A and B. Count gains minus losses, each times its crumb chance, and what remains is C’s chance times (0.8 minus 0.5).

pg:9.t: Climbing, nudge by nudge. Pip adds the gradient times a step size alpha (alpha) equals 2 to the preferences, then works out the new gradient, and repeats. The gradient only describes the slope right where Pip stands, so it takes many small steps. After 5 nudges the expected return is 0.67, after 20 it is 0.78, and C’s chance has grown to 0.94. The gains shrink as Pip nears the best possible 0.8.

pg:10.t: Small nudges, small changes. Why chances? First, they change smoothly. Suppose Pip had guesses A 0.2, B 0.51, C 0.49 and always picked the biggest. Move B and C by 0.02 each, to 0.49 and 0.51, and its choice flips completely from B to C. With preferences A 0, B 0.01, C minus 0.01, moving B and C by 0.02 each only shifts the chances from B 0.34, C 0.33 to B 0.33, C 0.34. Learning becomes a gentle slide, not sudden jumps.

pg:11.t: Any strength you like. Second, actions need not be a short list. Suppose Pip must jump a gap with any strength it likes. A table of guesses would need an entry for every possible strength. A policy can instead be a bell curve over strengths, set by two numbers: its centre mu (mu) and its spread sigma (sigma). The same idea applies: nudge mu toward strengths that landed better, and sigma can be learned too. Later reels show exactly how.

pg:12.t: Random on purpose. Third, some problems need a random policy. In rock, paper, scissors, any fixed choice gets beaten once the opponent spots it; the best play is a third each. This matters against opponents that adapt, or when Pip cannot see everything; in the fixed maze one move per cell is enough. Picking the biggest guess, even with epsilon-greedy’s random moves, cannot learn a mix like a third each. A policy of chances can.

pg:13.t: Back in the maze. The same idea works in Pip’s maze. Each cell gets its own four preferences, one per move, and its own softmax. With 16 cells that is 64 numbers. In each cell the four arrows show the chances: the longer the arrow, the more likely the move. All preferences start at 0, so every arrow is a quarter, the random Pip from the first reel. Raise one preference, and its arrow grows.

pg:14.t: The catch. Everything so far used the hidden crumb chances. The gradient needed them, and Pip does not have them. In the maze it would also need the rulebook, because where each move leads decides which rewards follow. So Pip must estimate the gradient from its own tries: pick a door, see what happens, nudge. That is the next reel, REINFORCE. Its nudges are noisy, which is the theme of the reels after it.

pg:15.t: Your turn. Tap a door to raise its preference by 0.5. Tap the floor to reset. Watch the chances, the expected return, and the gradient arrows telling you which way is uphill. Try raising A a few times, then C. Or tap all three doors once each: the chances do not change.

pg:16.t: Where it is used. Policy gradient methods train controllers for simulated and real robots, where actions are motor strengths. P P O, a policy gradient method from 2017, trained OpenAI Five, which beat the Dota 2 world champions in 2019. AlphaGo’s policy network was improved by policy gradient in self-play, and P P O-style training is used to fine-tune chatbots from human feedback.

pg:17.t: Recap. A policy gradient method keeps the policy itself as adjustable numbers and nudges them to raise the expected return. Softmax turns preferences into chances. The gradient says which way to nudge each preference: here, toward doors that beat the current average. Chances change smoothly, handle any action, and can stay random on purpose.

reinforce:0.t: REINFORCE. The simplest policy gradient: weight actions by the episode’s return.

reinforce:1.t: Learning from tries. In the last reel, Pip climbed toward the best door using the exact gradient. But that needed the hidden crumb chances, which Pip does not have. REINFORCE fixes this. Pip simply tries: it picks a door with its current chances, sees what happens, and nudges its preferences. No hidden chances, no rulebook, only its own experience.

reinforce:2.t: One try. All preferences start at 0, so each door has chance 0.33. Pip rolls its dice and picks door C. A crumb appears: reward 1. The idea is simple: an action followed by a good return becomes more likely. So C’s preference goes up, and the other two go down a little.

reinforce:3.t: The nudge, exactly. Each preference moves by step size alpha (alpha) times return times a factor. For the chosen door the factor is 1 minus its chance: 1 minus 0.33 equals 0.67. For every other door it is minus its chance, minus 0.33. With alpha equals 0.5 and return 1: C gets plus 0.33, A and B minus 0.17. Had the reward been 0, nothing would change at all.

reinforce:4.t: How surprising was the choice?. That factor is the gradient of the log-probability, the log of the chosen door’s chance. The nudge is scaled by the return and by how surprising the choice was. A door picked with chance 0.9 gets a factor of only 0.1; one picked with chance 0.1 gets 0.9. Why? Likely doors get picked, and nudged, often; rare doors seldom, so each nudge counts more. The card shows the division by the chance exactly cancels how often a door is picked.

reinforce:5.t: On average, uphill. One try is a rough guess. Here Pip tries 2,000 times without changing its chances, and we average reward times factor for each door. Each line is a running average; the dashed lines are the exact gradient from the last reel: minus 0.10, 0 and plus 0.10. After 2,000 tries the averages are minus 0.10, 0 and 0.10. REINFORCE’s nudges are noisy, but on average they point uphill.

reinforce:6.t: A whole walk. Now the maze: dry floor, plus 1 onto the cheese, minus 1 onto the cat, both end the walk, gamma (gamma) 0.9. All preferences start at 0. REINFORCE waits for the walk to finish, like Monte Carlo, and credits every move with the return that followed it, since a move cannot change earlier rewards. Textbook REINFORCE also shrinks late moves’ nudges by 0.9 per step since the start; like most implementations, we leave that out.

reinforce:7.t: Walk 1. Walk 1 takes 15 moves. Pip wanders, bumps into walls 6 times, and finally steps up from the cell below the cat onto the cat: reward minus 1. The walk is over, so every move now gets its return: minus 1 for the last one, minus 0.90 for the one before, and so on back to minus 0.23 for Pip’s first move. The labels show the return of the last move made in each cell.

reinforce:8.t: Every move pushed down. Now the nudges. Each move’s preference changes by alpha times its return times its factor, with alpha equals 0.2. All returns were negative, so every move Pip made became less likely. Fair for the last move, up into the cat: in that cell its chance drops from 0.25 to 0.21. But Pip’s first move, up from the start, was a fine move. Its chance drops too, to 0.24, punished only because this walk happened to end badly.

reinforce:9.t: The first cheese. Walk 5 is the first to reach the cheese, after 39 moves. The last move gets return 1, but Pip’s first move only 0.02: the cheese was too many steps away to matter much. So learning starts near the cheese, where returns are big, and spreads back toward the start as walks get shorter.

reinforce:10.t: 300 walks. A new chart. Along the bottom: walk number. Up the side: that walk’s return from the start. Dots: gold for cheese, rose for cat. Long walks score near 0, so bottom ticks also mark cat walks, rose, and stopped walks, grey. The line averages the last 25 walks. Early walks are long and score near 0. Then the returns climb: the average of the last 25 walks reaches 0.50, near the best possible 0.53.

reinforce:11.t: What Pip learned. After 300 walks, following the biggest arrow from the start gives a route of 7 moves to the cheese, the shortest possible. At the start, “up” now has chance 0.87. Along the way, 23 walks ended on the cat and 24 were stopped at 100 moves. Stopped walks scored 0 and changed nothing. Off the route, cells were rarely visited, so their arrows stay rough.

reinforce:12.t: Same recipe, other dice. Run REINFORCE again with different dice. The thin lines are five runs, each the average of its last 25 walks. Around walk 100 they range from 0.13 to 0.33: some runs learn early, some late. The thick line averages 100 runs. It climbs smoothly, to 0.45 over the last 25 walks. A single run is a very noisy version of it.

reinforce:13.t: Why so noisy?. Each walk’s luck colours every move in it. One random detour into the cat punishes all the good moves before it, as walk 1 showed; one lucky walk rewards the bumps along the way. The bars count Pip’s 300 walks by their return from the start, from minus 0.53 to 0.53. Every nudge is scaled by returns like these, so the nudges swing as widely. This is high variance: right on average, but each single estimate jumps around. The next reel calms it.

reinforce:14.t: Your turn. Drag the step size alpha. Each setting reruns 100 runs of 300 walks with the same dice. The thick line is their average return; the thin lines are runs 1 to 5. Small alpha learns slowly but steadily. Big alpha learns faster at first, but watch the count of runs that end up stuck.

reinforce:15.t: Too big a step. With alpha equals 1, 8 of 100 runs get stuck. In run 15, the early walks hit the cat 7 times and never the cheese. The big pushes left most big arrows pointing left or down, away from the cheese. From walk 52 on, all 249 walks hit the 100-move stop: return 0, no nudge. No chance is exactly 0, so an ending could still come, but here it practically never does. Big steps on noisy estimates can wreck a policy.

reinforce:16.t: Where it is used. Ronald Williams published REINFORCE in 1992. AlphaGo, described in 2016, improved its policy network this way: games against earlier versions of itself, with each move nudged by whether the game was won or lost. REINFORCE-style updates are still used today, for example to fine-tune language models on a reward score, usually together with the noise-calming tricks of the next reels.

reinforce:17.t: Recap. REINFORCE learns a policy from complete episodes. After each one, every action’s log-probability is nudged by step size times the return that followed it. Rare choices get bigger nudges, so on average the nudges follow the true gradient. But one episode’s luck colours every action, so single updates are noisy, and big steps can wreck the policy.

baseline:0.t: Baselines  and  Advantage. Not “was it good?” but “was it better than usual?”

baseline:1.t: A crumb behind the worst door. Back in the door room with plain REINFORCE, 14 picks into a run. B’s crumbs have made B the favourite, though C is better. Now Pip opens door A, the worst door, and a crumb appears: reward 1. So A becomes more likely, though it pays only 2 times in 10. An empty door gives reward 0: no change. A picked door is pushed up or left alone; it loses chance only slowly, when other doors pay.

baseline:2.t: Better than usual?. Think of grading on a curve. A score of 75 is great if the class usually gets 60, and poor if it usually gets 90. What matters is the score compared with what is usual. So Pip keeps a baseline, a yardstick for a usual reward, and nudges by reward minus yardstick instead of the reward itself. Better than usual: push up. Worse than usual: push down.

baseline:3.t: The advantage. Reward minus yardstick has a name: the advantage. It says how much better this try went than usual. A simple yardstick is the average of all of Pip’s rewards so far in this run. At first a third each, Pip gets a crumb about half the time, so the yardstick is near 0.5. A crumb from A then gives advantage 1 minus 0.5 equals plus 0.5; an empty door gives 0 minus 0.5 equals minus 0.5, a push down.

baseline:4.t: Same direction, on average. Does subtracting a yardstick bend the direction Pip learns in? No, because the yardstick does not depend on which door Pip picks. Take door A, yardstick 0.5. Picked, a third of the time, A’s preference loses 0.5 times 0.67 equals 0.33. Not picked, two thirds of the time, it gains 0.5 times 0.33 equals 0.17. On average: a third of 0.33 minus two thirds of 0.17, which is 0. The same holds for every door and any yardstick.

baseline:5.t: Smaller spread. So the average nudge stays minus 0.10, 0, plus 0.10, the exact gradient. What changes is the spread: how far a single nudge typically lands from that average, measured in preference units. Here each dot is one possible single-try nudge to C’s preference; its size shows how often it happens. Combining all three doors, the spread is 0.56 plain and 0.38 with the yardstick.

baseline:6.t: Less spread, faster learning. Now 500 runs of 200 picks each, with and without the average-reward yardstick, alpha equals 0.5. Both use the same dice. Along the bottom: picks. Up the side: Pip’s chance of picking C. Lines: the average over runs. Shaded: where the middle 80 percent of runs lie. After 50 picks the chance of C averages 0.78 plain and 0.84 with the yardstick, and the shaded band is much narrower.

baseline:7.t: Fewer stuck runs. Look at single runs at pick 200. Plain REINFORCE leaves 32 of 500 runs with C’s chance still below one half: a few lucky crumbs from A or B pushed them the wrong way, and empty doors change nothing; only C’s crumbs slowly pull them back. With the yardstick, 3 of 500. Empty doors now push down, so a wrong lead gets corrected.

baseline:8.t: Your turn. Drag the yardstick: a fixed number from 0 to 1, or Pip’s running average reward. Each setting reruns the same 500 runs. Any yardstick from 0.25 to 1 beats none here. A yardstick of 1 is the mirror of plain REINFORCE: crumbs change nothing, empty doors push down. It helps less: 0.83 after 50 picks, against 0.85 with 0.75. The running average is not the best, but needs no tuning.

baseline:9.t: One yardstick is not enough. Back to the maze, with REINFORCE and the same alpha equals 0.2 as before. Here one average won’t do: late in training, Pip’s return from the start is usually around 0.46, from the cell left of the cheese 0.99. The numbers are Pip’s yardsticks after 300 walks, learned as the next step shows. So Pip keeps a yardstick per cell: its value V of s, the usual return from that cell under its current chances, as in the values reel.

baseline:10.t: Learning the yardsticks. Pip learns V of s like the Monte Carlo reel, from returns, with no rulebook: after each walk, each visited cell’s yardstick moves a tenth of the way toward the return that followed. Each move is nudged by its advantage: return minus its cell’s yardstick, using the yardsticks from before the walk; only then are they updated. Preferences and yardsticks learn side by side.

baseline:11.t: Better or worse than usual. Walk 201: Pip steps from the cell left of the cheese straight onto it. Return 1, yardstick there 0.99: advantage plus 0.01, a gentle push up. Walk 202: in that same cell Pip’s dice pick left, then right, right: the cheese comes on the third move, return 0.81. Advantage minus 0.18: that move gets pushed down. Plain REINFORCE would have pushed it up, since its return was positive.

baseline:12.t: How much calmer?. Freeze Pip’s chances and yardsticks after walk 50, 150 and 300; run 2,000 walks from each. Measure the variance of one walk’s nudges: the average squared distance from their mean, added up over all 64 preferences, with and without yardsticks. After walk 50 the young yardsticks are poor guesses and make it worse: 2.43 becomes 3.25. After 150 they cut it by a factor of 3.5, after 300 by 8.3. The average direction never changes; a poor yardstick only adds noise.

baseline:13.t: An honest result. Over 100 runs in this maze the average curves almost overlap: last 25 walks, 0.45 plain and 0.45 with yardsticks. The spread between runs, the standard deviation of each run’s last-25 average return, shrinks a little: 0.034 to 0.024. Why so little? Most learning happens early, while returns are near 0 and the yardsticks are still poor. The door room, where the usual reward sat far above 0, showed the big effect. Baselines help most when returns share a large common level.

baseline:14.t: Where it is used. Nearly every modern policy gradient method subtracts a baseline. Actor-critic methods, A 2 C and P P O among them, learn V of s with a second network and nudge by an advantage: return minus V of s, or a refinement of it. For language models, methods like RLOO and G R P O sample several answers to the same question and use their average reward as the yardstick: the door-room idea, almost exactly.

baseline:15.t: Recap. A baseline is a yardstick for the usual return. Nudging by return minus baseline, the advantage, pushes up only what went better than usual and pushes down what went worse. It does not change the average direction, only the noise. It helps most when returns share a big common level; a common yardstick is the state’s value V of s, which the next reel learns step by step.

actorcritic:0.t: Actor-Critic. One network acts, another grades every move.

actorcritic:1.t: Pip’s chances, again. Same maze as before: stepping onto the cheese pays plus 1, onto the cat minus 1, and either ends the walk; gamma (gamma) is 0.9; a walk is stopped after 100 steps and then scores 0. Pip has no rulebook. In every cell Pip keeps four preference numbers, one per move, and softmax turns them into chances. All start at 0, so every arrow is a quarter. Arrow length shows the chance.

actorcritic:2.t: The long wait. REINFORCE with a baseline learns only when the walk is over. Here is Pip’s very first walk: 15 steps, then the cat. Until that last step, nothing was learned. And then every move of the walk is judged by the return that followed it, which includes the luck of every later move. The very first step up gets blamed for a cat met 14 moves later.

actorcritic:3.t: An actor and a critic. Split Pip in two. The actor is the chances: it picks the moves. The critic is a value notebook: for each cell, a guess of the return to expect from there with the current chances. Think of an athlete and a coach. The athlete tries a move; the coach says at once, better than I expected, or worse. Both keep learning.

actorcritic:4.t: The critic learns by T D. The critic learns exactly as in the T D reel. After each step: target equals reward plus 0.9 times guess where Pip landed, or just the reward if the walk ended. The gap, target minus the guess where Pip was, is the T D error delta (delta). The guess moves a fifth of the way: plus 0.2 times delta, the T D reel’s step size. The critic starts blank, every guess 0, and it must keep up as Pip’s chances change.

actorcritic:5.t: delta grades the move. Before the move, the critic expected the guess of Pip’s cell. After it, Pip has one real reward plus the guess where it landed. If that beats the expectation, delta is positive: the move went better than expected, so make it more likely. Negative: less likely. The actor’s update is REINFORCE’s, with delta in place of return minus yardstick: the baseline idea, with the rest of the walk replaced by the critic’s guess. And it happens right after the move.

actorcritic:6.t: One step, in numbers. Walk 1, last step: from the cell below the cat, Pip moves up, onto the cat. delta equals minus 1 plus 0 minus 0 equals minus 1. The actor lowers up: its preference changes by 1 times delta times (1 minus 0.25), to minus 0.75; each other move rises by 0.25. Chances: up 0.11, the others 0.30. That 1 is the actor’s step size, the alpha of the REINFORCE reel. Why 1? It moves chances clearly but not all at once; the slider later tries others. The critic’s guess there drops to minus 0.20.

actorcritic:7.t: Quiet until the end. What about the first 14 steps of walk 1? Each had reward 0 and landed on a cell whose guess was 0, so delta equals 0 plus 0.9 times 0 minus 0 equals 0. No push at all. So on walk 1 actor-critic is even quieter than REINFORCE, which pushed every move of the walk once it ended. A blank critic needs news from the cheese or the cat, and that news spreads back slowly, one walk at a time. That is why actor-critic will start slower.

actorcritic:8.t: Learning mid-walk. Walk 11. Pip has met the cat from the cell right of it before, so that cell’s guess is minus 0.20. On step 18 Pip moves up into that cell: delta equals 0 plus 0.9 times ( minus 0.20) minus ( minus 0.03) equals minus 0.15, a push away from that move, mid-walk. Dots mark steps whose delta is at least 0.01 either way: gold better, rose worse; 6 came before the cheese. Pip left that cell once more on the way, which lifted its guess to minus 0.17, so at the cheese delta equals 1 minus ( minus 0.17) equals 1.17.

actorcritic:9.t: After 300 walks. Let the pair learn for 300 walks. The arrows straighten along the short path, and the critic’s numbers fill in behind them. After walk 300, the critic’s guess for the start is 0.52. The best possible return is 0.9 to the power 6, 0.53: seven steps to the cheese. 7 of Pip’s last 10 walks took exactly 7 steps.

actorcritic:10.t: Two signals for one move. Freeze Pip after walk 50: from the start it goes up with chance 0.44. Take 40 walks that begin with up. Each dot is what REINFORCE with a baseline would use for that first move: the walk’s return minus a yardstick, here the critic’s guess for the start, 0.13. The dots spread from 0.01 to 0.41: each one carries the luck of the rest of its walk.

actorcritic:11.t: Steady but biased. Now the critic’s signal for the same move: delta equals 0 plus 0.9 times 0.23 minus 0.13 equals 0.08. On this dry floor a move always lands in the same cell, and the critic is frozen, so delta is the same number every time: no noise at all. But the dots average 0.30, not 0.08. That average estimates the true grade: the real return after up, minus the critic’s guess for the start. delta also uses the guess for the cell above, which lags behind how well Pip now does: that is bias. Returns are unbiased but noisy; delta is steady but can be wrong.

actorcritic:12.t: A fair race. Now a race over 300 walks: actor-critic against REINFORCE with a baseline. Both use actor step 1, bigger than the baseline reel’s 0.2, so the race fits in 300 walks. The yardstick learns with step 0.1, as in the baseline reel; the critic with 0.2, as in the T D reel. Run k of both uses the same dice seed; 100 runs each. The chart: across, walks 1 to 300. Up, the return from the start, averaged over the 100 runs and over 10 neighbouring walks. Dashed: the best possible, 0.53.

actorcritic:13.t: Slow start, strong finish. REINFORCE with a baseline gets going sooner: after 50 walks it averages 0.33, actor-critic 0.23. The blank critic is the reason: its delta stays near 0 until news from the cheese has spread back to the start. From walk 69 on, actor-critic leads. After 300 walks: 0.52 against 0.50.

actorcritic:14.t: Calmer, too. Each dot is one run: its average return over its last 100 walks. The dashed line marks 0.4; big dark dots are runs still below it. REINFORCE with a baseline: 4 of 100 runs below 0.4. In 3 of them Pip ended up wandering: 90 or more of the last 100 walks hit the 100-step limit and scored 0, so return minus yardstick is about 0 and the pushes fade. Actor-critic: 0 runs below 0.4, the lowest at 0.50.

actorcritic:15.t: Fair step sizes?. The yardstick learned with step 0.1, the critic with 0.2, and step sizes matter. So we reran both with the other one’s step. REINFORCE with a baseline and yardstick step 0.2: 0.32 after 50 walks, 9 runs below 0.4. Actor-critic with critic step 0.1: 0.10 after 50 walks, 0 runs below 0.4. Same picture either way: REINFORCE with a baseline starts faster and leaves more runs behind.

actorcritic:16.t: Your turn. Drag the actor step size and rerun both methods on the same seeds. The chart title counts the runs that end below 0.4. Big steps learn fast but trust each push more. Watch which method copes with step 2, and which one is quicker with small steps.

actorcritic:17.t: A rushed critic. The critic is only a guess, and how fast it learns matters. With critic step 0.5 it spreads news faster, 0.34 after 50 walks against 0.23 at 0.2. But each walk now jerks the guesses around, the grades jerk with them, and 7 of 100 runs end below 0.4. At 0.05 the critic is calm but slow: 0.05 after 50 walks. A wrong critic steers the actor wrong.

actorcritic:18.t: Where you’ve seen this. In 1983, Andrew Barto, Richard Sutton and Charles Anderson balanced a pole on a cart with two learning parts: one chose the pushes, an adaptive critic graded them. That is the actor and the critic. Today A 2 C, A 3 C, P P O, D D P G, T D 3 and sack are all actor-critic methods, with neural networks in both roles. The next reels look at running many workers at once, and at better grades than a single step.

actorcritic:19.t: Recap. Actor-critic splits Pip in two: the actor holds the chances, the critic learns a value notebook by T D. After every step, the critic’s T D error grades the move, and the actor nudges it up or down. No waiting for the walk to end, and steady grades instead of noisy returns. The price: a critic that is wrong, or still blank, grades wrongly. That is bias.

gae:0.t: n-step Returns  and  G A E. How far should you look before trusting the critic’s guess?

gae:1.t: How far should Pip look?. Same maze: plus 1 for the cheese, minus 1 for the cat, either ends the walk; gamma (gamma) is 0.9. Pip’s actor needs a grade for each move: how much better it went than the critic expected. Actor-critic graded with one real step plus the critic’s guess. REINFORCE with a baseline used the whole real return. Is there something in between, and is it better?

gae:2.t: Two grades, one move. Recall the actor-critic reel: Pip frozen after walk 50, moving up from the start. This time we run 2,000 walks that begin with up, not 40. The one-step grade, the T D error, is 0.08 every time. The whole-walk grade, return minus the critic’s guess for the start, averages 0.294 but swings from walk to walk; 40 walks are drawn as dots. The gold line is the true grade, 0.297: the value of up from the start under these chances, worked out by us with the rulebook, minus the critic’s guess for the start.

gae:3.t: Bias and noise. The one-step grade has no noise, because on the dry floor up always lands in the same cell. But it is 0.22 too low every single time: the critic’s guess for that cell still lags. A mistake that leans the same way every time is bias. The whole-walk grade is right on average: 0.294 against 0.297, a gap that is just the luck of 2,000 walks. But each walk’s luck moves it: its spread is 0.13. That walk-to-walk jumping is variance, or noise.

gae:4.t: n steps, then the guess. The traces reel met the n-step target: add the next n real rewards, discounted by 0.9 per step as in a return, then 0.9 multiplied n times times the critic’s guess where Pip is after n steps. Its grade is that target minus the guess where Pip started. n equals 1 is the T D error. If the walk ends within n steps, there is no guess to add: the grade is the whole real return minus the guess. Any n in between is a dial.

gae:5.t: Turning the n dial. Here are the grades of the same move for n equals 1, 2, 4, 8 and the whole walk, from the same 2,000 walks. As n grows, the average slides toward the true grade, from 0.08 to 0.27 at n equals 8, while the spread grows from 0 to 0.16. More real steps: less bias, more noise than one step. Here n equals 8 is even noisier than the whole walk (spread 0.13): its grade also depends on the critic’s guess wherever Pip happens to be after 8 moves, and those guesses differ from cell to cell.

gae:6.t: G A E: mix every n. Why pick one n? Generalised advantage estimation, G A E, averages all of them with fading weights; the grade is the advantage of the baseline reel. n equals 1 gets weight 1 minus lambda, n equals 2 gets (1 minus lambda) times lambda, n equals 3 that times lambda again, and so on. The weights add up to 1, so it stays an average; weight for n longer than the walk goes to the whole-walk grade. lambda (lambda), between 0 and 1, sets how fast the weights fade. The bars show them for lambda equals 0.5 and lambda equals 0.9.

gae:7.t: A neat shortcut. The mix has a simple form. Take each step’s T D error along the walk: delta zero for the first move, delta one for the next, and so on. A two-step grade is delta zero plus 0.9 delta one, because the guess in between cancels; here delta one equals 0.9 times 0.37 minus 0.23 equals 0.10. Mixing all n gives delta zero plus 0.9 lambda times delta one plus (0.9 lambda) squared times delta two plus ... Later surprises count less, like the traces reel’s fading marks. For this walk with lambda equals 0.9, the grade is 0.28. One move, delta three, bumped into the wall.

gae:8.t: Your turn. Drag lambda and watch the grades of the same move. Gold is the true grade, teal the average of all the walks. At 0 the dots stack on one wrong spot; at 1 they centre on the truth but spread wide. The typical miss combines both: the square root of bias squared plus spread squared, how far one grade usually lands from the truth.

gae:9.t: Which lambda is best?. Across: lambda from 0 to 1. Rose: the bias, blue: the spread, black: the typical miss, which combines both. Lower is better. With this critic, frozen after walk 50, the typical miss keeps falling all the way, so it is smallest at lambda equals 1: 0.13, against 0.22 at lambda equals 0. The critic still lags, so trusting it less pays.

gae:10.t: A better critic. Now freeze Pip after walk 80. Two things changed: the critic caught up, so the one-step grade is off by only 0.02; and Pip’s chances improved (up 0.82 instead of 0.44), so walks wander less and long grades are calmer, spread 0.07 at lambda equals 1. Now the best lambda is 0: typical miss 0.02, against 0.07 at lambda equals 1. Even with calmer walks, the trusted critic wins: the best lambda depends on how far you can trust the critic.

gae:11.t: Learning with G A E. Now let Pip learn with G A E grades: after each walk, every move gets its G A E grade; the actor is nudged by it (step 1) and the critic moves toward grade plus its guess (step 0.2). 100 runs per lambda, same dice. Across: walks; up: the return from the start, averaged over runs and 10 neighbouring walks. After 50 walks the average return is 0.24 with lambda equals 0, 0.37 with lambda equals 0.5, and 0.34 with lambda equals 1.

gae:12.t: Middle ground. lambda equals 0 starts slowest: its grades lean on a blank critic, the bias we saw. lambda equals 1 starts fast but stays noisy: 7 of 100 runs end below 0.4, against 1 for lambda equals 0. lambda equals 0.5 is fastest after 50 walks, with 2 runs below 0.4. lambda equals 0.9 does no better than lambda equals 1 here (8 runs below 0.4 against 7, a difference of one run in 100). Late on, lambda equals 0 ends best (0.52): by then the critic is good, as in the walk-80 picture.

gae:13.t: The price: waiting. A G A E grade needs the T D errors of the moves that come after, so Pip cannot grade a move the moment it makes it. Here Pip waits for the end of each walk. Real systems cut experience into chunks, a few hundred or a few thousand steps, and let the critic’s guess stand in for whatever comes after the cut.

gae:14.t: In practice. G A E was introduced by John Schulman and colleagues in 2015. With neural networks as actor and critic, lambda equals 0.95 together with gamma equals 0.99 became a common default; the P P O paper used exactly that. So G A E is the same dial as T D(lambda) in the traces reel, now used to grade moves for the actor instead of to update values.

gae:15.t: Recap. An n-step grade adds n real rewards, then trusts the critic: small n is steady but biased when the critic is off, large n is unbiased but noisy. G A E mixes every n with weights that fade by lambda, which is the same as summing T D errors weighted by (0.9 lambda) per step. The best lambda depends on how far the critic can be trusted.

ppo:0.t: P P O. Improve the policy, but not too much at once.

ppo:1.t: Pip starts from scratch. Same maze, dry floor: plus 1 for the step onto the cheese, minus 1 onto the cat, both end the walk, gamma (gamma) is 0.9. A walk still going after 100 steps is stopped and scores 0. Pip’s four chances per cell, drawn as arrows, start at a quarter each. Of 1000 test walks, 179 reach the cheese, 643 the cat, 178 are stopped. Its score, the return it can expect from the start, worked out exactly with the rulebook, is minus 0.03; the best possible is 0.53.

ppo:2.t: One update. Each update, Pip walks 10 times: a batch. Each move gets an advantage: the return that followed it minus the critic’s value of the cell. The critic here is exact, so we can watch the actor alone. Then the move made gains alpha (alpha) times advantage times (1 minus its chance), the others lose alpha times advantage times their chance; divide by 10, the number of walks. alpha equals 3.

ppo:3.t: Walks are precious. This batch cost ten walks. The update uses it once, then throws it away. In a real game or on a real robot, collecting walks is the slow, expensive part; computing is cheap. So learn more from each batch: go over the same walks 10 times, 10 passes, each one an update with alpha equals 3. Careful: ten such passes can push up to ten times as far as one, a very big step, unless something stops them.

ppo:4.t: The ratio. After the first pass the chances have changed, but the walks came from the old ones. So P P O weighs each move by the ratio: new chance divided by old chance of that move in that cell. Example: the step onto the cheese, from the cell left of it. Its old chance was 0.25. After one pass it is 0.321, so the ratio is 1.285: new Pip would make that move about 1.29 times as often.

ppo:5.t: What each pass climbs. Each pass makes an objective bigger: the average of ratio times advantage over the batch’s moves. Why the ratio? The walks came from old Pip. Weighting each move by new chance divided by old chance turns an average over old Pip’s moves into an estimate for new Pip: moves new Pip makes more often count more. At ratio 1 the slope of new divided by old is the slope of log(new chance), so the first pass is exactly the ordinary update.

ppo:6.t: Ten passes, no brakes. Pip takes 10 passes over its first batch, pushing ratio times advantage each time, with no brake. Of 1000 test walks, not one now ends: Pip wanders and bumps until it is stopped, meeting neither cat nor cheese. So the score goes from minus 0.03 to 0.00. That looks harmless. It is not: watch what happens next.

ppo:7.t: Why never finish?. The batch: 5 walks hit the cat, 1 the cheese, 4 were stopped at 100 steps with return 0. The critic expected less than 0 everywhere, down to minus 0.54 beside the cat. So all 400 moves of the stopped walks had a positive advantage, 0.05 on average. Pushed ten times over, “keep wandering” beat “reach the cheese”. One ordinary pass sees the same advantages but pushes once: the score barely moves, to minus 0.01, and later batches can correct it.

ppo:8.t: Stuck for good. Now every walk is stopped. In the next batch, 10 of 10 walks stop at 100 steps, every return is 0, and the critic, exact for a Pip who never finishes, says about 0 everywhere. The largest advantage is 0.0002. With no surprises there is nothing to learn from. The chart shows this run’s score after each update: forty updates later it is still 0.00.

ppo:9.t: Clip the ratio. P P O, Proximal Policy Optimization, adds a brake. Clip the ratio to a band around 1: from 1 minus epsilon to 1 plus epsilon, with epsilon (epsilon, not the one from epsilon-greedy) usually 0.2. So 0.8 to 1.2. For a move with positive advantage, follow ratio times advantage up to 1.2; beyond that the objective stays flat, so there is no reward for pushing further. Below 0.8 the line continues: making a good move rarer is still penalised.

ppo:10.t: When the advantage is negative. For a move with negative advantage, it mirrors: lowering the ratio helps only down to 0.8, then the objective goes flat. But raising that bad move’s chance still costs, with no cap. P P O keeps whichever of the two numbers, clipped or not, is lower. It removes the reward for going too far, never the penalty.

ppo:11.t: Flat means stop. On a flat stretch the objective has no slope, so that move stops pushing. The cheese step again, over 10 passes. Without the clip its ratio climbs to 2.50. With epsilon equals 0.2 it overshoots on the first pass, to 1.29, then stays there. The first pass starts at ratio 1, inside the band, so the clip cannot hold it back yet. Nothing else in that cell moves it afterwards.

ppo:12.t: The same batch, with the brake. Same first batch, same 10 passes, now clipped at 0.2. Score minus 0.01; 457 of 1000 test walks still end, fewer than the blank policy’s 822. The brake limits how far the bad advice goes; it does not undo it. Average K L divergence, how different old and new chances are: 0.015, against 0.544 unclipped. Later batches correct it. The chart adds this clipped run, blue: 0.46 after 10 updates, 0.52 after 40.

ppo:13.t: Fifty runs. Now 50 runs with different dice, 40 updates each, averaged. Teal: the ordinary update, one pass per batch. Rose: 10 passes, no clip. Blue: 10 passes, clipped at 0.2. No clip: 11 of 50 runs got stuck. One pass: 0.32 after 10 updates, 0.50 after 40. Clipped passes: 0.39 and 0.52, none stuck. Even counting the crashes, unclipped passes lead early. All compared per walk collected; ten passes cost ten times the computing.

ppo:14.t: Ten passes, one big step?. Each pass uses alpha equals 3, so ten unclipped passes can push about as far as one pass at alpha equals 30. Rose: one pass at alpha equals 30. Teal: ten passes at alpha equals 0.3, a tenth of the push each. One pass at alpha equals 30: 20 of 50 stuck, the too-big step again. Ten passes at alpha equals 0.3 are as safe and as slow as one ordinary pass: 0.31 against 0.32 after 10 updates. The clip is what lets ten full passes through: 0.39, none stuck.

ppo:15.t: Your turn. Drag epsilon. Each setting reruns the same 50 runs: 10 passes per batch, alpha equals 3. The line is the average score; the card counts runs stuck near 0. A tight band is safe but learns slowly. A wide band lets more through. With no clip, 11 of 50 runs get stuck.

ppo:16.t: A brake, not a wall. The clip only stops a move from pushing itself further. Other moves in the same cell still shift its chance. After the clipped update, 172 of the batch’s 769 ratios lie outside 0.8 to 1.2, from 0.30 to 1.43. So P P O is a soft limit, not a guarantee. Practical versions often also stop the passes early once the average K L passes a small threshold, such as 0.015.

ppo:17.t: Where it is used. Schulman and colleagues at OpenAI introduced P P O in 2017. Simple to code and forgiving to tune, it became a common default. A scaled-up P P O trained OpenAI Five, which played Dota 2 from 2018 and beat the world champions in 2019. In 2022, InstructGPT used P P O to steer a language model toward answers people preferred, the reinforcement step of R L H F. There, the cell is the text so far and the move is the next word.

ppo:18.t: Recap. Reusing a batch for several passes squeezes more learning out of each walk, but unchecked passes can push the policy far past what the batch supports, and a wrecked policy may never recover. P P O clips the ratio, new chance divided by old chance, to 1  plus or minus  epsilon, so a move stops earning credit once it has moved enough.

sac:0.t: Entropy  and  Soft Actor-Critic. Reward the agent for keeping its options open.

sac:1.t: Back in the door room. The door room from the policy gradient reel. Behind doors A, B and C a crumb, reward 1, appears with a hidden chance: 0.2, 0.5 and 0.8. Pip picks one door per visit, and the visit ends. Pip’s policy is a pie of chances made from three preferences by softmax. It starts at a third each.

sac:2.t: A critic for each door. Pip learns as an actor-critic. The critic keeps a score per door, starting at 0. After each pick it studies 8 random picks from its memory of the last 200, the replay idea from D Q N, moving that door’s score a tenth of the way toward the crumb it got. The actor uses all three scores at once: the policy gradient reel’s nudge, chance times (score minus the pie’s average score), times a step of 3. No sampled returns needed.

sac:3.t: Why old picks still count. REINFORCE and P P O judged moves by the returns of Pip’s own recent walks, so walks made under an older policy were stale. This critic learns something else: what each door pays, like D Q N’s Q-values. A crumb behind C is evidence about C, whoever picked it and whenever. The actor is trained against the critic’s scores, not against its own returns. So the critic may replay old picks: the method is off-policy. sack works the same way.

sac:4.t: An unlucky start. Here is Pip’s first run. In its first 30 picks it tries A 2 times, B 28 times, and C never. B pays 14 crumbs, so its score climbs, while C’s score stays at its starting 0. After B’s first crumbs, the actor pushed B’s chance up within a few picks, so Pip tried the other doors even less. Luck decided the first picks; the rule did the rest. We chose this run to show getting stuck; the next steps show how often it happens.

sac:5.t: Stuck on B. The chart shows Pip’s three chances, pick by pick: A blue, B orange, C teal. By pick 400 the chance of B is 1.00. In all 400 picks Pip never tries C, so the critic’s score for C stays 0.00, far below its true 0.8. The critic only learns about doors Pip picks. A’s score is left over from its 2 early tries, and B’s jumps around because each study moves it a tenth. Pip collects about half a crumb per visit instead of 0.8, with almost no way out.

sac:6.t: Not one unlucky run. Run it 200 times with different dice. In 36 of the 200 runs, by pick 400 Pip’s favourite door is not C. It is the trap from the Exploration versus Exploitation reel: a learner that stops trying a door never finds out it was wrong. Pip needs a reason to keep trying doors it currently rates low.

sac:7.t: How spread out?. A door’s surprise is minus log of its chance: a door Pip almost never picks would be very surprising, a sure door not at all. Entropy is the average surprise. It measures how spread out the chances are. A third each: entropy 1.10, the most possible for three doors. Chances 0.1, 0.1, 0.8: 0.64. Always the same door: 0.

sac:8.t: A bonus for staying spread. Now change what Pip aims for: average reward plus alpha times entropy. alpha (alpha) is the temperature: how many crumbs one unit of spread is worth. Careful: in earlier reels alpha was a step size; here it is not. For the actor, a door’s worth becomes its score plus alpha times its surprise, and the nudge uses worth instead of score. That is exactly the uphill direction of the new aim. Rare doors earn a bonus, so their preferences do not sink forever.

sac:9.t: Why not random picks?. Why not simply pick a random door 1 time in 5, as epsilon-greedy does? Because the actor’s own aim would still push its pie toward certainty, and the random picks would go to good and bad doors alike, forever. With the bonus, staying spread is part of the aim itself. The actor keeps spare chances where they cost little: on doors whose scores are close to the best.

sac:10.t: Turning the temperature. If Pip knew the true crumb chances, the best pie for a temperature would give each door a chance in proportion to e to the power of its crumb chance divided by alpha. At alpha equals 0.2: A 0.04, B 0.18, C 0.79. That is softmax with each preference set to crumb chance divided by alpha, and it is where the actor’s rule settles once the critic is right. Cold, near 0: always C. Hot: closer to a third each.

sac:11.t: Same dice, with a bonus. Rerun Pip’s first run with alpha equals 0.2. The dice are the same, so it starts the same way, but once its chances differ the picks drift apart. The bonus keeps C in play: by pick 400 the chance of C is 0.85 and its score 0.83. Over 200 runs, the favourite at pick 400 is not C in 2 runs, against 36 without the bonus.

sac:12.t: Curiosity has a price. Even when it has found C, the curious Pip keeps a few percent on A and B. Averaged over all 200 runs, stuck ones included, its chance of C at pick 400 is 0.79, against 0.82 without the bonus. Crumbs per visit over the first 400 picks: a tie, 0.72 and 0.72. So at alpha equals 0.2 curiosity costs about what it saves before anything changes. A cooler alpha equals 0.1 is already ahead: 0.75 per visit. The bigger payoff comes when the world changes.

sac:13.t: The world changes. After pick 400, door A suddenly pays a crumb 95 times in 100. The certain Pip picks A not once in the next 600 picks and never finds out. The curious Pip tries A 306 times; A leads its pie from pick 550. Over 200 runs, A is the favourite at pick 1000 in 190 runs with the bonus, 5 without.

sac:14.t: Your turn. Drag the temperature alpha and rerun the 200 runs. The pie is the best pie for that temperature if Pip knew the chances; the numbers are what learning Pips actually did. Too cold and Pip gets stuck and misses the change; too hot and it wastes visits on bad doors. Which alpha collects the most after the change?

sac:15.t: A jump instead of doors. Now a different task, sketched in the policy gradient reel. Pip stands on a ledge and picks a jump strength: how many metres it flies, any number. The cheese lies 0.7 metres out. Landing right on it pays 1; short or long pays less, along the curve below: a miss of 0.15 metres pays about 0.37. Strengths are not a menu, so the policy is a bell curve: a centre, the strength Pip aims for, and a spread, how far its jumps scatter around it.

sac:16.t: Bell curves too. A bell’s entropy grows with its spread: 0.69 more each time the spread doubles. Without a bonus the bell narrows toward one strength. With it, the bell keeps the width where the reward lost by spreading balances the bonus. Strengths are kept between 0 and 1.2 metres. Exact numbers for a bell centred on the cheese: alpha equals 0.01 keeps a spread of 0.01 metres, alpha equals 0.03 keeps 0.02, alpha equals 0.1 keeps 0.04.

sac:17.t: Soft values. In longer tasks the bonus is added to the reward at every step. Then the critic’s value of a situation counts future bonuses too: a spot with several good ways on is worth more than a spot with only one, so the agent learns to prefer places that keep options open. Why “soft”? The best pie is a softmax of the values: a soft version of always taking the maximum. As alpha shrinks to 0 it becomes the hard maximum again.

sac:18.t: Soft Actor-Critic. sack (Haarnoja, Zhou, Abbeel and Levine, 2018) puts this into an actor-critic for continuous actions. Its actor cannot list every strength, so it draws a few from its bell, asks the critic which way each should move, and shifts and reshapes the bell. It replays old experience, since its critic learns values. It keeps two critics and uses the smaller score: the actor is drawn to spots where a critic is too high by luck, and two critics rarely share a lucky error. Later, alpha was tuned automatically.

sac:19.t: Where it’s used. sack is a standard choice for continuous control, from simulated robots to real ones. The same group trained a real four-legged robot, Minitaur, to walk with about two hours of real experience: short for a real robot, where every trial costs time and wear. They also taught a robot hand to turn a valve. Entropy bonuses are common elsewhere too: many policy gradient methods add a small one to keep exploring.

sac:20.t: Recap. Entropy measures how spread out the chances are: the average surprise. Adding alpha times entropy to the reward keeps Pip curious, so an unlucky start or a changed world does not trap it. The temperature alpha sets the price of curiosity. sack puts this bonus into an actor-critic for continuous actions.

ddpg:0.t: Continuous Control: D D P G  and  T D 3. D Q N for steering wheels and robot joints.

ddpg:1.t: How hard to jump?. Back to the jump from the sack reel. Pip stands on a ledge and picks a jump strength: how many metres it flies. Any number will do: 0.5, 0.71, 0.7034. The cheese lies 0.7 metres out. Landing right on it pays 1; a bit short or long pays less, following the curve below. The reward is paid on landing.

ddpg:2.t: A row of ledges. In this reel the cheese ledge is narrow, from 0.4 to 1.0 metres. Land off it and Pip falls into the stream: reward 0, and the run is over. Land on it and Pip walks to its front edge and faces the same picture again: the next crumb, again 0.7 metres out. Two more changes. Wind shifts each landing by a few centimetres. And crumbs vary in size, from nothing to double, 1 on average, so the reward is the curve’s value times the crumb. Real rewards are noisy too. gamma (gamma) is 0.9.

ddpg:3.t: No menu to pick from. D Q N kept one Q-value per move and took the biggest: up, right, down or left, four numbers to compare. Here the move is a number, and there are endlessly many of them. Taking the max means searching them all, at every jump. Chop strengths into steps? A robot arm with 7 joints and 10 settings each has 10 million combinations to compare, every single step.

ddpg:4.t: A critic for any strength. The critic scores any strength: Q of s, a, the reward to expect from jumping a now and the actor’s clean answer ever after, each later jump multiplied by another 0.9. Here the situation s is always a gap’s edge. Dashed: the true Q once the actor answers 0.7, from the rules. Jumping 0.7 is then worth 9.06; past the cliffs at 0.4 and 1.0 Pip falls. Pip does not have this curve: the critic must learn it.

ddpg:5.t: An actor that just answers. The actor looks at the situation and answers with one strength. No chances, no dice: same situation, same answer. That is a deterministic actor. Earlier reels needed chances so that a small nudge made a small change; a strength is a smooth number, so nudging it already does that. In real tasks the actor is a network, situation in, action out; here it is one number, starting at 0.3 metres. Pip falls.

ddpg:6.t: Teaching the critic. The critic learns like D Q N: target equals reward plus 0.9 times its score for the next jump. D Q N used the best next move; here the critic asks the actor what it would jump next. A fall ends the run: the target is just the reward, 0. Jump 217: Pip jumps 0.81 and lands at 0.74: reward 0.94 times crumb 1.14 equals 1.07. Next the actor would jump 0.68, scored 2.10. Target 2.96, above the critic’s 2.51, so its curve is nudged up there.

ddpg:7.t: Try a little around it. A deterministic actor always gives the same answer, so the critic would only ever see one strength and could not tell whether a harder or softer jump is better. So while training, every jump gets random noise added: a bell curve with a spread of 0.1 metres around the actor’s answer. D D P G explored with noise like this too. The noise is only for the jumps Pip makes: the target’s next jump uses the actor’s clean answer.

ddpg:8.t: Climb the critic’s slope. How should the actor improve without trying every strength? It asks the critic: if I jumped a little harder, would your score go up? That is the slope of the critic’s curve at the actor’s strength. Then it steps uphill: new strength equals old plus 0.01 times slope. At jump 45 of Pip’s first run, the actor says 0.47, the critic’s slope there is 2.77, so the actor moves to 0.50.

ddpg:9.t: Many knobs. In a real task the actor is a network with many knobs. The critic’s slope says how much the score rises per extra metre of strength. For each knob, ask too how much the strength moves when that knob turns a little. Multiply the two. That product, the chain rule, says how much turning each knob raises the score; backpropagation computes it, and every knob moves a small step times it. So it is still a policy gradient. Here the actor is one number, so the second factor is 1.

ddpg:10.t: Borrowed from D Q N. Two tricks from the Deep R L reels keep this steady. A replay buffer: every jump is kept, and after each jump the critic studies 8 random old ones, not just the latest. Target networks: the score of the next jump comes from slow copies, moved 2 percent toward the real ones after each jump, so targets do not shift under the critic’s feet. The actor gets a slow copy too, because the target asks it for the next jump.

ddpg:11.t: D D P G. Actor climbing a critic, plus replay, target copies and noise: that is D D P G, Deep Deterministic Policy Gradient (Lillicrap and colleagues, 2015). Here is Pip’s first run, sped up. Of the first 50 jumps, 35 end in the stream. By jump 100 the actor says 0.70, and it stays near 0.7. In jumps 100 to 400 Pip falls only once: the exploring noise can still send it off the ledge.

ddpg:12.t: The critic catches up. Gold: the critic’s score for the actor’s own jump, every 50 jumps. Dashed: that jump’s true worth. The actor found 0.7 by about jump 100; the critic needs about 1250 jumps: a worth near 9 is built one reward plus 0.9 times an older guess at a time, as in the T D reel, and the slow copy slows it more. Dips: the actor drifted, to 0.59 at jump 11250, so every jump paid less. At jump 12000: critic 9.02, truth 8.80.

ddpg:13.t: Too optimistic. From jump 4000 on, this critic is too high by 0.41 on average: it believes in reward that will never come. Close-up at jump 9650: critic 9.48, truth 9.06. Why? The actor goes where the critic’s curve is highest, including spots that are too high by the luck of the samples. Every target leans on that inflated score, so the error is copied back, jump after jump. The Double D Q N reel saw the same thing: taking the max picks lucky guesses.

ddpg:14.t: Not just bad luck. Is that one unlucky run? Run D D P G 8 times with different dice. The chart shows the critic’s score of its own jump minus the true worth, averaged over the 8 runs, from jump 4000 to 12000, once the critics have caught up. Above the dashed zero line the critic is too optimistic, below too pessimistic. D D P G stays above zero: over those jumps it is too high by 0.39 on average, and too high in 8 of the 8 runs.

ddpg:15.t: T D 3, fix one: two critics. In 2018, Scott Fujimoto, Herke van Hoof and David Meger proposed T D 3, Twin Delayed D D P G: three fixes. The first: train two critics, each studying its own random handful of old jumps, and build one shared target for both from the smaller of their two scores. The actor climbs the first critic. A lucky high guess is rarely shared by both. Over the same 8 runs, the average gap shrinks from 0.39 to minus 0.03.

ddpg:16.t: Fix two: let the critic settle. Second: update the actor and the slow copies only every second jump, while the critics learn after every jump. Why? The actor chases the critic’s peak; if the critic is still wobbling, the actor chases the wobble. In this small task it changes nothing you can see: the gap is minus 0.03, the same as with two critics alone. The T D 3 authors aimed it at large networks, whose critics take longer to settle.

ddpg:17.t: Fix three: blur the target. Third: when scoring the next jump for a target, jiggle the actor’s strength a little, a spread of 0.03 metres, at most 0.06, so a narrow false peak in the critic cannot pull the target up. All three fixes read minus 0.22, but that is mostly built in: with jiggled next jumps the critic values a slightly clumsier jumper, truly worth 0.26 less. Against that worth, T D 3 is off by less than 0.01 (dashed line). The T D 3 authors argued a small underestimate is safer anyway.

ddpg:18.t: Your turn. Drag to switch T D 3’s fixes on one at a time: thin lines are the 8 runs, the thick line their average. For T D 3 the gap is measured against the jiggled jumper it really values. Each run’s average gap: D D P G 0.18 to 0.60, two critics minus 0.14 to 0.09. Pip’s jump is about equally good in all four: with one hump, false optimism has nowhere to lure the actor. In big tasks it can.

ddpg:19.t: Where it’s used. D D P G (2015) learned more than 20 simulated physics tasks, like swinging up a pole, grasping, walking and driving, many straight from camera pixels. T D 3 (2018) clearly beat it on standard simulated robot benchmarks such as Hopper and HalfCheetah. Today T D 3 is a common starting point for continuous control, robot arms included. Soft Actor-Critic, in its own reel, also uses two critics, but with a policy that has spread.

ddpg:20.t: Recap. When the action is a number, nobody can take a max over all of them. D D P G lets a deterministic actor climb the slope of a critic Q of s, a, with noise for exploring, a replay buffer and slow target copies. The actor seeks the critic’s peaks, so the critic drifts too optimistic. T D 3 takes the smaller of two critics, which removed the optimism here, delays the actor and blurs the target action.

modelbased:0.t: Model-Based R L. Learn how the world works, then plan in your head.

modelbased:1.t: No rulebook. Pip’s maze again. Stepping onto the cheese pays plus 1, onto the cat minus 1, and either ends the walk. Other steps pay 0, a bump leaves Pip in place, and gamma (gamma) is 0.9. Pip has no rulebook: before a move, it cannot tell where it will land. In the Q-learning reel it learned from experience alone, and its first four walks took 24, 20, 28 and 31 steps.

modelbased:2.t: One walk, one number. Here is that first walk again, sped up. Pip keeps four numbers per cell, one per move, all starting at 0, so each update nudges 0 toward 0 plus 0.9 times 0 and nothing moves. Only the last step, onto the cheese, changes a number: “up” below the cheese, from 0 to 0.2. Pip saw 24 steps of the maze; the other 23 left no trace.

modelbased:3.t: Write it down. What if Pip also wrote down what each move did: in this cell, this move landed me there and paid this much? A bump counts too: pushed up here, stayed put. After walk 1 the notebook holds 14 entries, in the 7 cells Pip visited, out of 64 cell and move pairs; some moves were repeated. This notebook is a learned model: Pip’s own copy of part of the rulebook.

modelbased:4.t: Counting. On Pip’s dry floor one look at a move is enough. On the M D P reel’s wet floor, “right” from the start was tried 1000 times: 795 moved right, 102 slid up, 103 stayed. Count divided by tries is the model’s guess of each chance: 0.795, 0.102, 0.103, near the true 0.8, 0.1, 0.1. Planning would average over the landings with these chances; an imagined step would draw a landing with them. Here the floor stays dry.

modelbased:5.t: Planning in the notebook. Now plan with it, as in the value iteration reel: value of a cell equals the best, over moves, of reward plus 0.9 times value where that move lands. Start from zeros and sweep. One difference: Pip may only use moves in its notebook. Moves it never tried are left out, because it has no idea where they lead. Here 7 sweeps change something; sweep 8 changes nothing, so the planning stops.

modelbased:6.t: A route after one walk. Taking the best noted move in each cell, Pip walks from the start to the cheese in 7 steps, the shortest possible. Its real experience so far: one walk of 24 steps. After that same walk, plain Q-learning knew one move, the one below the cheese. Writing things down got far more out of the same experience: better sample efficiency, learning per real step.

modelbased:7.t: Planning costs thinking. Planning is not free. That plan took 8 sweeps over 14 entries: 112 updates. Each new walk adds entries, and a fresh plan would sweep them all again. Here that is cheap. In a world with millions of states, sweeping everything after every step is not. Richard Sutton’s Dyna spreads the planning thin instead: a little after each real step.

modelbased:8.t: Dyna-Q, part one: a real step. Dyna-Q runs Q-learning as usual. After each real move, the target is the reward plus 0.9 times the biggest number in the cell where Pip landed, and the move’s number goes a fifth of the way toward it: alpha (alpha) equals 0.2. Pip still takes the biggest number, with one move in five random: epsilon (epsilon) equals 0.2. New: it also writes the move into its notebook.

modelbased:9.t: Part two: imagined steps. Then, before its next real move, Pip practises in its head 10 times: it picks a random notebook entry, reads where that move lands and what it pays, and applies the same update, as if it had made the move. No real step is taken, and imagination can only replay moves Pip really tried. Unlike a replay memory, which stores every move as it happened, the notebook keeps one entry per cell and move: a rulebook Pip could also plan with.

modelbased:10.t: The first walks. Walk 1 is the same 24 steps for both methods: every number is 0, so imagining changes nothing until the cheese is found. Walk 2 also takes 20 steps for both. But by its end Q-learning has 2 nonzero numbers and Dyna-Q has 16. On walk 3, Q-learning wanders 28 steps; Dyna-Q walks 7.

modelbased:11.t: The race. One run can be lucky, so race on 20 runs with different dice, seeds 1 to 20; both methods get the same 20. In the chart, across is the walk number, 1 to 30. Up is the number of steps that walk took, averaged over the 20 runs. Grey is Q-learning, teal is Dyna-Q with 10 imagined steps per real one.

modelbased:12.t: Real steps saved. Over the first 10 walks, Q-learning used 642 real steps on average and Dyna-Q 319, about half. In walks 21 to 30 both average about 9 steps a walk, not 7, because one move in five is still random. The price is thinking: Dyna-Q made 10 imagined updates for every real one, about 5500 updates per run against about 900.

modelbased:13.t: The catch: the world changes. After 50 walks with Dyna-Q, Pip’s arrows take the bottom route and the start’s best number is 0.53. Then the cat wakes up and moves to the bottom row, right onto that route. The notebook does not know. It still says the bottom row is safe, and the numbers built from it agree. Pip follows its confident plan and meets the cat after 3 steps.

modelbased:14.t: Real steps fix it, slowly. That step overwrites its entry: “right here lands on the cat, minus 1”. On walk 2, Pip stops in that cell and bumps up and down 11 times: those bump numbers still say 0.59 and 0.58, learned when the cell led to the cheese. A bump’s target is 0.9 times the cell’s own best number, so they shrink slowly, until they drop below “left”. Then a random move hits the cat again. After walk 2, the arrows go over the top.

modelbased:15.t: A belief nobody checks. The new plan goes over the top. But 3 notebook entries, the rose minus 1 tags, still say that stepping into the old cat cell costs minus 1. The plan keeps away, so only a random move could check, and imagination keeps replaying those entries, reinforcing the mistake. A known fix, Dyna-Q+ in Sutton and Barto’s textbook, adds a small bonus to moves not tried for a long time, so Pip goes back to check.

modelbased:16.t: Your turn. Drag the number of imagined steps per real step. 0 is plain Q-learning. The chart reruns the same 20 runs and compares with Q-learning in grey. Watch the first walks shrink as Pip imagines more, then stop shrinking: once the notebook is mostly learned, extra imagining adds little, and the random moves remain.

modelbased:17.t: Where it came from. Richard Sutton introduced Dyna in 1990: learn a model, and mix real updates with imagined ones. Learned models matter most where real experience is slow or costly, as with robots. PILCO, in 2011, learned to swing up a real cart-pole within a handful of trials. The next reels search ahead with a model (tree search, AlphaZero, MuZero) or learn a model from pictures (World Models, Dreamer).

modelbased:18.t: Recap. A model says, for each state and action, where you land and what it pays. If nobody hands you one, learn it by writing down, and counting, what really happened. Then plan with it, or use it for imagined practice between real steps, as Dyna does. In Pip’s maze that halved the real steps. But a wrong model gives confident wrong plans.

mcts:0.t: Monte Carlo Tree Search. Grow a search tree toward the most promising moves.

mcts:1.t: Pip versus the cat. Pip and the cat play noughts and crosses: a 3 by 3 board, three in a row wins. Pip goes first and draws cheese; the cat draws paws. A full board with no line is a draw. We keep score in Pip’s points: a win is 1, a draw  one half, a loss 0. The cat wants Pip’s points low.

mcts:2.t: Pip’s move. Another game, two moves in: Pip took the middle right, the cat answered in the top left corner. Now it is Pip’s turn, with 7 empty squares. Pip knows the rules exactly: where each move puts a mark and when a game ends. That rulebook is a model of the game, so Pip can play moves out in its head before choosing one.

mcts:3.t: A tree of futures. Draw the current board at the top. Below it, one branch for each of Pip’s 7 moves. Below each of those, the cat’s 6 replies, and so on until the games end. This is a search tree; each spot in it is a node. Counting every partial game from here, even when two move orders reach the same board, the tree has 6,900 nodes. That is small enough to check them all. In Go, with about 250 moves per turn, it is not.

mcts:4.t: Play it out at random. A cheap way to judge a move: play it, then let both sides make random moves until the game ends. That is a playout. Here Pip tries bottom left, and the random game ends in a Pip win: 1 point. One playout is a coin flip. The average over many playouts is an estimate of how good the move is. Averaging random trials is what Monte Carlo means.

mcts:5.t: Averages from playouts. So run 2000 playouts after each of Pip’s 7 moves. Each number on the board is the average of Pip’s points over the 2000 random games that start with a move there. The centre looks best, 0.69. Top right comes second at 0.65; bottom middle is worst at 0.43. Should Pip play the centre?

mcts:6.t: The careless cat. We checked every way the game can go, working back from the ends of the games: Pip always takes the most points, the cat the fewest. Then only top right wins. The centre and bottom left draw; the other four lose, even bottom right, which the playouts rated 0.60. Top right wins because Pip threatens the right column, the cat must block, and Pip’s centre then makes two threats. The playouts missed it: their cat rarely defends. A good move must hold up against a careful opponent.

mcts:7.t: Let the tree think for both. Monte Carlo Tree Search, M C T S for short, keeps the playouts but grows a tree on top of them. Inside the tree, both sides choose with U C B, as at the cheese arcade: each node is an arcade, its moves are the machines. At the cat’s turn the score uses the cat’s points, 1 minus Pip’s. Imagined pulls cost nothing, but U C B still spends loops where the choice is decided. Averages drift as the tree grows, so the arcade’s guarantee does not carry over directly; a 2006 proof shows this version still finds best play, given enough loops.

mcts:8.t: One loop, four steps. Each node keeps n, how often a loop passed through it, and the total of Pip’s points. Average equals total divided by n, a Monte Carlo value estimate. Select: from the top, follow the best U C B score down to a node with an untried move. Expand: add that move as a new node. Simulate: one random playout. Back up: add its points to every node on the path. If the walk instead reaches a finished game, nothing is added or played out: its real result is backed up.

mcts:9.t: The first seven loops. At first the top node has untried moves, so each loop simply adds one of Pip’s moves, in random order, and plays it out once, like trying each arcade machine once. Results, left to right in the picture: top middle  one half, top right 1, middle left 0, centre  one half, bottom left 1, bottom middle 1, bottom right 0. Pip’s points, from one coin flip each.

mcts:10.t: Loop 8: U C B chooses. Now every move has n equals 1 and the top node has N equals 7. Each bonus is 1 times the square root of (2 times log 7 divided by 1) equals 1.97. The three moves that won score 2.97; ties go to the move added first, so loop 8 walks down to bottom left. That node has untried replies, so one of them, picked at random, is added: the cat’s reply in the centre. Its playout ends in a cat win, 0 points. Bottom left now shows n equals 2, average 0.5.

mcts:11.t: The tree grows. Loop after loop, the same four steps. Under each move, the brown dots are the cat’s replies; bigger dots were visited more. Deeper levels are drawn as bars, gold where Pip moves, brown where the cat moves: the wider the bar, the more nodes at that depth. Moves that keep scoring well get walked through again and again, so their branches grow deeper. Weak moves still get an occasional look, because their bonus creeps up while they are ignored.

mcts:12.t: After 1000 loops. Top right has been visited 292 times, the centre 202, and no other move more than 138. Top right also has the best average, 0.67 against 0.63. M C T S plays the move it visited most. A rarely visited move can have a lucky average, but it cannot pile up visits unless it keeps scoring. Averages also count loops where Pip explored weak follow-ups or a random playout blundered, so even a sure win averages below 1. The search can stop at any time and still answer.

mcts:13.t: Where the effort went. Those 1000 loops built 796 nodes, top one included, out of 6,900. 205 loops added none: they walked down to a finished game, 108 of them under top right. Top right’s branch has 184 nodes, 5 moves deep; bottom middle’s only 62, 3 deep. Value iteration also plans with a model, but sweeps every position. M C T S looks deep where it matters and stays shallow elsewhere, so it can work in games far too big to search completely.

mcts:14.t: How many loops are enough?. Is 1000 loops luck? Run the whole search 100 times, each with different random playouts, for several budgets. Left to right: loops per decision, 10, 30, 100, 300, 1000 and 3000. Upward: in how many of the 100 runs M C T S chose that move. Gold: top right, the winning move. With 10 loops, only 13 runs: about a random guess among 7. With 1000 loops, 80; with 3000, 100.

mcts:15.t: The tree first agrees with the playouts. Add the centre, in teal. Up to 300 loops, M C T S picks the centre more and more: 70 runs of 100 at 300 loops. A shallow tree’s averages are mostly random-playout averages: at 300 loops the tree’s own average, over the 100 runs, is 0.68 for the centre against 0.63 for top right, close to the playouts’ 0.69 and 0.65. With more loops the tree reaches the cat’s replies. Under the centre, the cat’s most visited reply becomes its one good answer, middle left; under top right, the tree finds Pip’s plan. At 3000 loops: top right 0.87, not 1, since exploring loops and random playouts still blunder; centre 0.65.

mcts:16.t: Your turn. Drag the number of loops per decision. The board shows one search: the share of loops that went through each move, with the move it would play highlighted. Below, the result over 100 searches. With few loops the visits spread out. The centre peaks at 300 loops, chosen in 70 of 100 searches. By 3000, every one of the 100 searches plays top right.

mcts:17.t: The weak spot: random playouts. Random playouts are a crude judge: here they rated the centre above the only winning move, and M C T S needed about 1000 loops to see past that. Even in this tiny game, 3000 loops built 1,098 nodes, a sixth of the whole tree. In Go, a random game says little about who is really ahead, and the tree can never cover a meaningful part of the game. Go programs added handmade rules to make playouts less random. The next reel replaces them with something learned.

mcts:18.t: Where it is used. In 2006 Rémi Coulom named Monte Carlo tree search in his Go program Crazy Stone, and Kocsis and Szepesvári published UCT, the U C B rule at every node used here. The program MoGo soon used UCT for Go. For the next decade the strongest Go programs were built on M C T S. They reached strong amateur level but still lost to top professionals on the full board. AlphaGo, in 2016, kept the tree search and added learned networks.

mcts:19.t: Recap. M C T S grows a search tree from the current position, at most one node per loop: select by U C B, expand, simulate a random playout, back up the result. Both sides choose by U C B inside the tree, so the search learns to expect good replies. It goes deep where moves look strong, and plays the most visited move. Its weak spot is the random playout.

alphazero:0.t: AlphaZero. Self-play plus tree search plus one neural network.

alphazero:1.t: A better judge. Back to Pip’s puzzle from the tree search reel: cat in the top left corner, Pip on the middle right, Pip to move. Only top right wins. Random playouts rated the centre higher, 0.69 against 0.65, and the search needed about 1000 loops to see past them. What if Pip could learn to judge a position, instead of playing it out at random?

alphazero:2.t: One network, two answers. AlphaZero uses one small neural network. It reads the board, which squares hold cheese, which hold paws and whose turn it is, and gives two answers. The value: Pip’s expected points from this position. The prior: for each empty square, how promising that move looks, as shares adding up to 100 percent. Ours has 32 hidden units and 970 knobs; before training they are random.

alphazero:3.t: A judge inside the search. The search loop stays: select, expand, back up. But there is no random playout. When a loop reaches a new node, the network looks at it once: its value is backed up the path, and its priors are stored for the node’s moves. If the loop reaches a finished game, the real result is backed up instead: the rules say who won.

alphazero:4.t: The prior steers the bonus. AlphaZero swaps U C B’s bonus for one that uses the prior: score equals average plus c times prior times the square root of N divided by (1 plus n). As before, N counts visits of the node, n visits of the move, and the average uses the chooser’s points. c equals 1.5 weighs the bonus. A move the network likes gets tried early; one it dislikes waits, but its bonus grows while it is ignored. A move never tried counts as a draw,  one half. Unlike U C B, this rule has no proof behind it; it was chosen because it works.

alphazero:5.t: Where the lessons come from. No human games, no hints. The network plays against itself: network plus search choose every move, for Pip and for the cat. This is self-play. Every game starts from the empty board, with 40 loops of search per move.
