To make games differ, the first 4 moves are drawn at random in proportion to the search’s visits, and random noise is mixed into the priors at the top of each search, where the move is chosen, so moves the network dislikes still get tried. Later moves take the most visited move.

alphazero:6.t: What one game teaches. Here is the very first self-play game, with the untrained network. Under each board: the share of the search’s visits that went to the move played. The cat’s 13% move ignores Pip’s diagonal: one of the 4 random opening draws. The game ends in a Pip win. Every position becomes a lesson with two answers: the search’s visit shares, written pi (pi), and the final result, z. Training shrinks two errors: the value’s miss on z, and a standard measure of mismatch between two sets of shares, cross-entropy, between the prior and pi.

alphazero:7.t: Search as a teacher. Why copy the search? Because search plus network chooses better than the network alone: it looks ahead, and checks the network’s guesses against positions further down. Training the prior toward pi makes the network’s instinct more like its own careful thinking. The value head learns what a position is worth from how whole games turned out, z: a Monte Carlo target, not a T D one.

alphazero:8.t: The loop. One generation: play 50 self-play games, then train the network on the lessons of the last 4 generations, shown 8 times each, each position also rotated or mirrored at random. Older games, played by a clumsier network, are dropped. The trained network then plays the next 50 games. We run 12 generations, 600 games in all. Each nudge changes the knobs a little toward the lessons, like the gradient steps of earlier reels.

alphazero:9.t: Watching it learn. How good is the instinct? We hold the answer key: for every position where the choice matters, 3,191 of them, we know the best moves. Left to right: generations. Upward: the share of those positions where the prior’s favourite is a best move. Untrained: 40%. After generation 4: 73%. It peaks at 87% after generation 8 and ends at 85% after 12. Nobody showed it a good move. The truth enters through the rules: finished games report their real result, in the search and as z.

alphazero:10.t: Its instinct on our puzzle. After training, the network looks at Pip’s puzzle. Its prior gives top right 39%, the centre 23% and bottom right 20%. Its value: 0.63 of a point for Pip; the truth is 1, a sure win. So the instinct already leans the right way, but the value is unsure. Next, the search checks it.

alphazero:11.t: The search checks the instinct. Give the search 50 loops; the first one only asks the network about the current board. Then it sends 37 through top right, 6 through the centre, 4 through bottom right and 2 through bottom left. Top right’s average climbs to 0.86. Random-playout tree search needed about 1000 loops for this. Why so few? The value head judges each new position directly. After bottom right, for example, the network gives the cat’s reply in the top right corner a 52% prior. It is the cat’s only reply that does not lose.

alphazero:12.t: The teacher stays ahead. Is the search really a better teacher? Take 300 random positions where the choice matters. The trained network alone picks a best move in 267. With 10 loops of search: 285. With 40: 293. With 200: 299. Before training the gap was even wider: 120 alone, 285 with 40 loops. The search’s visit shares are a better target than the network’s own guesses, and that gap is what keeps the loop improving. But only 20 of the 300 have six or more empty squares; from the rest, 40 loops often reach the end of the game.

alphazero:13.t: Against perfect play. We let it play a perfect player: 30 games as Pip and 30 as the cat. With perfect play this game is a draw, so a draw is the best anyone can get. Untrained, even with 40 loops of search, it lost 19 of its 30 games as the cat, and 0 as Pip. Untrained, its search did well on random positions but not here: one wrong early move loses a game. Trained, the network alone lost 1 game of 60, with 40 loops 1, with 200 loops 0. Its prior is wrong in 15% of positions that matter, but these games reached 142 such positions and it erred in 1.

alphazero:14.t: Your turn. Drag through the generations. The board shows the network’s prior on Pip’s puzzle; the chart marks how often its favourite is a best move overall. At generation 0 the prior is close to even. Watch when top right takes the lead, and when the search with 40 loops starts to pick it.

alphazero:15.t: The catch. Even this toy took 600 games with 40 loops per move. Go needs vastly more: AlphaZero played tens of millions of self-play games for each of chess, shogi and Go, on thousands of special chips. And look at what the search does every loop: it plays moves by the rules to reach new positions. AlphaZero must be given the rules. Atari games and the real world come with no rulebook. That is the next reel.

alphazero:16.t: AlphaGo to AlphaZero. In 2016 DeepMind’s AlphaGo beat Lee Sedol, a top Go player, 4 games to 1. It learned first from human games and still used playouts. In 2017 AlphaGo Zero dropped both and learned by self-play alone; it beat that AlphaGo 100 games to 0. Then AlphaZero, preprint 2017, journal paper 2018: given only the rules, the same method learned chess, shogi and Go, and won matches against leading programs.

alphazero:17.t: Recap. AlphaZero replaces random playouts with a network that gives a value and a prior for each position. The search uses the value at new nodes, and the prior to decide which moves to try. It learns by self-play: the value learns how games ended, the prior learns the search’s visit shares. Better network, better search, better lessons. It still needs the rules.

worldmodels:0.t: World Models  and  Dreamer. Learn to dream the game, then practise inside the dream.

worldmodels:1.t: Back in the meadow. Pip has left the maze for the open meadow. Its position is two numbers, x and y. A move goes 0.15 up, right, down or left, plus a small random wobble. Landing inside the cheese circle pays plus 1, inside the cat circle minus 1, and either ends the walk. gamma (gamma) is 0.9. In the D Q N reel, Pip trained on 8000 real moves. For a robot, every real move costs time and wear.

worldmodels:2.t: Too big for a notebook. In the model-based reel, Pip wrote down what each move did in each cell: a learned model, its own copy of the rulebook. Then it practised in its head. Here Pip never stands on exactly the same spot twice, so no notebook could list every spot. The fix is the one the values got in the function approximation reel: a network that guesses for spots it has never seen.

worldmodels:3.t: A world model. Pip’s world model is two small networks. The move predictor takes Pip’s four measurements and which move it makes, one switch per move, and guesses the change in x and in y: the change, because it is nearly the same everywhere, which is easier to learn than the new position. The reward predictor takes the four measurements of the landing spot and guesses the reward there. Together they are a learned simulator.

worldmodels:4.t: Learning from 500 real moves. First, real experience: Pip wanders with random moves from random spots, 500 real moves in all. Only 4 of them landed on the cheese and 7 on the cat. Each network is trained as in the function approximation reel: guess, compare with what really happened, nudge every knob a little toward the truth, thousands of times over these same moves.

worldmodels:5.t: How good are its moves?. Teal arrows are the move predictor’s guesses for “right” from a few spots; grey shows the move without wobble. Near the right fence the guesses poke a little past it: few of the 500 moves showed that bump. On 2000 fresh real moves its guess is off by 0.029 on average. Even a perfect predictor of the average move is off by 0.022: the wobble cannot be predicted. A move is 0.15.

worldmodels:6.t: How good are its rewards?. The reward predictor, drawn as squares: gold where it says cheese (a guess above 0.5), rose where it says cat (below minus 0.5). Dashed: the real circles. Its cheese covers 64 percent of the real circle, its cat only 34 percent. An honest caveat: “to cheese” and “to cat” are computed from where they sit, so Pip gets the reward layout for free; the predictor only learns how near counts, from 4 cheese and 7 cat landings.

worldmodels:7.t: Dreaming. Now Pip can dream. From the start, it picks a move, asks the move predictor where it lands, then predicts the next move from that guessed spot, and so on. No real step is taken. Dashed: a dream of a fixed list of ten moves, up four times, then right, then up. Solid: the same moves made for real. Reality reaches the cheese after 10 moves; the dream says cheese after 9.

worldmodels:8.t: Dreams drift. How far do dreams drift? From 200 random spots, make 15 random moves for real and in the dream. Teal: the average gap for the learned model. Grey: a perfect predictor of the average move, which only misses the wobble. After 1 step the gap is 0.030; after 15, 0.137, against 0.074 for grey. Each dreamed step starts from the last guess, so errors pile up. Grey grows too: the wobble adds up even for a perfect model.

worldmodels:9.t: Practice in the dream. Now train the D Q N reel’s Q-network, same settings, entirely inside the dream: 8000 dreamed moves, zero real ones. Each dream starts at a spot Pip really visited and lasts at most 15 moves, since long dreams drift. A dream step pays 0 unless the reward predictor says cheese or cat, which ends the dream. Of 860 dreams, 271 stray past the fence at some point, a spot the real Pip can never reach: the move predictor never quite learned the fence.

worldmodels:10.t: Waking up. Time to wake up. The dream-trained network now steers the real Pip, always taking its best move, from the D Q N reel’s 30 test spots. It reaches the cheese from 27 of the 30 spots and meets the cat 3 times. All it ever saw of the real meadow were those 500 random moves.

worldmodels:11.t: A fair test. Is that luck? Four runs with different dice. D Q N on its own 500 real moves, which allows only 400 updates, reaches the cheese from 7, 1, 0, 3 of the 30 spots. Dream-trained Pip: 27, 30, 26, 29. Pip’s 500 random moves fed straight to a Q-network, with as many updates as the dream run, 7900: 1, 1, 0, 0. So it is not just more updates: the model fills in what those few moves never showed.

worldmodels:12.t: The catch: a flawed dream. The catch. The dream’s cat covers only a third of the real one. In run 3, dream-trained Pip met the real cat from 4 of the 30 spots. For 2 of those 4 fatal landings the dream had predicted minus 0.44 and minus 0.38: not below minus 0.5, so plain grass, and nothing in practice warned against them. At the other 2 the dream did predict the cat; the small network’s own mistakes or the wobble did the rest.

worldmodels:13.t: Your turn. Drag the number of real moves the move predictor learns from, then watch its dream of the fixed ten moves and the drift chart. Retraining takes a moment. From 30 real moves, the dream is off by 0.75 after 15 steps, about 5 moves’ length. From 2000, by 0.09. More real experience makes the dream more trustworthy, but grey shows a floor no model can beat.

worldmodels:14.t: From pictures. Real agents often see pictures, not positions, and predicting every pixel is wasteful. In 2018, David Ha and Jürgen Schmidhuber’s World Models squeezed each game frame into a short list of numbers, a latent state, and learned to predict the next list. In a VizDoom game, the controller, the small part that picks the actions, trained entirely inside that dream, still worked in the real game. Pip’s four measurements already play the latent state’s part.

worldmodels:15.t: Dreamer. Danijar Hafner and colleagues’ Dreamer (2019) learns such a latent model from pixels and trains an actor, a policy network, and a critic, a value network, on dreamed chains of 15 steps started from real moments, as Pip’s dreams were. It keeps collecting real experience and retraining the model, so the dream is checked against reality. DreamerV3 (2023) used one set of settings across many tasks and collected diamonds in Minecraft from scratch.

worldmodels:16.t: Recap. When the world is too big for a notebook, learn a world model with networks: where a move lands and what it pays. Then let the policy practise inside the dream, almost for free. Keep dreams short, because errors pile up, and keep checking the dream against reality: the policy inherits whatever the dream gets wrong. In bigger problems a policy can even seek out the dream’s errors, a known risk this toy did not show.

shaping:0.t: Reward Shaping. Add hints so the agent isn’t searching in the dark.

shaping:1.t: A bigger maze. Pip has a bigger maze for this reel, so the cheese is harder to find: 8 cells across, 6 up, five rocks, the cheese top right, the start bottom left. No cat, to keep things simple. The rules are as before: plus 1 on the step onto the cheese, which ends the walk; every other step pays 0; gamma (gamma) equals 0.9. A walk that has not found the cheese after 1000 steps is called off.

shaping:2.t: The learner. Pip learns with Q-learning, as in the Q-learning reel: four numbers per cell, one per move, all starting at 0. It takes the move with the biggest number, ties broken at random, and one move in five is random. After each move, the move’s number is nudged a fifth of the way, alpha (alpha) equals 0.2, toward the reward plus 0.9 times the best number where Pip landed.

shaping:3.t: Searching in the dark. Every number starts at 0, so every choice is a coin toss. Pip’s first walk took 207 steps. Each update said “0 stays 0”. Only the last step, onto the cheese, changed anything: one number out of 168 rose to 0.2. All that wandering taught Pip nothing. A reward that almost never shows up is called a sparse reward.

shaping:4.t: How slow is slow?. To see the speed, run 20 Pips, each with its own luck, for 30 walks each. The chart’s line goes across from walk 1 to walk 30; its height is how many steps that walk took, averaged over the 20 Pips. Lower is better: the shortest way takes 12 steps. Without hints, the first 10 walks average 151 steps. By walk 30 it is 16.

shaping:5.t: Give hints: hot and cold. We, the designers, know how far each cell is from the cheese: columns plus rows. Here no rock makes the real way longer. Pip does not know this. So we add a hint to the reward, like the game hot and cold: plus 0.1 for a step that brings Pip one closer, minus 0.1 for a step away, 0 for a bump. Adding extra rewards like this is called reward shaping.

shaping:6.t: Much faster. The teal line is the same 20 Pips with hot-and-cold hints. Their first 10 walks average 20 steps instead of 151. Why? Every step now carries a little news, so the numbers start pointing toward the cheese long before Pip ever reaches it.

shaping:7.t: A tempting shortcut. A designer thinks: why punish steps away at all? Just reward progress, and make it stronger: plus 0.3 for every step closer, nothing otherwise. It sounds like the same hint. Watch what Pip learns.

shaping:8.t: Pip dances. After 30 walks, Pip follows its biggest numbers from the start, with no random moves. It runs toward the cheese, then steps back and forth beside it. Without random moves it would never eat. 16 of the 20 Pips end up dancing: 8 right beside the cheese, the rest farther away, a sign their learning is unfinished. Even early, this hint slows learning: 271 steps per walk over the first 10 walks, against 151 with no hints.

shaping:9.t: Why dancing pays. Beside the cheese, Pip has two plans. Eat now: plus 1, plus 0.3 for the step closer, then nothing: 1.3. Or dance: a free step away, plus 0.3 back, again and again. Counted with the 0.9 discount, the dance is worth 1.42. Beside the cheese, the hint did not just speed things up. It changed what is best. Pip is not broken; it found the best way to collect our hints. This is called farming a reward.

shaping:10.t: Why hot and cold was fine. With hot and cold, a step away takes back what the step closer gave: plus 0.1, then minus 0.1. Out and back, the hints sum to nothing; with the discount, almost nothing, plus 0.01, far too little to beat the cheese here. Call minus a tenth of the distance a cell’s potential. Each hint is the new cell’s potential minus the old one’s, so along any walk the middle terms cancel: only start and end count.

shaping:11.t: The safe recipe. In 1999, Andrew Ng, Daishi Harada and Stuart Russell made this exact. Give each cell any potential, 0 once the walk is over, and pay hint equals 0.9 times potential of the new cell minus potential of the old one. Counted with the discount, any whole walk’s hints from a cell then add up to minus its potential, loops included. So every move’s number in that cell shifts by the same amount, and the ranking of moves is unchanged: the best plan stays best. This is potential-based shaping.

shaping:12.t: Choosing a potential. Any potential is safe, but a good one also helps. A natural choice is a rough guess of how much reward is still to come. Ours: 1 minus the distance divided by 12. It is 0 at the start, 12 steps away, and 0.92 beside the cheese. On the cheese the walk is over, so its potential is 0. The step onto the cheese pays plus 1 of reward and a hint of minus 0.92: the guess is cashed in.

shaping:13.t: What the hints feel like. From a cell 8 steps away: a step closer pays plus 0.042, a bump minus 0.033, a step away minus 0.108. So getting closer pays, wasting a step costs a little, going back costs more. These small costs are not a step cost that changes the plan: the cheese step pays them back, so every plan’s total is the same. What matters is the form of the recipe, with the 0.9 built in.

shaping:14.t: Same total, every time. Check it from the start, where the potential is 0. Three walks: the shortest route, Pip’s first wandering walk with these hints, 53 steps, and a walk that dances beside the cheese for 1000 steps. Their hints, counted with the discount, add up to 0, 0 and 0. Dancing earns nothing extra. Only the reward differs: the route’s cheese is worth 0.31 from the start, the dance 0.

shaping:15.t: Fast and safe. Gold: 20 Pips with the potential hint. Their first 10 walks average 21 steps, almost as fast as hot and cold, and all 20 end on a 12-step route. The best numbers Pip heads for are the usual ones minus the cell’s potential. At the start, where the potential is 0, that is 0.31, the same as without hints. The teal hot-and-cold line hides under the gold one.

shaping:16.t: Safe is not the same as fast. The guarantee is about what is best, not speed. Put hot and cold’s potential, minus a tenth of the distance, into the exact recipe: now even a bump earns a small positive hint, so moves Pip has tried look better than untried ones. The first 10 walks average 412 steps: slower than no hints at all. This potential differs from ours mostly by a constant. A constant cannot change the best plan, but because Pip’s numbers all start at 0, it changes how fast Pip learns.

shaping:17.t: Your turn. Pick one of four hints: none, hot and cold, plus 0.3 per step closer, or the potential hint. The picture shows one Pip after 30 walks, following its biggest numbers with no random moves. The card gives averages over all 20 Pips. Which hints speed Pip up, and which one teaches it the wrong thing?

shaping:18.t: In the real world. The word comes from animal training: B. F. Skinner taught pigeons by rewarding small steps toward a trick. In R L, Jette Randløv and Preben Alstrøm in 1998 rewarded a simulated bicycle for progress toward a goal, with no penalty for riding away. It learned to ride in circles, collecting reward on every loop, just like Pip’s dance. That story helped motivate the 1999 recipe. Hand-made hints are still common in robot learning.

shaping:19.t: Recap. Sparse rewards make learning slow: most steps teach nothing. Shaping adds hints so every step carries news. Careless hints change what is best and get farmed. Hints of the form gamma times potential(new) minus potential(old) can never change the best plan; a good potential also makes learning fast.

hacking:0.t: Reward Hacking. You get what you reward, not what you meant.

hacking:1.t: A chore for Pip. Back in Pip’s maze: cheese plus 1, cat minus 1, both end the walk, gamma (gamma) equals 0.9. Today there are also three crumbs lying around. We want Pip to tidy up: pick up the crumbs, then go to the cheese. Pip, as always, knows nothing of what we want. It only feels the rewards we hand out.

hacking:2.t: Writing the reward. We have a crumb sensor, so we write: plus 0.2 for every step that ends on a crumb. Cheese and cat stay as before, and a walk stops after 50 steps. The sensor only checks where Pip stands, so a crumb never disappears. Pip learns with Q-learning, as in the Q-learning reel: one move in five random.

hacking:3.t: What Pip learned. After 100 walks, Pip follows its biggest numbers from the start, no random moves. It walks 2 steps to the crumb on the left, and then bumps into the rock beside it, again and again. Each bump is a step that ends on a crumb: plus 0.2, every single step. Pip never goes near the cheese.

hacking:4.t: Why bumping wins. Stand on the crumb and bump forever: 0.2 every step. With the 0.9 discount that is worth 2. From the start: 1.8. Heading straight for the cheese without lingering, along the bottom over two crumbs, is worth only 0.84. Even beside the cheese, the best move under this reward is to turn away. From the cell left of it, eating is worth 1, heading back to the left crumb 1.46. From the cell below it, the right crumb is next door: 2.

hacking:5.t: Reward hacking. Pip broke no rule. It found the best way to collect exactly what we rewarded: steps that end on a crumb. What we meant, tidy up and then eat, was never in the numbers. When an agent scores well by a route its designers did not intend, it is called reward hacking, or specification gaming.

hacking:6.t: High score from the first walk. Each bar is one training walk; its height is the points Pip scored, the plain sum of its rewards, gold if it reached the cheese. The score is high from walk 1: once a step onto the crumb paid plus 0.2, that move had the only number above 0, so Pip repeated it. Only 1 of the first 10 walks reached the cheese, the last on walk 6. Over the last 50: 8.7 points per walk, 0 cheeses.

hacking:7.t: Goodhart’s law. Economists know this as Goodhart’s law. In Marilyn Strathern’s words: when a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure. Touching crumbs was a fine sign of tidying, as long as nobody optimised it. Once Pip optimised it, the sign and the goal came apart.

hacking:8.t: Patch the reward. Fix the loophole: each crumb pays plus 0.2 once, then it is gone. Pip’s state must now include which crumbs are left, because the same cell now pays or not depending on that. A new run of 300 walks, more than before because there are eight times as many states: Pip takes the 2 crumbs on its way and eats the cheese in 7 steps, skipping the left crumb. That is the best plan under this reward: fetching all three is worth 0.73, against 0.84, because the detour delays the cheese.

hacking:9.t: Patches don’t scale. Patching worked here because we watched Pip and saw the trick. In a big world we cannot list every loophole in advance, and an agent that searches hard will find the ones we missed. A patch also changes the problem: Pip had to track which crumbs were left. And each fix is a new reward with its own gaps: ours still does not say “collect every crumb”, so Pip skipped one.

hacking:10.t: A boat that never finished. This happens with real agents. In 2016, OpenAI trained an agent on the boat racing game CoastRunners, where points come from hitting targets along the course. It found a lagoon where three targets kept coming back, and circled there, crashing and catching fire, never finishing the race. It still scored more than finishing would. Like Pip, it was rewarded for points, not for the race.

hacking:11.t: More from the list. Victoria Krakovna and colleagues at DeepMind keep a public list of such cases. A few: a simulated robot arm, rewarded for the height of a block’s bottom face, flipped the block over instead of stacking it. A simulated hand, judged by people watching through a camera, learned to hover between the camera and the ball so it looked like grabbing. A Tetris program learned to pause the game forever, so it would never lose.

hacking:12.t: Why it matters more for strong agents. Pip found its trick in a 20-cell maze. A stronger agent searches far more possibilities, so it finds gaps a weaker one would miss. In 2022, Alexander Pan, Kush Bhatia and Jacob Steinhardt found that more capable agents exploited badly specified rewards more. Chatbots tuned with a reward model, a network trained to predict which answers people prefer, face the same pull: an answer can score well with that model without being better for people.

hacking:13.t: What helps. There is no complete cure. Watch what the agent does, not just its score. Test it in situations it did not train on. Patch rewards when you find a loophole. And do not push too hard on a reward you do not fully trust. When chatbots are tuned, a penalty usually keeps the new model’s answers close to those of the model before tuning, so it cannot drift far toward odd answers that only the reward model likes.

hacking:14.t: Your turn. Choose how much each step on a crumb pays. Pip trains for 100 walks, then follows its biggest numbers from the start. How small must the crumb reward be before Pip goes for the cheese? A twist: only above about 0.07 is bumping truly the best plan. Below that Pip still bumps: it found the crumb long before the cheese, and rare random moves never carry it far enough to learn better. That part is not hacking but unfinished exploration, the problem from the bandit reels.

hacking:15.t: Recap. An agent optimises exactly what you reward, not what you meant. Gaps between the two get found: Pip bumped a rock on a crumb, a boat circled for points. When a measure becomes a target, it stops being a good measure. The stronger the optimiser, the more this matters: watch behaviour, test widely, and patch.

curiosity:0.t: Curiosity  and  Intrinsic Motivation. Reward the agent for being surprised.

curiosity:1.t: A much bigger maze. Pip has moved to a big maze: 12 columns by 9 rows, 108 cells, with walls between them. The cheese sits in the far top right corner. The shortest route from the start takes 21 steps. There is no cat here. Same rules as before: plus 1 on the step onto the cheese, then the walk ends and Pip starts again at the bottom left. Every other step pays 0. A move into a wall leaves Pip where it is, and still counts as a step.

curiosity:2.t: A reward that almost never comes. Until Pip steps onto the cheese for the first time, every step pays 0: a sparse reward, as in the shaping reel. Why not add hints? With walls everywhere, "closer as the crow flies" can point into dead ends, and the designer may not know the maze at all. So Pip learns nothing about the cheese until it stumbles onto it once. Everything depends on how it explores before that.

curiosity:3.t: Pip’s learner. Pip keeps a guess for every cell and move. After each step it moves that guess halfway toward the reward plus 0.9 times the best guess in the new cell. This is Q-learning, with gamma (gamma) 0.9. Pip takes the best-guess move, except 1 move in 10 at random: epsilon-greedy, epsilon (epsilon) 0.1. Step size and epsilon differ a little from earlier reels. All guesses start at 0; with no reward yet they stay 0, every move ties, and ties are broken at random.

curiosity:4.t: Wandering in circles. Watch 1000 steps of this random walk, sped up. Shading shows how often Pip stood in a cell: the darker, the more visits. After 1000 steps Pip has seen only 57 of the 108 cells. It stood on the start cell 52 times and on one cell nearby 64 times. Random steps keep undoing each other, so Pip circles near home.

curiosity:5.t: Found, eventually. Pip keeps wandering. It finally steps onto the cheese at step 2274, more than a hundred times the 21 steps of the shortest route. Was this run unlucky? A bit, but it was typical. Over 101 runs with different luck, the middle run, the median, needs 1738 steps to find the cheese the first time.

curiosity:6.t: A reward from inside. Children explore because new things are interesting, not because anyone pays them. Let’s give Pip the same drive: an intrinsic reward, a bonus Pip pays itself for going somewhere new. The cheese is an extrinsic reward: it comes from the world. Pip adds the two and learns from the sum, with the same learner. Doesn’t an added bonus change what is best, as in the shaping reel? Yes, on purpose. We come back to that.

curiosity:7.t: Counting visits. The simplest novelty bonus: Pip counts how often it has stood in each cell. On arrival it pays itself 0.1 divided by the square root of the count, this visit included. The bars show the bonus for the first ten visits to a cell: 0.1 on the first, 0.05 on the fourth, and 0.01 on the hundredth. Familiar cells get boring, but slowly, while unvisited cells keep the full 0.1.

curiosity:8.t: Untried moves look promising. One more change. A move Pip has never tried starts with the guess 1, not 0. Why 1? A move into an endless run of new cells, each paying 0.1, would be worth 0.1, plus 0.9 times 0.1, plus 0.81 times 0.1, and so on: exactly 1. So "untried" means "maybe fresh ground": optimism, as in the bandit reels. The surprise explorer later starts at 1 too. For the random walker, with only the cheese as reward, the matching start was 0.

curiosity:9.t: The counting explorer. Same maze, same luck seed. Now each visit makes a cell a little more boring, so Pip’s guesses point toward the least visited parts of the maze, and the shading spreads like a flood. This Pip steps onto the cheese at step 348, after seeing 64 cells. By that step the random walker had seen 18; it needed 2274 steps for the cheese.

curiosity:10.t: A chart of exploring. One run proves little, so here are averages over 101 runs. The chart: left to right, steps taken. Upward, how many of the 108 cells Pip has seen at least once by then. A line that reaches the top has seen the whole maze. The grey line shows the fastest possible case, one new cell per step.

curiosity:11.t: Counting covers the maze. Gold, the random walker: after 1000 steps it has seen 50 cells on average. Teal, the counting explorer: 97, almost all of them. The random walker is still at 68 after 2000 steps. Being pulled toward rarely visited cells turns wandering into a sweep.

curiosity:12.t: Time to the first cheese. Now the race to the first cheese. Each bar is the median over 101 runs. Random walker: 1738 steps. Counting explorer: 314, more than five times faster. Is it just the hopeful start of 1? With that start but no bonus, the median is 560: it helps, but those hopes fade once each move is tried. The bonus keeps pulling Pip onward.

curiosity:13.t: Curiosity as surprise. A second kind, from Pathak and colleagues in 2017: pay for surprise. For each cell and move, Pip keeps chances for what it will see next; here, what it sees is the cell it lands in. The prediction error is 1 minus the chance it gave to what it actually saw. Bonus: 0.1 times that. After each move the chances shift halfway toward what was seen. A new move: chance 0, error 1. Then 0.5, 0.25, 0.125.

curiosity:14.t: Surprise works too. The surprise explorer, same seed: it steps onto the cheese at step 738. Over 101 runs its median is 769 steps: slower than counting, 314, but far faster than the random walker, 1738. In this maze moves are not random, so surprise is really a count per cell and move that halves with each try. Two likely reasons it is slower: it fades faster than the square root, and it is kept per move rather than per cell.

curiosity:15.t: The noisy TV. Now a TV sits 6 steps from the start, showing static: one of 64 patterns, picked by chance each time. On that cell Pip sees the cell plus the picture, so it must guess the picture too, and no chance can beat 1 in 64. So the error stays near 1: the bonus there averages 0.099, forever. Pip reaches the TV at step 103 and mostly stays: each bump into a wall leaves it on the TV cell, with a fresh picture.

curiosity:16.t: Trapped by noise. In 3000 steps this Pip spent 2333 on the TV cell, saw only 46 cells, and never found the cheese. Over 101 runs of 5000 steps, the median time to the cheese is 2724, counting the 28 runs that never found it as more than 5000. Counting is not fooled: it counts the cell, not the picture. But if Pip counted every different picture as a new place, static would be new every time, and counting would fall into the same trap.

curiosity:17.t: Can a bonus be farmed?. After the hacking reel, a fair question: can Pip farm its own bonus? A count bonus fades as the count grows: the hundredth visit pays only 0.01. Farming it pays less and less, so in the end the cheese’s plus 1 wins. A surprise bonus fades only if the world can be predicted. Noise never can, so it pays about 0.099 forever. The noisy TV is reward hacking of an inner reward.

curiosity:18.t: Your turn. Tap a cell to put the TV there. The slider picks the explorer: left is surprise, right is counting; its name shows beside the slider and above the maze. Pip replays 3000 steps, same seed, sped up. Try the TV far away, or in a dead end. When does surprise get hooked, and does counting ever care?

curiosity:19.t: Where you meet this. Pathak and colleagues used prediction-error curiosity to let agents explore the game Doom and Super Mario Bros with little or no game reward; their Mario agent got through part of the first level on curiosity alone. Count bonuses were stretched to game screens by Bellemare and colleagues in 2016, with big gains on Montezuma’s Revenge, the Atari game where D Q N scored 0. A 2018 study by Burda and colleagues showed the noisy TV trap in practice.

curiosity:20.t: Recap. When reward is sparse, random exploring wanders in circles. An intrinsic reward for novelty sends the agent toward fresh ground. Count visits and pay more for rare places, or pay for prediction error. Beware the noisy TV: pure randomness stays surprising forever. Next: what to do when places never repeat, so there is nothing to count.

imitation:0.t: Imitation Learning. Skip the reward: just copy an expert.

imitation:1.t: Meet Mo. This is Mo, an old mouse who has lived in Pip’s maze for years. In every cell, Mo knows a good move. Pip could learn by trial and error, as in earlier reels, but that takes many walks and many meetings with the cat. Here is a shortcut: watch Mo, and copy. That is imitation learning.

imitation:2.t: Two kinds of paws. The floor is wet, as in the M D P and policy reels. Pip’s moves go as intended 8 times in 10 and slide sideways 1 in 10 each way. Mo’s old paws grip: Mo never slides. Rewards are as usual: plus 1 for the step onto the cheese, minus 1 onto the cat, and either ends the walk. But a copier never looks at rewards. It only sees what Mo does.

imitation:3.t: Recording a demonstration. Mo walks from the start to the cheese while we write down every step as a pair: the cell Mo was in, and the move Mo made. Cell 16, up. Cell 11, up. And so on. One recorded walk is a demonstration. Mo’s takes 7 steps: up the left side, then along the top.

imitation:4.t: Three demonstrations. Mo walks the route 3 times. Mo never slides, so every walk is the same: 21 examples, all in the same 7 cells. In the other 9 cells, nobody has ever seen Mo. Those cells get a grey question mark.

imitation:5.t: Behaviour cloning. Each example is like a quiz question with its answer: “in cell 16, which move?” “Up.” Learning a rule from questions with known answers is called supervised learning. Used on demonstrations, it is behaviour cloning: in each cell, give Mo’s answer. Had Mo answered differently on different visits, Pip would take the most common answer.

imitation:6.t: Cells without examples. But Pip’s rule must answer in every cell. Our copier uses a simple stand-in for what a trained network does: an empty cell copies the nearest cell with an example, counting steps across the grid. On a tie, the lower-numbered cell wins. Those answers are guesses. 5 of the 9 push into a rock or a wall. In cell 8, right beside the cat, the guess is “right”: onto the cat.

imitation:7.t: Looks just like Mo. Pip walks with its copy. Walk 3: no slides, 7 steps, cheese. On Mo’s route the copy is perfect, because every cell there holds Mo’s example. If Pip never slid, cloning would be all it needs.

imitation:8.t: One slide. Walk 194. On its very first move Pip tries up and slides right, into cell 17. Mo never stood there, so the copy guesses: “up”. Up leads to cell 12? No: Pip slides again, into cell 18. There the guess “up” pushes into the rock. Bump, bump. Then a slide back into cell 17.

imitation:9.t: Errors pile up. Pip climbs to cell 12 and bumps another rock, until a lucky slide puts it back on Mo’s route. Near the end it slides down into cell 8, and the guess says right: onto the cat. That is compounding error: a slip leads to a cell Mo never showed, a guess there leads further off, and no example shows the way back. 9 of Pip’s 15 steps were in cells without an example.

imitation:10.t: A thousand walks. Now 1000 walks from the start, same dice for both rules. Each bar is 1000 walks: gold reached the cheese, rose the cat, grey was stopped after 100 steps. Top: Pip with Mo’s whole rule card, a perfect copy in every cell. Bottom: the clone. The card reaches the cheese 861 times, the clone 784. 293 clone walks entered a cell without an example; only 156 of those reached the cheese.

imitation:11.t: More of Mo won’t help. Would more demonstrations help? Thirty walks by Mo give 210 examples, but still the same 7 cells, because Mo never leaves the route. The clone is exactly the same, and so is its score: 784. The trouble is not how much data, but where it comes from. Mo’s examples cover Mo’s cells; Pip’s slides take it to its own. This mismatch is called distribution shift.

imitation:12.t: dagger: ask about Pip’s cells. In 2011, Stéphane Ross, Geoff Gordon and Drew Bagnell proposed a fix: let the learner walk, and ask the expert about the cells the learner actually reaches. Mo watches Pip and says, for every cell Pip stood in, “here, I would go ...”. Add those answers to the examples, clone again, repeat. The method is called dagger, short for Dataset Aggregation.

imitation:13.t: Round 1. Pip walks 5 times with its clone, slides and guesses included: 62 steps. Mo labels every one, so there are now 83 examples. 4 cells get Mo’s answer for the first time: cells 8, 12, 17 and 18. With them, the clone reaches the cheese 857 times in 1000, up from 784.

imitation:14.t: Round by round. This chart follows the rounds. Across: round 0, plain cloning, to round 4. Up: how many of the 1000 test walks reach the cheese. The dashed line is Pip with Mo’s whole card. Rounds 2 and 3 add examples but no new cells, so nothing changes. In round 4 all 16 cells hold Mo’s answer, and the clone scores 861, exactly the card’s score. That is the ceiling: a copier matches its teacher, never beats it. And Mo’s card suits paws that grip: from cells 4, 10 and 14, one sideways slide lands on the cat.

imitation:15.t: The price of asking. dagger needs the expert on call, answering about awkward places it would never get into itself. For driving, that means labelling recordings of a learner’s drives, which is slow. And the learner must practise for real, mistakes included. In return, the guarantee improves. Count the mistakes beyond the expert’s over a walk of many steps. One early slip can leave a clone lost for every step that follows, so in the worst case its extra mistakes grow with the square of the walk’s length. dagger trains on the learner’s own cells, so they grow only in proportion to it.

imitation:16.t: Your turn. Slide through the dagger rounds, from 0, plain cloning, to 4. Plum arrows are Mo’s examples; gold arrows with a dot are the clone’s guesses. Tap a cell to drop Pip there and watch one walk with that round’s clone, slides and all. Each tap rolls new dice.

imitation:17.t: Where it is used. Around 1990, ALVINN at Carnegie Mellon learned to steer a van from camera images by copying a human driver. In 2016, NVIDIA trained a car to steer from about 72 hours of human driving. To teach recovery, it added camera views shifted off-centre, labelled with the steering that leads back: dagger’s idea, without an expert on call. Robots often learn from demonstrations given by remote control, and chatbots begin by imitating human-written text.

imitation:18.t: Recap. Behaviour cloning turns an expert’s demonstrations into examples and copies the expert’s move in each state: plain supervised learning, no rewards needed. Its weak spot: small mistakes lead to states the expert never showed, and the errors compound. More expert walks don’t reach those states. dagger asks the expert about the states the learner actually visits.

irl:0.t: Inverse R L. Watch the expert, figure out what they want.

irl:1.t: What does Mo want?. In the last reel, Pip copied Mo’s moves cell by cell. Copying has a second weakness: it breaks when the maze changes. Mo’s arrows point where the cheese used to be. So here Pip asks a deeper question: not “what does Mo do?” but “what does Mo want?” Normal R L goes from a reward to behaviour. Inverse R L goes backwards, from behaviour to the reward that explains it.

irl:2.t: Why the goal travels. Think of a friend who always takes the longer road home. You might guess they care more about avoiding traffic than about distance. That guess is a reward, and it is useful: in a new city, you can predict their route without ever having seen it. Moves belong to one place. A goal can be reused anywhere.

irl:3.t: Mo’s walk, dry floor. The floor is dry in this reel, so every move goes where it points. Mo walks from the start to the cheese in 7 steps, up the left side and along the top. Pip knows the maze: where each move leads. It does not know the rewards. Inverse R L usually assumes this: the learner can plan, but has to find out what is worth planning for.

irl:4.t: Rewards from features. Pip describes every step with three features: does it reach the cheese, does it reach the cat, and the plain fact that a step was taken. A guessed reward is one weight per feature. Reward of a step equals cheese weight if it lands on the cheese, plus cat weight if it lands on the cat, plus the step weight, always. The maze’s usual rewards are the weights plus 1, minus 1 and 0.

irl:5.t: Adding up a walk. Add each feature over the walk, with the usual discount: one more 0.9 per step of delay. Mo reaches the cheese on step 7: cheese total 0.9 to the sixth equals 0.53. Cat total 0. Step total 1 plus 0.9 plus ... plus 0.9 to the sixth equals 5.22. A walk’s return under any guess is then weight times total, added up. With the usual weights it is 0.53, the familiar return of a 7-step walk to the cheese.

irl:6.t: Many rewards fit. Which rewards make Mo’s walk a best walk? The usual ones do. So does “only cheese counts”. And so does all zero: then every walk scores 0, and Mo’s is as good as any. All zero explains every behaviour at once. A reward where steps are fun does not fit: then the best walk never ends. Andrew Ng and Stuart Russell, who framed inverse R L in 2000, pointed out this ambiguity.

irl:7.t: Pick the clearest win. So Pip needs a rule for choosing. A natural one: keep a list of rival behaviours, built up one at a time, and pick the reward under which Mo’s walk beats them all by the widest margin. All zero gives a margin of 0, so it is out. A walk with exactly Mo’s feature totals scores the same as Mo under every guess, so it is never a rival. Doubling every weight changes no choice but doubles every gap, so the guesses are kept the same size: the three weights squared add up to 1.

irl:8.t: Round 1: Mo against the Wanderer. Start with one other behaviour: the Wanderer, every move random. Its totals, worked out exactly from the rules: cheese 0.01, cat 0.04, steps 9.54. Mo takes far fewer steps. So the reward with the widest margin says mostly “steps are bad”: cheese plus 0.12, cat minus 0.01, step minus 0.99. The cheese weight is tiny partly because a step total is about 5 while a cheese total is at most 1: how features are scaled sways the choice.

irl:9.t: Planning with guess 1. Pip plans the best walk under guess 1. With steps that costly, the quickest ending wins: Pip runs to the cat in 5 steps instead of reaching the cheese in 7. That is not what Mo does, so guess 1 is wrong. But it is useful: the cat run joins the list of behaviours Mo must beat.

irl:10.t: Round 2: beat both. Now find the reward under which Mo beats both the Wanderer and the cat run by the widest margin: cheese plus 0.71, cat minus 0.70, step minus 0.08. Mo wins by 0.75 against each. Pip plans with guess 2, and the plan has exactly Mo’s feature totals. Mo’s route and the route along the bottom and up the right side tie: both are 7 steps to the cheese. The planner tries up first, so it takes Mo’s. Nothing is left to beat, so the search stops.

irl:11.t: What Pip found. Divide guess 2 by its cheese weight: cheese plus 1, cat minus 0.99, step minus 0.11. Close to the maze’s real rewards, plus 1 and minus 1, plus a small dislike of steps that Mo’s walk cannot rule out. Why stop when the plan matches? If Pip’s plan collects the same feature totals as Mo, it earns the same return as Mo under every reward built from these features, Mo’s true one included. Pieter Abbeel and Andrew Ng built their 2004 method on this.

irl:12.t: A new maze. Now the maze changes. The cheese moves to the bottom right, cell 20. The cat now sleeps in cell 18, and the rocks sit in cells 7 and 14. Mo has never walked here. Copying Mo’s rule card fails: Pip goes up and along the top to cell 5, where the cheese used to be. Mo’s full rule card from the old maze has no arrow there, because cell 5 held the cheese, so the nearest arrow says right: into the wall, again and again until the walk is stopped.

irl:13.t: Plan with what Mo wants. Pip plans in the new maze with guess 2. The plan goes up and around the cat: 8 steps to the cheese, through cells 11, 12, 13, 8, 9, 10, 15. A route through cell 17 is just as short; the planner tries up first. It is exactly the best route under the maze’s real rewards. The moves did not transfer; the goal did.

irl:14.t: Your turn. Pick a reward guess, then tap any cell to move the cheese there. Pip plans with the guess in Pip’s usual maze and walks the plan. Watch guess 1 run for the cat whenever the cheese is farther away than the cat, and all zero have no reason to go anywhere. Guess 2 finds the cheese wherever you put it in this small maze. In a much bigger maze, a far-off cheese could lose to a nearby cat.

irl:15.t: Noisy experts: maximum entropy. Real experts are not perfect: they take different routes on different days. In 2008 Brian Ziebart and colleagues proposed maximum entropy inverse R L: assume the most random behaviour that still matches the expert’s feature totals. That works out as: each walk’s chance grows like e to the power of its return under the guessed reward. The weights are tuned until these chancy walks match the expert’s totals on average. Ziebart’s team learned how taxi drivers weigh road types, speeds and turns from GPS traces.

irl:16.t: Where it is used. Pieter Abbeel and colleagues used apprenticeship learning, built on inverse R L, to fly aerobatic manoeuvres with a model helicopter from an expert pilot’s demonstrations, around 2007 to 2010. Inverse R L is also used to model drivers and pedestrians. Its costs: a planner runs inside every round, the features are chosen by hand, and some ambiguity always remains. gale (2016) never writes the reward down: a second network learns to tell the expert’s moves from the learner’s, and the learner is rewarded for fooling it.

irl:17.t: Recap. Inverse R L watches behaviour and works out the reward behind it. A reward is a reusable description of the goal: plan with it in a new maze, where copied moves fail. Many rewards explain the same behaviour, even all zero, so a rule must choose: the widest margin, matching feature totals, or maximum entropy.

offline:0.t: Offline R L. Learn from a fixed log of data, with no new trials.

offline:1.t: Learning without walking. In the on/off reel, Pip learned from the Wanderer’s diary without taking a single step itself. Now make that the whole rule: a fixed record of old experience, and no new walks, ever. This is offline R L. It matters wherever trying things is costly or dangerous: you cannot test random treatments on patients, but hospitals keep years of records.

offline:2.t: Pip’s old diary. Months ago, Pip walked 50 times with Mo’s rule card on the wet floor: 8 times in 10 a move goes where it points, 1 in 10 it slides to each side. Every step was written down: cell, move, reward, landing cell. 433 steps; 46 walks reached the cheese and 4 the cat. Slides took Pip into all 16 cells, but in each cell the diary holds only one move: the arrow of Mo’s card.

offline:3.t: With a table, no harm done. First, replay the diary with a table, as in the on/off reel: four numbers per cell, drawn as four triangles, with Q-learning’s update and many readings. Moves the diary never tried keep their starting number, 0. Here that is harmless. In every cell the tried move scores above 0, so Pip follows Mo’s arrows. On 1000 test walks it reaches the cheese 861 times. The start’s number, 0.38, is above the true 0.33 only because this diary was lucky: 46 of 50 walks reached the cheese.

offline:4.t: Big problems need a network. But in big problems, a table is impossible: the function approximation reel showed why. A network computes the numbers from a description of the state instead. Pip’s tiny network takes the column and the row, scaled to between minus 1 and 1, passes them through 8 hidden units, and gives four numbers, one per move: 60 knobs in all. It gives every move a number, tried or not.

offline:5.t: Replaying with the network. Same idea as the table. Each round, for every diary step, the target is the reward plus 0.9 times the biggest of the network’s four numbers at the landing cell, or just the reward if the walk ended there. Then the targets are held fixed while all the knobs together take 60 small steps toward them. 30 rounds in all. Nothing else changes, and Pip never takes a new step.

offline:6.t: Numbers that cannot be true. After 30 rounds, the start cell’s numbers are: up 2.20, right 1.63, down minus 0.69, left 2.88. Only “up” appears in the diary. But no walk can earn more than 1: the cheese pays plus 1 once, and the discount only shrinks it. Under the best possible rule, the start is worth 0.33. The untried “left”, 2.88, is pure invention.

offline:7.t: How the error grows. This chart follows the start cell’s biggest number. Across: the round, 0 to 30. Up: the number. The dashed lines mark 1, the most any walk can earn, and the best value really possible. Round 0 is the random starting knobs. It climbs past 1 and ends at 2.88. Why? The max in every target picks the biggest number at the landing cell, and untried moves have made-up ones. The max finds the most optimistic invention, and the next round builds on it. This is extrapolation error.

offline:8.t: Nobody ever checks. Online, the mistake would fix itself: Pip would try “left”, bump into the wall, earn nothing, and lower the number a bit with every try. Offline, nobody ever tries it. So Pip trusts it. Walking with the biggest number in each cell, it pushes into the wall at the start again and again. On 1000 test walks it reaches the cheese 0 times. In 10 of 16 cells its choice is a move the diary never tried.

offline:9.t: Stay close to the data. The fix sounds simple: don’t trust moves the diary never tried. If the data says nothing about a move, assume it is not great. Offline methods do this in different ways. Some only ever pick moves that look like the diary’s. Others lower the numbers of untried moves, so the max stops finding inventions. The next step shows one of those.

offline:10.t: Conservative Q-learning. C Q L, from Aviral Kumar, Aurick Zhou, George Tucker and Sergey Levine in 2020, adds a second push to every round. At every diary step it adds a penalty: a soft maximum of that cell’s four numbers, minus the number of the diary’s own move. Lowering it pushes all four down, the biggest hardest, and the diary’s move back up. A move the diary tried is held up by its targets. An untried move only gets pushed down. A dial, alpha (alpha), sets how hard: here 0.5.

offline:11.t: After C Q L. Same diary, same starting knobs, same 30 rounds, now with C Q L. The start cell: up 0.44, right minus 2.12, down minus 4.96, left minus 3.06. The diary’s move is on top, a little above its real worth under Mo’s card, 0.33, and far below 1. The chart’s new line stays down. On the test walks Pip reaches the cheese 845 times in 1000, against 0 without C Q L. One invention survives: in cell 14 it says up, into the cat. That is why it stays below the diary’s rule, 861.

offline:12.t: How hard to push. Too gentle, and inventions survive: at alpha 0.05, cheese 141. At 0.5 the numbers are sane, but the cell 14 invention costs walks: 845. At 5 Pip copies the diary exactly, 861, but the start’s number, 1.27, is above 1 again. So strong pushes give the best walks here, middle ones honest numbers. With one tried move per cell, C Q L cannot beat the diary’s rule. Combining the best parts of varied walks is offline R L’s promise, not shown here.

offline:13.t: Your turn. Slide alpha, the strength of C Q L’s push, from 0, plain offline Q-learning, to 5. Each setting trains its own network on the same diary. Rose arrows are choices the diary never tried. Tap a cell to drop Pip there and watch one walk with that network’s choices, slides and all.

offline:14.t: Other ways to stay close. I Q L, implicit Q-learning, from Ilya Kostrikov, Ashvin Nair and Sergey Levine in 2021, never asks about untried moves at all: its targets use only moves that appear in the data. Where a cell has several logged moves, it learns which did best and leans toward those. Earlier methods, such as BCQ, batch-constrained Q-learning, in 2019, restrict the learner to moves that resemble the data’s. All share one idea: in offline R L, what the data does not show, you should not trust.

offline:15.t: Where it matters. Offline R L is studied wherever logs are plentiful and experiments are costly: treatment records in healthcare, logs of what people clicked in recommendation systems, and recorded runs of robots. Often it gives a careful warm start, followed by a little cautious practice in the real world. The toy here shows the main danger, not how large systems behave.

offline:16.t: Recap. Offline R L learns from a fixed record, with no new trials. With a network, untried moves get made-up numbers, and Q-learning’s max hunts down the most optimistic: extrapolation error. Nothing corrects it, because nobody tries those moves. The cure is to stay close to the data: C Q L pushes untried moves down, I Q L never asks about them.

rlhf:0.t: R L H F. How chatbots are tuned with human preferences.

rlhf:1.t: Bot, the answer machine. Pip asks Bot a question: how do I get to the cheese? Bot is a tiny stand-in for a language model. A real one writes word by word; Bot just picks one of eight whole answers, each with a chance. Bot learned these chances by copying example answers that people wrote, as in the imitation reel. Some are good, many are not.

rlhf:2.t: What is a good answer?. From the start, the way to the cheese is up three, then right four, passing just above the cat. So some answers help and some do not. Could we write the rule as code? Count the words: the longest answer repeats itself, and people dislike it. Look for direction words: Down, then left, has them and is wrong. For real questions, a rule for helpful and honest is far harder still.

rlhf:3.t: Easy to compare. But people can easily say which of two answers they prefer. Bot answers twice, a person picks one. Here the people are simulated; Mo, the old mouse with glasses, stands in for them. Each answer has a hidden taste score that drives their choices. Bot never sees it, only the comparisons.

rlhf:4.t: How people choose. People are noisy. Our simulated person picks answer A with chance 1 divided by (1 plus e to the minus gap), where the gap is A’s taste minus B’s: the Bradley–Terry model. The chart shows this curve. Across: the taste gap. Up: the chance of picking A. Equal taste gives 0.5. The two answers above have a gap of 3, so A wins with chance 0.95, not always.

rlhf:5.t: 400 comparisons. Bot answers twice, 400 times over, and the simulated people pick. Most pairs are two of Bot’s common answers. Bot’s rare repeated answer, the last row, turns up in only 11 of the 400 pairs. It wins 4 and loses 7. Keep an eye on it.

rlhf:6.t: A reward model. Now we build a reward model: a program that scores any answer, trained to agree with the comparisons. Real ones are large networks reading the whole text. Ours counts three things and gives each a weight: every word, every up or right, every down or left. Score equals the sum. Training picks the weights that make the people’s choices most likely under the same curve.

rlhf:7.t: Scores for every answer. Trained weights: 0.084 per word, 0.910 per up or right, minus 0.337 per down or left. The two good answers score 2.24 and 2.41, well above the rest. On the comparisons it agrees with 60% of the choices. That sounds low, but people’s own hidden taste would agree with only 60%: in 97 pairs both answers tasted the same, a coin flip. But the repeated answer scores 4.31, the highest of all. It says up and right four times, and the scorer only counts.

rlhf:8.t: Practice with P P O. Now the reward model is the judge, and it can score thousands of answers at no cost. Bot improves its chances with P P O, from the P P O reel. Each update Bot answers 32 times. An answer’s advantage is its reward minus the batch’s average. Bot takes 4 passes over the batch, with the ratio clipped to 0.8 to 1.2. Bot’s answers are one step long, so the batch average serves as the critic.

rlhf:9.t: Two ways to keep score. Two charts will track Bot. Top: the average reward-model score of Bot’s answers, what P P O is pushing up. Bottom: people’s verdict, the chance a person prefers the new Bot’s answer over the original Bot’s. 0.5 means no better. We can compute it exactly from the hidden taste. Bot cannot. Both start at the dot.

rlhf:10.t: Leash off. Run P P O with only the reward-model score as reward. At first both lines rise: Bot learns the good answers, and by update 34 people’s verdict is 0.87. But now and then Bot gives its rare repeated answer, which scores higher still, and P P O piles onto it. By update 100 the score is 4.30, Bot gives the repeated answer 99.6 times in 100, and people’s verdict is 0.37: worse than the original.

rlhf:11.t: Reward hacking. The reward model learned that up and right are good, and that is true in Bot’s usual answers. Repeating them is not, but in its 11 comparisons there was too little to learn from, and three weights cannot say repeating is bad. Maximising a learned score finds exactly such gaps. This is reward hacking: a high score, a worse answer.

rlhf:12.t: A leash. The fix is a leash to the original Bot. Each answer’s reward loses beta (beta) times log of new chance divided by original chance. Averaged over the tuned Bot’s answers, that log is the K L divergence from the P P O reel, weighted by the new chances instead of the old: how far Bot has moved. Bot settles where every answer’s leashed reward is equal: each final chance is the original chance times e to the power of score divided by beta, rescaled to add up to 1. With beta equals 1 the repeated answer grows from 1 in 100 to only 0.22.

rlhf:13.t: Leash on. Same run with beta equals 1. The score rises less, to 2.15. People’s verdict rises to 0.65: people now prefer the tuned Bot’s answer about 65 times in 100. The good answers climb to 0.27 and 0.23. The repeated one still grows, from 0.01 to 0.22: the leash holds it back, it does not erase the blind spot.

rlhf:14.t: Your turn. Drag beta, the strength of the leash. Each setting reruns P P O for 100 updates. The bars show Bot’s final chances, the card the reward-model score and people’s verdict. Too loose, and Bot hacks the scorer. Too tight, and Bot barely changes. Of these settings, beta equals 1 does best with people, 0.65.

rlhf:15.t: Not a cure. The best Bot here, always the good answer with the cat warning, would get a verdict of 0.91 from people. The leash got 0.65: safer, not perfect. The reward model is only as good as the comparisons behind it. So teams can collect fresh comparisons on the tuned model’s new answers and retrain the reward model. Real teams cannot see people’s hidden taste, so they choose beta, and when to stop, by asking people to rate the tuned model.

rlhf:16.t: Where it is used. Christiano and colleagues, in 2017, taught simulated robots and Atari players from people comparing short video clips; a backflip took about 900 comparisons. In 2022, InstructGPT (Ouyang and colleagues) tuned GPT-3 with comparisons, a reward model, and P P O with a K L penalty. People preferred a 1.3 billion parameter InstructGPT to the 175 billion parameter GPT-3. This recipe, R L H F, shaped later chat assistants.

rlhf:17.t: Recap. When a good answer is hard to write down, ask people to compare two answers. Fit a reward model so that bigger score gaps mean more reliable preferences. Then tune the model with P P O against that score, on a K L leash to the original, because a learned scorer has blind spots that an unleashed optimiser will find.

pomdp:0.t: Partial Observability (P O M D P). What to do when you can’t see the whole picture.

pomdp:1.t: A maze built for fog. This reel uses a new maze, built to show one problem. A corridor of seven cells, numbered 1 to 7, with three rooms below it: the cheese under cell 4, a cat under cell 1 and under cell 7. The rules are the usual ones: plus 1 for stepping onto the cheese, minus 1 onto a cat, either one ends the walk, gamma (gamma) 0.9. Each walk starts in one of the seven cells, picked at random.

pomdp:2.t: Fog. Now the fog comes in. Pip sees only its own cell, and even there only which sides are walls and which are open. No cheese, no cats, no cell numbers. What Pip senses is its observation. Where it really is, the cell, is still the state, but Pip cannot see it.

pomdp:3.t: Only four feelings. Walking the corridor, Pip can feel only four different things. Cell 1: a wall on the left, an opening below. Cell 7: the mirror image. Cell 4: open left, right and below. And cells 2, 3, 5 and 6 all feel exactly the same: walls above and below, open on both sides. Call that feeling corridor.

pomdp:4.t: Twins that need opposite moves. Look at cells 3 and 5. They feel identical, yet from cell 3 the cheese is to the right, and from cell 5 it is to the left. The same goes for cells 2 and 6. So what Pip feels does not tell it what to do. In the M D P reel’s words, the observation is not Markov: what happens next depends on more than what Pip can sense.

pomdp:5.t: A name for it: P O M D P. Underneath, nothing changed: states, moves, rewards and gamma are still an M D P. Add one thing, which observation each state gives, and you have a partially observable M D P: a P O M D P, said “pom-dee-pee”. The true state is still Markov. It is just hidden behind the observations.

pomdp:6.t: A rule from what Pip feels. The simplest policy maps the current observation straight to a move. It has no memory, so it is called memoryless. Three entries are easy: left end, go right; junction, go down; right end, go left. But a memoryless rule has one entry for “corridor”, so all four corridor cells must get the same move.

pomdp:7.t: Corridor means right. Say the rule is “corridor: go right”. From cells 1 to 4 that works. But start Pip in cell 5: right to 6, right to 7, the right end says left, back to 6, which feels like corridor: right again. Pip shuttles forever. So this rule reaches the cheese from 4 of 7 starts. “Corridor: go left” fails on the other side, also 4 of 7. Up and down only bump.

pomdp:8.t: Roll a die?. One trick helps a little: in the corridor, flip a coin between left and right. Pip now reaches the cheese from every start, but it dithers. Averaged over the 7 starts, the return is 0.62, against 0.49 for “always right”. If Pip could see its cell, it would walk straight there: 0.84. No memoryless rule can do that. With the full state a fixed rule is always enough; under fog, a random one can beat every fixed one.

pomdp:9.t: Fix one: remember. Give Pip a one-item memory: the move it just made. Now “corridor, and I was going right” and “corridor, and I was going left” are different situations, each with its own entry. Rule: in the corridor keep going the way you were going; with no memory yet, go right. From cell 5: right, right, the end turns it around, then left, left, left, down. Cheese in 6 steps.

pomdp:10.t: Learning in the fog. Can Q-learning, from the Q-learning reel, find such rules itself? Same settings: one move in five random, alpha (alpha) 0.2. Across: walk 1 to 300. Up: the return, averaged over the last 20 walks and over 20 runs with different seeds. Grey dashed: a Pip that sees its cell. Rose: learning from what Pip feels; it stalls near 0.37. Early walks often meet a cat, so the lines start below 0. Why does rose stall? Its one corridor entry mixes twins that need opposite moves, and a greedy rule can never be the coin flip.

pomdp:11.t: Memory pays, slowly. The teal line learns from what Pip feels plus its last move. At first it is no better, since it has more situations to fill in; then it pulls ahead: 0.54 against 0.37 over the last 100 walks. After 300 walks, the rose runs’ best moves reach the cheese from 3.5 of 7 starts on average. The teal runs’: 6.85. All lines include the random exploring moves, so even grey stays below 0.84.

pomdp:12.t: Fix two: a belief. Fix two needs more knowledge. Suppose Pip has the map: where each move leads and what each cell feels like, but not its own position. Then it can keep a belief: the chance that it is in each cell, shown as shading. At the start, 1 in 7 for each cell, about 0.14. Then Pip feels “corridor”. Only cells 2, 3, 5 and 6 feel like that: 1 chance in 4 each.

pomdp:13.t: Move, then look. Pip moves right. It doesn’t know from where, so it shifts every chance one cell right: cell 2’s chance goes to 3, cell 6’s goes to 7, and so on. Then it feels: corridor again. Cells 4 and 7 do not feel like that, so their chances are wiped out. Cells 3 and 6 remain, and the chances are scaled back up to add to 1: one half each.

pomdp:14.t: Certain. Pip moves right once more: the chances shift to cells 4 and 7. It feels the right end, which only cell 7 feels like. Belief: cell 7, for certain. Now Pip knows where it is, and the map’s plan applies: left, left, left, down. Moving right was away from the cheese, but it bought information. That is 6 moves in all, as many as the memory rule needed. Here “go right until sure” is a hand-made plan; in general, choosing moves from a belief is a planning problem of its own.

pomdp:15.t: Shaky whiskers. Real sensors err. Say a feeling is right 9 times in 10, otherwise one of the other three at random; moves still never skid. A look now lowers chances instead of wiping them out. With the same readings, Pip ends 0.96 sure of cell 7. If the middle reading had wrongly said “junction”, cell 7 still gets 0.66: starts in 5 or 6 explain it, since right from cell 7 is a bump. Cell 5 gets 0.33: a start in 3, with only the last reading wrong.

pomdp:16.t: Your turn. Pip starts in a hidden random cell, any of 1 to 7. Tap left, right or down to move it, and watch the belief after each move and feel. Down ends the walk where there is a room. Tap the card for a new walk. Use the slider to make the whiskers unreliable, and see how much longer it takes to be sure.

pomdp:17.t: Memory or belief?. Why is a belief enough? Built with the map from every past move and look, it holds all the history can say about where Pip is, so choosing moves from it is Markov again. But it needs the map and one number per state: hopeless for big worlds. Memory needs no map. Deep R L agents often use a recurrent network, such as an LSTM: it reads one observation at a time, and the usual R L training shapes what it keeps.

pomdp:18.t: Where you meet fog. In poker you cannot see the other cards, so good players and programs reason about what an opponent might hold, given how they have bet. That is a belief. A self-driving car loses sight of a cyclist behind a bus, and must remember that the cyclist is probably still there. In the D Q N reel, the Atari player fed in four recent screen images: a short memory, so motion could be seen.

pomdp:19.t: Recap. In a P O M D P the agent gets observations, not the state. Different states can look the same, so a rule on observations alone can fail, as Pip shuttled in the corridor. Two fixes: memory of recent observations and moves, which Q-learning can learn without a map; or a belief, chances over states, updated after every move and look, which needs the map.

hrl:0.t: Hierarchical R L. Think in sub-goals, not individual muscle twitches.

hrl:1.t: A bigger maze. Pip has moved into a house: four rooms of 5 by 5 cells, joined by four doors, A to D. Walls are shaded. Pip starts in the top-left corner of room 1; the cheese sits in door D, between rooms 3 and 4. Rules as before: plus 1 for stepping onto the cheese, which ends the walk, gamma (gamma) 0.9. There is no cat. The shortest route takes 13 steps.

hrl:2.t: Tiny steps, a long way. First, plain Q-learning, as in the Q-learning reel: a number for each move in each cell, one move in five random, alpha (alpha) 0.2. All numbers start at 0, so walk 1 is pure wandering. In this run, walk 1 took 840 steps to stumble onto the cheese. Over 20 runs with different seeds, walk 1 took 665 steps on average. The dots mark the cells Pip passed through.

hrl:3.t: Think in big steps. You don’t plan a trip to the kitchen one footstep at a time. You think: leave this room, go down the hall, into the kitchen. Each big step hides many small ones. For Pip: from room 1, go to door B; from door B, go to door D. Two big steps instead of thirteen small ones.

hrl:4.t: An option. A big step needs a little policy of its own. Here is “go to door B”: an arrow in every cell of room 1, plus door A, all leading to door B. It can start anywhere in room 1 or in door A, and it stops at door B. A mini-policy with a start zone and a stopping rule is called an option. We drew 8 of them by hand, one for each door of each room.

hrl:5.t: A bigger menu. Pip’s menu now has the 4 moves plus the options that can start where it stands: 2 inside a room; in a doorway, one from each room it joins, such as “go to door A” and “go to door D” in door B. Picking an option is one decision: Pip follows its arrows until it stops. The one-in-five random pick happens only at decisions; inside an option Pip just follows the arrows. Nobody tells Pip which choice is good: options are only extra choices we handed it.

hrl:6.t: Learning numbers for options. Each option gets a number too. If it stops after k steps, the target is the discounted reward collected on the way, plus 0.9 to the power k times the best number, over moves and options, where it stopped. Only the chosen option’s number changes. Walk 1 of this run ends with “go to door D”. The plus 1 comes on its step 4, so it counts 0.9 to the power 3: 0.729. The number moves a fifth of the way, alpha equals 0.2: 0.146.

hrl:7.t: Walk 1, side by side. Same seed, same rules, walk 1. Plain Q-learning, gold, wanders for 840 steps. With options, teal, Pip needs 39 steps and 16 decisions. Why so much faster? A random option carries Pip a whole room at a time, so even pure wandering crosses the house quickly. Over 20 runs, walk 1 takes 35 steps with options on average, against 665.

hrl:8.t: Sixty walks. Now 60 walks per run. Across is the walk number; up is the steps that walk took, averaged over the same 20 seeds for both learners. The dashed line is the shortest route, 13. Gold, plain Q-learning, needs many walks to come down. Teal, with options, is near the bottom almost at once. Over all 60 walks: 6,714 steps against 1,060.

hrl:9.t: Manager and worker. After 60 walks, follow the best choices. Plain: 13 decisions, one per step. With options: 2 decisions, “go to door B” then “go to door D”, over the same 13 steps. Think of a manager that picks the next big step, and a worker, the option’s arrows, that takes the small steps. The manager’s problem is tiny: a few decisions per walk.

hrl:10.t: Why news travels faster. In plain Q-learning, the cheese’s plus 1 creeps back about one cell per walk, so the start learns of it only once a chain of 13 numbers has filled in. Across the 20 runs, the start’s best number first rose above 0 after about 23 walks on average. With options the chain is two links long: start to door B, door B to cheese. Average: after about 5 walks.

hrl:11.t: When options get in the way. Now move the cheese to the far corner of room 4, seven steps from any door. Same options, same 20 seeds, walk 1, stopped after 5,000 steps. Plain Q-learning finds the cheese in 974 steps on average. With options, 19 of the 20 runs hit the limit. Why? One choice in three is an option, and every option ends at a door, so Pip keeps being yanked back. After finding the cheese it recovers, slowly. Average steps with options against plain: walk 20, 1,915 against 260; walk 60, 44 against 26.

hrl:12.t: The hard part. Options help only when their stopping points suit the task. We drew ours by hand, knowing where the doors were. An agent that has to discover good options by itself faces the hard, still open problem of hierarchical R L. Some methods look for bottlenecks such as doorways, that many good routes pass through. Others, like option-critic (2017), learn options and their stopping rules from reward alone.

hrl:13.t: Other ways to split the work. The options framework comes from Sutton, Precup and Singh, 1999. Other designs split the work differently. In feudal designs, going back to Dayan and Hinton in 1993, a manager hands out goals and is rewarded by the task itself, while the worker is rewarded only for reaching the manager’s goals. In goal-conditioned versions, the manager picks a target state, like “be at door B”, and one worker policy learns to reach any target.

hrl:14.t: Your turn. Slide to move the cheese: door D, door C, the middle of room 4, or its far corner. Both learners rerun, 10 seeds, 30 walks each, walks stopped at 3,000 steps. Where do the options shine, and where do they hurt? Look at how close the cheese is to a door.

hrl:15.t: Where it is used. Robots often combine skills, such as reach, grasp and place, written by hand or learned one at a time, with a higher-level policy that picks the next skill. DeepMind’s FeUdal Networks, in 2017, used a manager that sets goals for a worker in Atari games such as Montezuma’s Revenge. It helps most when tasks are long and rewards are rare, and the sub-goals fit the task.

hrl:16.t: Recap. Hierarchical R L plans with big steps and small ones. An option is a mini-policy with a start zone and a stopping rule; picking one is a single decision that may take many steps. With options that fit the task, Pip explored and learned far faster. With ill-fitting options it did worse. Finding good options automatically is the hard part.

marl:0.t: Multi-Agent R L. When several learners share one world.

marl:1.t: Not alone any more. In every reel so far, Pip was the only one learning. The cheese, the cat, even the wet floor followed fixed rules: the same move in the same cell gave the same chances, every time. Now meet Tam, a second mouse in the same maze, with a pink bow. Tam learns too. Several learners sharing one world: that is multi-agent R L.

marl:2.t: The others are part of the world. From Pip’s point of view, Tam is part of the world, like the floor: what happens after Pip’s move can depend on what Tam does. And for Tam, Pip is part of its world. But the floor never changes its habits. Tam does, as it learns. So the chances in Pip’s world keep shifting. A world like that is called non-stationary.

marl:3.t: One room, two doors. To see it clearly, shrink the maze to one room. Each round, Pip and Tam each pick a door at the same moment, without seeing the other’s choice. The big door is heavy: it opens only if both push it, and then each gets a big cheese, worth 1. Pushing it alone gets nothing. The small hole always has a crumb, worth 0.3, for each mouse that goes there. The round ends there, and the payoff is paid at once.

marl:4.t: The payoff table. All four cases fit in a table. Rows are Pip’s door, columns are Tam’s. Each box shows Pip’s payoff, then Tam’s. Both do best together, at the big door: 1 each. So Pip and Tam are a team. But the big door is a gamble: it pays only if the other comes too. The hole is safe. Game theorists call this a stag hunt: two hunters catch a stag only together, while a hare is safe alone.

marl:5.t: How each mouse learns. Each mouse keeps two numbers: its guess of the payoff of each door. Both start at 0. Each round it takes the door with the bigger number, a coin toss if they are equal. One round in five it picks at random, to keep trying both. After the round, it moves the number for its door a fifth of the way toward the payoff. Neither knows that the other is learning. These are independent learners.

marl:6.t: The first rounds. Round 1: all numbers are 0, so both toss a coin, and both pick the hole. Each gets 0.3, and its number for the hole goes from 0 to 0.06. Now the hole has the bigger number, so both keep going there. Round 6: one of Pip’s random rounds sends it to the big door. Tam is at the hole, so the door stays shut: payoff 0, and Pip’s 0 for the big door stays 0.

marl:7.t: The big door, alone. Before round 100, Pip tried the big door 11 times, all at random. Tam was at the hole every time, so each try paid 0. Is Pip wrong to keep 0 for the big door? Not really. Tam goes to the big door only in its random rounds, half of one in five: one round in ten. So the big door pays 0.1 on average, less than the crumb’s 0.3. For Tam’s current habit, the hole really is better.

marl:8.t: A lucky round. Round 100: both happen to make a random choice, and both pick the big door. It opens! Each number for the big door jumps from 0 to 0.2. Then each happens to try it once alone, and drops to 0.16. Round 112: another random double. 0.16 plus 0.2 times 0.84 equals 0.33, just above the hole’s 0.3. Now both prefer the big door.

marl:9.t: Same door, different world. This line shows the world from Pip’s side. Across: rounds 1 to 200. Up: the chance that the big door pays for Pip in that round, which is Tam’s chance of picking it. Round 1 shows 0.5, since Tam’s first pick is a coin toss. Nothing about the door changed. Tam changed: the chance jumped from 0.1 to 0.9 after round 112. On the wet floor, a move’s chances stayed fixed. Here Pip’s lessons can go stale at any time.
