marl:10.t: A hundred pairs. Now 100 pairs of mice, each with its own dice, play 200 rounds. Each dot is one pair: gold when both prefer the big door, teal when both prefer the hole, grey otherwise. After 50 rounds, 66 pairs share the hole. After 200, still 47; 53 reached the big door. A pair at the hole is stuck in a sensible way: whoever switches alone gets 0. Only a lucky double gets them out.

marl:11.t: Now against the cat. Teammates share a goal. Opponents do not. New game: Pip runs to one of two doors, with cheese behind each, and the cat waits at one door. Same door: caught, Pip gets minus 1, the cat plus 1. Different doors: Pip eats, plus 1, and the cat gets minus 1. What one wins, the other loses. This is called zero-sum: pure competition.

marl:12.t: Chasing each other. Pip and the cat learn exactly like the two mice: two numbers each, one round in five random. The strips show each one’s favourite door before every round: gold for left, teal for right. The cat learns Pip’s favourite and waits there, so that door starts to cost Pip, and Pip switches. Then the cat follows. Pip’s favourite changed 19 times in 200 rounds. Neither ever settles.

marl:13.t: No resting point. The best way to play here is the rock, paper, scissors answer from the policy reel: a coin toss between the doors. If both play that way, neither gains by changing alone, so there is nothing left to learn. Such a resting point is called an equilibrium; the pair stuck at the hole was one too. Our learners never hold it. Each always has a favourite, taken nine rounds in ten, which the other can exploit. Pip went left 98 of 200 times: close to half, but only on average.

marl:14.t: Your turn: be the cat. You are the cat. Tap a door to wait there. Pip learns from every round, exactly as before. Its two numbers are shown below. A cat that always waits at the left door caught this Pip just once in 30 rounds; against 1000 Pips with other dice, 3.4 times on average, mostly in Pip’s random rounds. A cat tossing a coin catches Pip about half the time: Pip escaped 515 of 1000 rounds in our run. Can you catch Pip more than half the time?

marl:15.t: Train together, act alone. One popular fix for the shifting world: centralised training with decentralised acting. While practising, a helper, often called a critic, learns a number for each pair of doors, like the payoff table. It sees what neither mouse can: the big door pays 1 when both come. Each mouse is nudged toward doors the helper rates highly. When acting, the helper is gone and each mouse decides alone. MADDPG, from 2017, is one such method; this reel doesn’t run it.

marl:16.t: Playing against yourself. In games where both sides play by the same rules, like chess, an agent can train against copies of itself. As it improves, so does its opponent, so practice is never too easy and never hopeless. This is self-play; AlphaZero learned chess and Go this way. An uneven game like runner against cat needs both roles trained. And self-play can still go round in circles, as our learners did, so big systems also play against older copies.

marl:17.t: Out in the world. In April 2019, OpenAI Five, five copies of one network trained mostly by self-play, beat OG, the reigning world champions of the video game Dota 2. The same year, DeepMind’s AlphaStar reached Grandmaster level in StarCraft II, training a league: many agents, old and new, that play against each other. Both took enormous amounts of practice. The shifting world of this reel is one reason multi-agent training is hard.

marl:18.t: Recap. In multi-agent R L, several learners share a world. To each one, the others are part of that world, and because they keep learning, the world is non-stationary. Teammates can get stuck on a safe but poor habit; opponents can chase each other forever. Helpers that see everything during training, and self-play, are common ways to cope.

sim2real:0.t: Sim-to-Real  and  Domain Randomisation. Train in simulation, then deploy on a real robot.

sim2real:1.t: Practice is expensive. Pip has a new job: a real running track, with cheese at the end. Practising on the real track is slow, and a mistake can be painful: the cat sleeps just past the cheese. So the engineers build a simulator: a computer copy of the track. In it, Pip can practise thousands of walks in seconds, many copies at once, and nobody gets hurt.

sim2real:2.t: The rules of the track. Cells are numbered 0 to 7; Pip starts on 0. Each step it either walks one cell or runs two. Arriving on the cheese, cell 6, pays plus 1. Going past it means landing on the cat, cell 7: minus 1. Either ends the walk. Sooner is better: each step of delay multiplies the reward by 0.9, the discount gamma (gamma). The result is the walk’s return: three runs give 0.9 times 0.9 equals 0.81, six walks only 0.59.

sim2real:3.t: A dry simulator. In the simulator the floor is perfectly dry: a run always goes exactly two cells. Practice walks start in random cells, so Pip learns what to do in every cell. Its habit is one choice per cell. The best habit for this floor: run everywhere, except next to the cheese, where a run would overshoot. When walking is no better, Pip runs. From cell 0 that is run, run, run: 0.81.

sim2real:4.t: The real floor is polished. The real track is polished. When Pip runs, it sometimes skids one cell further and needs an extra step to get back on its feet. The lost step counts even when the skid lands on the cheese or the cat. Walking never skids. The chance of a skid, the slip chance, is not known exactly: the engineers only guess it is somewhere between 0 and 0.4. The difference between the copy and the real thing is called the reality gap.

sim2real:5.t: One skid, at the worst moment. Pip takes its dry habit onto the real track. Say the real slip chance is 0.2. Run, run: fine. From cell 4 it runs again, which in the simulator always landed exactly on the cheese. This time it skids one cell further, past the cheese, onto the cat. The habit never had to plan for a skid, because the simulator never made one.

sim2real:6.t: A thousand real walks. One walk could be bad luck, so the engineers test 1000 walks at slip chance 0.2. Each dot is one of the first 100: gold reached the cheese, rose met the cat. 133 of the 1000 walks met the cat. The average return is 0.58, far below the 0.81 the simulator promised.

sim2real:7.t: Tuned to one exact world. The dry habit is not stupid. It is perfect for the floor it practised on, and it squeezes every step out of it: it counts on each run landing exactly two cells on. That is the trouble with a single, exact simulator. Whatever the copy gets slightly wrong, the habit may rely on. Engineers can try to make the copy more accurate, but it is never perfect.

sim2real:8.t: Randomise the simulator. A different idea: domain randomisation. Before each practice walk, the simulator picks a new slip chance at random: 0, 0.1, 0.2, 0.3 or 0.4. Pip is not told which floor it has. Now the best habit is the one with the best average over all those floors, so it cannot rely on any single one. Here we find it by scoring all 64 possible habits on those floors, standing in for a learner.

sim2real:9.t: The randomised habit. The habit that wins: run until two cells from the cheese, then walk. From cell 4, a run might skid past the cheese, so it walks; from cell 3, a skid lands on the cheese, so running is safe. On the dry floor it is slower, 0.73 instead of 0.81: one extra step. That is the price of caution. Pip can’t see the floor, as in the fog reel; remembering skids would not help here, since even after two clean runs the floor may still be slippery.

sim2real:10.t: Back on the real track. The same test: 1000 real walks at slip chance 0.2. None meets the cat. The average return is 0.73, against 0.58 for the dry habit. Honest note: in this toy, practising on any single slip chance above about 0.05 would give the same safe habit; below that, a run from cell 4 is still worth the risk. Randomising matters because nobody knows which single value matches reality, and real worlds differ in many ways at once.

sim2real:11.t: Your turn. Drag the real slip chance; both habits are tested on 1000 real walks. Across: the slip chance; up: the average return; shaded: the practised range. On a dry floor the dry habit wins, 0.81 to 0.73; from 0.1 on, the randomised one wins. The dry habit recovers a little on slick floors: early skids often carry it past cell 4, the only cell where a skid hits the cat.

sim2real:12.t: Not a free lunch. Why is the randomised line flat, even beyond 0.4? Walking never skids, and a skid moves Pip three cells in two steps, like a run then a walk, so every walk takes four steps. Real robots are not so lucky: if reality lies outside the randomised range, the policy can break. Too wide a range can cost too, though not here: practising on slips up to 0.9 gives the same habit. In real tasks it can make a policy cautious and slow everywhere, or too hard to learn.

sim2real:13.t: Real robots. In 2017, Josh Tobin and colleagues trained a network to find objects in camera images using only simulated pictures, with random colours, textures and lighting: not an R L policy, but the same idea. It worked on real camera images it had never seen, well enough for a robot to grasp the objects. In 2018 and 2019, OpenAI trained a robot hand in heavily randomised simulation to turn a block, and later a Rubik’s cube. It worked on the real hand, though not every time.

sim2real:14.t: Recap. A simulator makes practice fast, cheap and safe, but it never matches the real world exactly. A policy tuned to one exact copy can rely on details reality does not share: the reality gap. Domain randomisation practises on many randomised versions, so the real world is just one more of them. The price is some caution, and the range must cover reality.

rainbow:0.t: Rainbow: Dueling  and  Distributional D Q N. Six fixes for D Q N, stacked into one strong agent.

rainbow:1.t: Six upgrades. Pip’s D Q N has a replay memory and a frozen copy for the targets, and the last reel added the Double D Q N trick. Each came from a different paper. In 2017, Matteo Hessel and colleagues at DeepMind stacked six such upgrades into one agent and called it Rainbow. Two of the six are new to you. This reel opens them up in the meadow: dueling heads and distributional learning. Then the whole list.

rainbow:2.t: Does the move matter?. Here is Pip’s trained network from the D Q N reel, run 1, after 8000 moves, without the Double trick. At the start, bottom left, its four Q-values are 0.39, 0.32, 0.31, 0.34. They are close: from out here, every move leaves a long way to go. Across the 30 test spots, the best Q-value runs from 0.41 to 0.95, while at a typical test spot the best and worst move differ by only 0.17. Where Pip stands often matters more than which move it makes.

rainbow:3.t: Spot plus move. Split each Q-value in two: a part for the spot, V, and a part for the move, its advantage A: Q equals V plus A. But adding 0.1 to V and taking 0.1 from every A leaves every Q the same, so the split needs a rule. The rule: subtract the average of the four A’s. Then V is the plain average of the four Q’s, the value of a random first move: not the values reel’s V, which weights moves by how often Pip picks them. Just a convenient middle point.

rainbow:4.t: Two heads. A dueling network builds this into its shape (Ziyu Wang and colleagues, 2016). The same hidden layer feeds two heads: one output for V, four for the advantages. Then Q equals V plus A minus the average of the A’s. This one was trained like Pip’s D Q N, same seeds. At the start it says V equals 0.39; the four A’s average minus 0.03. So the four Q-values come out 0.44, 0.35, 0.35, 0.41, and they average 0.39, the V.

rainbow:5.t: Why bother?. Each card in the replay memory is about one move: where Pip stood, which move, what followed. In a plain Q-network, the card is a lesson for that move’s output. A plain network’s outputs share hidden knobs, so a card nudges the other three a little too, but only indirectly. In a dueling network, V sits inside every Q-value, so every card trains V directly, whatever the move. The advantage head only has to learn the differences, small in most of the meadow.

rainbow:6.t: Two maps. Here is what the dueling network learned, run 1, after 8000 moves. Left: V at every spot, deeper gold for higher. It rises toward the cheese and is lowest just below and left of the cat, where every route has to go the long way round. Right: how much the move matters there, the largest advantage minus the smallest. It is strongest all around the cat, where one wrong step costs a lot, and palest in the bottom-left corner and in a band below the cat, where several moves are about equally good. The two heads split the question as hoped.

rainbow:7.t: A fair race. Does it learn faster? Eight runs of each, same seeds: the same dice for starts, wobble and random moves, and the same 30 test spots, tested every 500 moves. Orange: plain. Teal: dueling. Thin: single runs; thick: averages. After 8000 moves: 26.6 of 30 for plain, 27.9 for dueling. Single runs spread widely, so this gap is within the noise: about the same here, with four moves. Wang and colleagues saw clearer gains on Atari, with up to 18 moves.

rainbow:8.t: One spot, many futures. Now the second upgrade. Take one spot, below and right of the cat, and let Pip walk from it 1000 times, following its network with one move in five random, as in training. Each walk ends on the cheese, on the cat, or after 60 moves. The return of a walk counts the final plus 1 or minus 1, discounted by 0.9 for each move before it: cheese after 3 moves gives 0.9 times 0.9 equals 0.81. Drawn here: six walks that found the cheese and two that met the cat. Same spot, same habit, different luck.

rainbow:9.t: A histogram of returns. Now sort all 1000 returns into a histogram. Across: the return, from minus 1 on the left to plus 1 on the right, in slices 0.1 wide. Height: how many walks landed in that slice. Gold bars are walks that reached the cheese: 935 of them, spread by how many moves they took. Rose bars on the far left are walks that met the cat: 65. None ran out of time.

rainbow:10.t: The average hides it. A Q-value keeps just one number: the average return, here 0.56. Only 249 of the 1000 walks came within 0.1 of it; the rest scattered above and below, and the cat walks sit far off on the left. And it hides the risk: 7% of walks from here end on the cat. A single number cannot say whether 0.56 is a sure thing or a gamble.

rainbow:11.t: Same average, different risk. From the same spot, force the first move, then carry on as before. First move up, past the cat’s edge: average 0.50. First move down, away from it: average 0.47. Almost the same number. But up meets the cat in 11% of walks, down in only 4%. Two moves with nearly equal averages carry very different risks. Unforced, the network goes right here; down averages a little lower because its way round is longer.

rainbow:12.t: Learning a histogram. Distributional R L learns the whole histogram for every move (Marc Bellemare, Will Dabney and Rémi Munos, 2017). Their C 51 network gives, for each move, the chances of 51 fixed return values. The target: Pip moved right, reward 0. Take the histogram where it landed, squeeze it toward 0 by 0.9, add the reward. Here the histograms come from walks, not a trained network, and real C 51 uses the best move at the landing spot: this shows the idea.

rainbow:13.t: Back onto the bins. The squeezed bars no longer sit on the fixed return values. So each squeezed bar is split between its two nearest fixed values, more to the nearer one. Now the target is again one chance per fixed value. The network’s histogram for that move is then nudged toward the target. The loss measures how far apart the two histograms are (cross-entropy), much as squared error measured the gap between two numbers.

rainbow:14.t: Why it helps. Pip still picks moves by the average, which the histogram contains. Yet on Atari games, learning the whole shape gave clearly better scores than learning the average alone. Why exactly is still debated; one idea is that the histogram is a much richer lesson per card. It also opens the door to risk-aware choices, like preferring the move that rarely meets the cat, though C 51 itself did not do that.

rainbow:15.t: Your turn. Tap any spot on the meadow. Pip walks from there 400 times, following its network with one move in five random, and the histogram of returns appears below, with its average. Try spots in open grass, then spots touching the cat’s circle, then spots right next to the cheese. Where is the average a fair summary, and where does it hide a cat?

rainbow:16.t: All six. Rainbow stacks six upgrades on D Q N. You have now seen four of them: Double D Q N, dueling heads and distributional learning, plus prioritised replay, mentioned in the replay reel. The other two: multi-step targets use three real rewards, discounted as usual, then 0.9 cubed times a guess. Noisy networks add random wiggles to the knobs, learn how big the wiggles should be, and pick moves greedily on the wiggled Q-values, instead of one random move in five.

rainbow:17.t: What mattered. On 57 Atari games, Rainbow beat every one of its parts alone, and needed much less experience than D Q N to reach D Q N’s final scores. Removing one part at a time, prioritised replay and multi-step targets hurt most, distributional learning next. Dueling and Double D Q N changed the median game little (scores scaled to a human player’s), though some games cared. Small, compatible upgrades can add up.

rainbow:18.t: Recap. A dueling network splits each Q-value into the value of the spot, V, and the advantage of each move, A, with the average advantage subtracted so the split is unique. V learns from every card. Distributional R L learns the whole histogram of returns, which an average hides. Rainbow combined six upgrades to D Q N, and together they worked better than any one alone.

a2c:0.t: A 2 C  and  A 3 C. Many players learning at once beats one player alone.

a2c:1.t: One Pip, one maze. Same maze as the actor-critic reel: plus 1 for the cheese, minus 1 for the cat, either ends the walk, gamma (gamma) 0.9, and a walk is stopped after 100 moves. Pip is an actor, its chances, and a critic, its notebook. After every move the critic’s T D error grades that move. Everything Pip learns comes from one walk at a time, one move after another.

a2c:2.t: Look-alike moments. Moves that come one after another look alike: Pip is still in the same corner. In 8 moves in a row, Pip visits only 3.7 different cells on average, while its chances are still all a quarter. So a run of updates keeps pushing the same few cells. In Pip’s table, where each cell has its own numbers, that is mild. In a neural network, where all situations share the same numbers, a run of look-alike updates can drag it one way.

a2c:3.t: Copies of the maze. The fix: run many copies of the maze at once. Each copy has its own Pip, called a worker, with its own dice. Here there are 8. But there is only one set of chances and one critic, shared by all the workers. Whatever one worker’s moves teach, every worker uses from then on. A worker whose walk ends simply starts a new walk at the start and plays on.

a2c:4.t: A varied batch. Now take one move from each worker at the same moment. The workers drift apart, so their cells differ: on average 5.8 different cells among 8 moves, against 3.7 for one worker’s 8 moves in a row. Each update then mixes many situations at once. That is the first reason for workers: varied data.

a2c:5.t: A 2 C: play, wait, update. In A 2 C, every worker plays 5 moves with the shared chances, then waits. Then the 40 moves are pooled. Each move’s push uses its T D error, with the critic as it was when the round began. One update averages the workers’ summed pushes: the chances move by step 4, the critic by step 0.4. Then everyone continues. A 2 C stands for advantage actor-critic: the T D error plays the role of the advantage from the baseline reel. This lock-step version is called synchronous.

a2c:6.t: Why average?. One worker’s 5 moves carry the luck of that one walk. Averaging over 8 workers cancels much of that luck, so each update points more reliably the right way. That lets the steps be big: actor step 4, critic step 0.4, pushes added over each worker’s 5 moves. One worker alone is just the actor-critic reel’s method, updated every 5 moves with about four times its step. That is too big, as the next charts show; with eight it works. One worker with smaller steps is steadier, but slow.

a2c:7.t: Two clocks. We need a clock. Say a move takes one tick of time, and one move in four takes two: 1.25 ticks on average. So eight workers on eight computers make at most 6.4 moves per tick. In A 2 C the fast ones also wait for the slowest, 19 percent of the time, which leaves about 5.2. Top: the first 30 ticks of a 4-worker run; bars mean moving, dots waiting. Chart: across, ticks; up, the expected return from the start, worked out by us with the rulebook, which Pip never sees.

a2c:8.t: One worker against eight. 100 runs each, same dice. With step 4, one worker (grey) reaches 0.31 on average after 2500 ticks, and 42 of 100 runs are still below 0.4. Eight workers (teal): 0.52, 0 runs below 0.4. Dashed: one worker with both steps four times smaller. It is steadier but slow: 0.06 after 2500 ticks. On this clock, eight workers end far higher, and steadier.

a2c:9.t: Count moves, not ticks. Now the same runs, but across is the number of moves gathered by all workers together, up to 2,000. By then one worker with step 4 is at 0.31 on average; eight workers have only reached 0.03. So workers do not make Pip learn from fewer moves. They buy speed on the clock, by moving in parallel, and steadier updates. They need many computers, or many cores, to do it.

a2c:10.t: Your turn. Drag the number of workers: 1, 2, 4 or 8, all A 2 C with step 4, 100 runs each, on the tick clock. Watch the curve and the count of runs below 0.4. From 1 to 2 workers helps a lot, and 4 more still. Going on to 8 gains nothing here: 4 workers end at 0.53 with 14% waiting, 8 at 0.52 with 19%. Averaging 20 moves per update is already steady enough, and with 8 workers each round lasts a little longer.

a2c:11.t: A 3 C: no waiting. A 3 C, asynchronous advantage actor-critic (Mnih and colleagues, 2016), never waits. Each worker copies the shared numbers, plays its 5 moves, and sends its own update the moment it is done. Then it copies the latest numbers and goes on. Top: A 2 C with 4 workers. Each bar is a worker’s 5 moves, dotted lines are waiting, a black line is the shared update. Bottom: A 3 C, where every black dot is one worker’s update.

a2c:12.t: Stale copies. The catch: while a worker plays, the others update, so its copy is out of date. The white numbers count the updates it missed: 3.0 on average here with 4 workers, 7.0 with 8. Why does A 3 C work, when one worker’s push alone was too big? Each A 3 C push is scaled by step 4 divided by the 8 workers: 0.5, eight times smaller. A round’s eight small pushes add up to about one A 2 C update, arriving one by one. With 8 workers, A 3 C ends at 0.527 (best 0.531), A 2 C at 0.525; after 1,000 ticks 0.32 against 0.15.

a2c:13.t: A 2 C or A 3 C?. A 3 C ran its workers on the cores of one ordinary computer, no graphics card, and on Atari games it beat earlier graphics-card agents in about half their training time. A year later, OpenAI found that the synchronous A 2 C did as well, and its one big batch per update suits graphics cards. Our toy has no graphics card, so it only shows A 2 C’s cost, the waiting, and A 3 C’s cost, the stale copies. Real speed depends on the hardware.

a2c:14.t: Where it went. Running many copies of the world in parallel became standard. P P O, the next big method in this track, is usually trained exactly this way, with anything from 8 copies on a laptop to thousands in large labs. The asynchronous style lives on in large distributed systems such as IMPALA (2018), which corrects for the stale chances its workers act with.

a2c:15.t: Recap. Workers run copies of the world in parallel and share one actor and one critic. Their moves are more varied, and averaging their pushes steadies each update. A 2 C waits for all workers and makes one update per round. A 3 C lets each worker update on its own, with slightly stale copies. Workers save time on the clock, not moves.

trpo:0.t: T R P O: Trust Regions. Improve the policy, but never jump too far at once.

trpo:1.t: Pip’s policy, as chances. Same maze, dry floor: plus 1 for the step onto the cheese, minus 1 onto the cat, both end the walk, gamma (gamma) is 0.9. A walk still going after 100 steps is stopped and scores 0. Pip holds four chances per cell, drawn as arrows. After 10 ordinary updates from a blank start, its score, the return it can expect from the start, worked out exactly with the rulebook, is 0.36. The best possible is 0.53: seven steps straight to the cheese.

trpo:2.t: One update. Each update, Pip walks 10 times with its current chances: a batch, where REINFORCE used a single walk. For every move it made, it asks: did things go better than usual from here? That is the move’s advantage: the return that followed the move, minus the critic’s value of the cell. It is the simplest grade, and the critic here is exact, so we can watch the actor alone.

trpo:3.t: What the batch says at the start. At the start Pip moved up 10 times. Twice the walk later ran into the cat: advantages minus 0.59 and minus 0.79. Down and left both bump into a wall and waste a step, yet after 5 of the 8 down bumps the walk happened to go better than usual. So this batch says: less up, more of two useless moves. Added up, up scores minus 0.55, down 0.31, left 0.19. Right was never tried.

trpo:4.t: A normal step. For every move in the batch, the move made gains alpha (alpha) times advantage times (1 minus its chance) in preference, and each other move loses alpha times advantage times its chance. Then divide by 10, the number of walks. Usual step size: alpha equals 3. At the start, up drops from 0.55 to 0.49 and down rises from 0.24 to 0.28. The rest of the batch made the top row surer of right. The score rises from 0.36 to 0.39.

trpo:5.t: Why not a bigger step?. If a small step helps, a bigger one should help more and learn faster. Same batch, same direction, but alpha equals 100: about 33 times bigger. At the start, up falls from 0.55 to 0.00 and down climbs to 0.85. Pip now mostly walks into the wall. The score crashes from 0.36 to 0.01.

trpo:6.t: Bump, bump, bump. With the new chances, Pip bumps into the bottom wall again and again. In its next batch, 8 of 10 walks hit the 100-step limit and score 0. After the normal step, none did. The wrecked policy now collects poor walks, and poor walks are what it must learn from next.

trpo:7.t: Climbing back is slow. Both policies now keep learning with the usual alpha equals 3. The chart shows the score after each update: teal continues from the normal step, rose from the big one. The dashed line is the best possible, 0.53. The teal line reaches 0.51 after 40 updates. The rose line stays below 0.1 for 3 more updates, and is still only at 0.41 after 40.

trpo:8.t: The batch is a local map. Why did the batch mislead? Its advice is a slope: which way to nudge each preference, measured at the old policy. A slope is only reliable close to where it was measured, and every walk behind it came from the old policy. The chart moves along that direction with different step sizes, scored exactly. Small steps help, up to about alpha equals 5. Further out the same advice hurts, and at 100 the score is 0.01.

trpo:9.t: How far is too far?. So limit how far one update may move. But measure it in behaviour, not in preference numbers. In a cell with all preferences 0, adding 2 to up lifts its chance from 0.25 to 0.71. If up’s preference is already 10, the same plus 2 leaves its chance at 1.00. What matters is how different the chances become.

trpo:10.t: Surprise. First, a way to score one choice. The surprise at a choice is minus the log of its chance. A sure thing, chance 1, surprises 0. Chance one half gives 0.69, one quarter 1.39, one tenth 2.30. Rarer choices surprise more, without limit as the chance shrinks to 0. The curve shows surprise against chance.

trpo:11.t: K L divergence. Watch old Pip choose: the batch came from old Pip. On the moves old Pip makes, how much less likely does new Pip make them? Per move: log(old chance divided by new chance). Average it, weighted by old Pip’s chances: that is the K L divergence. Same policies give 0. At the start, new Pip almost never goes up, which old Pip did 0.55 of the time: that term alone is 4.01. The others add minus 0.18; single terms can be negative, the total never is. K L 3.83. After the normal step: 0.007.

trpo:12.t: The trust region rule. T R P O, Trust Region Policy Optimization (Schulman and colleagues, 2015), turns this into a rule: improve as the batch suggests, but keep the K L below a limit. The K L is worked out exactly in each cell Pip visited, then averaged over the visits. A common limit is 0.01. On this batch the big step has average K L 3.47. Even the normal step, 0.026, is over, although it did no harm: 0.01 is a habit from large networks, stricter than this small maze needs.

trpo:13.t: Halve until it fits. Real T R P O uses heavier maths to propose a step that should just fit. Our toy starts from the big step and halves until the K L fits and the batch still predicts a gain: weight each move’s advantage by new chance divided by old chance and add up. That total must beat the old policy’s. Here: six halvings, from 100 to 1.56, K L 0.008. Score 0.36 to 0.38, a little less than the plain alpha equals 3 step gave: safety costs some speed.

trpo:14.t: Forty updates, fifty runs. Now from a blank policy, 40 updates, averaged over 50 runs with different dice. Rose: plain steps of alpha equals 100. Teal: plain steps of alpha equals 3. Blue: T R P O, limit 0.01, halving from 100. Big plain steps: 46 of 50 runs got stuck near 0. Small plain steps: 0.32 after 10 updates, 0.50 after 40. T R P O starts slower, 0.17 after 10, because early on only steps of about 1 to 3 fit. It ends at 0.53, every run within 0.02 of the best, none stuck.

trpo:15.t: Which part does the work?. T R P O here does two things: it halves the step, and it checks the K L. Which one prevents the crashes? The rose line keeps the halving and the gain check but drops the K L check. Without the K L check, 46 of 50 runs get stuck, as bad as plain big steps. The batch predicts a gain even for huge steps: on the first update, 50 of 50 runs took the full alpha equals 100. The K L limit does the work.

trpo:16.t: Your turn. Drag the K L limit. Each setting reruns the same 50 runs of T R P O from a blank policy, always halving from alpha equals 100. The line is the average score; the card counts runs stuck near 0. Tiny limits are safe but crawl. Big limits let the big steps through: at limit 1, 15 of 50 runs get stuck.

trpo:17.t: A limit that adapts, at a price. A fixed small alpha also worked here, but the safe alpha changes as Pip learns. In run 0 the first 10 updates fit only steps of 0.78 to 3.13; at the end the full 100 fit, because with chances near 0 or 1 the (1 minus chance) factors and the advantages are small. The cost: at the old policy the K L is 0 and flat, so how fast it grows is set by its curvature. Real T R P O computes that curvature: second-order maths, slow and fiddly for big networks.

trpo:18.t: Where it was used. In 2015 T R P O trained simulated robots to swim, hop and walk, and played several Atari games straight from the screen pixels. Its steady improvement made it a standard baseline. In 2017 Schulman and colleagues, now at OpenAI, introduced P P O, which keeps the “don’t move too far” idea with a much simpler trick. P P O then largely replaced T R P O in practice.

trpo:19.t: Recap. A step that is too big can wreck a good policy, and the wrecked policy then collects poor walks to learn from. A batch’s advice is a local map: trust it only near the old policy. T R P O measures how far a step goes by the K L divergence between old and new chances, and only accepts steps within a limit.

muzero:0.t: MuZero. Plan like AlphaZero, without being told the rules.

muzero:1.t: Searching without a rulebook. Look again at AlphaZero’s search. Every loop, it plays moves by the rules to reach a new position, and the rules say when a game is won. Pip held the rulebook. Atari games, robots and most real problems come with no rulebook. Can Pip still search ahead? MuZero says yes: learn your own model of what moves do, and search inside it.

muzero:2.t: What should the model predict?. One idea: predict the next board exactly, square by square, like a picture. For a game screen that means every pixel, mostly details that never matter. MuZero asks less. Its model only has to predict what the search uses: the reward a move pays, the value of where it leads, and a prior over the next moves. Like the world-models reel, it plans in a learned model; unlike it, the model never predicts the board, and a search, not a policy trained in the dream, uses it.

muzero:3.t: Three small networks. h reads the real board once and turns it into a hidden state: here, 18 numbers, drawn as bars, above the line for positive, below for negative. g, the dynamics, takes a hidden state and a move and imagines the next hidden state, plus the reward for that move. f, the prediction, takes any hidden state and gives a prior and a value, like AlphaZero’s network. Ours have 5,519 knobs in all.

muzero:4.t: Rewards and values here. We keep Pip’s points. A move that ends the game pays its result as a reward: 1 for Pip’s win,  one half for a draw, 0 for a cat win. Every other move pays 0. The value is the points still to come, so once the game is over, it is 0. A move’s worth is then reward plus the value where it leads, with no discount. At the cat’s turns the search uses 1 minus that worth, as before. In AlphaZero’s reel the value included a finished game’s result; here MuZero must predict that result as a reward.

muzero:5.t: Imagining a line. From Pip’s puzzle, h reads the board. Then g imagines five moves in a row: Pip top right, cat bottom right, Pip centre, cat middle left, Pip bottom left. MuZero never sees those boards; we draw them faded, for us. Its predictions: rewards 0.00, 0.00, 0.02, 0.00, then 0.95 on the last move, which in the real game completes Pip’s diagonal. After it, the value is 0.00: nothing more to come. Earlier values stay below 1 on this sure win: f learned from a half-random player’s games, as we will see.

muzero:6.t: Searching inside the model. MuZero runs AlphaZero’s search with the model in place of the rules. Each new node: g gives its hidden state and the reward for the move, f gives its prior and value. Only the top position is real: there the game tells MuZero which squares are empty, as in the paper. Deeper, all 9 moves are allowed. The search alternates Pip and cat and is never told when an imagined game ends: after a winning move the model should predict reward and value near 0, so further moves add nothing.

muzero:7.t: How the model learns. Take a position from a recorded game and replay the next 3 real moves inside the model, starting from h. At every imagined step, the predictions are compared with what really happened: the reward that move really paid, how the game ended, and the move really played. Past the end of a game, the targets are reward 0 and value 0. The errors flow back through f, g and h; for the move shares the error measure is cross-entropy, as in AlphaZero. So the hidden state is shaped to hold whatever helps predict those three things, and nobody ever says what its 18 numbers should mean.

muzero:8.t: Our toy is simplified. Real MuZero learns from its own games, played with its own search, as AlphaZero did. In our tests that loop was too slow to learn well in a browser. So this toy learns from 3,000 recorded games by a player who makes a perfect move half the time and a random move otherwise; the move played is the policy target. Training ran ahead of time: 960,000 lessons, 3 moves unrolled each. The weights are stored in the reel. Apart from the legal moves at the top, the model never sees the rules.

muzero:9.t: Did it learn what matters?. Check every position where Pip is to move, and every move. Of the 1,834 moves that win at once, g predicts a reward above one half for 1,550. Of the 6,717 moves after which the game goes on, it predicts below one half for 6,345; the other 372 are imagined wins that the search may chase. The 80 moves that end in a draw get 0.50 on average. Nobody told it what three in a row is. It learned most of it from which moves ended games, because that helped predict rewards.

muzero:10.t: The puzzle, searched in its head. Now the search, with 50 loops inside the model. It sends 18 through top right, 8 through the centre and 11 through bottom right, a move that loses against best play. All 50 loops go through a move: the top is judged before they start. It plays top right. Top right’s average, 0.81, is the highest, but the centre’s, 0.76, is close. Every position below the top was imagined: no rules, no real boards. Here the search inside the model finds the winning move, as the real-rules searches did.

muzero:11.t: How good is it?. On 200 random positions where the choice matters, f’s prior alone picks a best move in 138; searching 50 loops in the model, 148. But our toy learned by imitation: is the model to blame, or that training? Test: the same h and f, searching with the real rules instead of g: 197. Against a perfect player: 17 losses of 60 searching in the model, 2 with the real rules. So here the learned model’s errors are the main cost; its search even dropped the prior’s right move in 19 positions, while fixing 29.

muzero:12.t: Your turn. Tap squares to imagine moves from Pip’s puzzle, Pip and cat taking turns. Each tap runs g once: you see the predicted reward and the value after it. The faded board shows what really happens; MuZero does not see it. Try the winning line, or a move onto a square that is already taken. The model was never told that is impossible. Tap the reset note to start again.

muzero:13.t: Where it is used. MuZero was published by Julian Schrittwieser and colleagues at DeepMind in Nature in 2020, after a 2019 preprint. Given the legal moves but not the rules, it matched AlphaZero in chess, shogi and Go, and set a new state of the art on a set of 57 Atari games, where the prior is over joystick moves and rewards are game points. Later versions learned from fixed records of past play, and a MuZero agent was trialled for compressing YouTube videos.

muzero:14.t: Recap. MuZero searches like AlphaZero, but inside a model it learned. h turns the board into a hidden state, g imagines a move’s next state and reward, f gives a prior and a value. The model is trained only to predict rewards, results and moves, never to draw the board. So it keeps what matters for choosing moves, and the search trusts it, errors included.

successor:0.t: Successor Features. Know where you’ll go, and new goals cost almost nothing.

successor:1.t: Back in the maze. Same maze, habit and rules as in the T D reel: dry floor, the arrows with one move in five random, plus 1 on the step onto the cheese, minus 1 onto the cat, either ends the walk, gamma (gamma) equals 0.9. After its 200 walks, T D gave Pip this notebook: 0.98 left of the cheese, 0.34 at the start. Each says how good a cell is, under this habit, for this cheese. They are noisy: the true values are 0.87 and 0.40, and that noise will follow us through this reel.

successor:2.t: What if the cheese moves?. Tomorrow someone swaps the cheese and the cat. Walls, habit, the two ending cells: all the same. Only what the ending cells pay has changed. Pip’s notebook is now wrong almost everywhere, because each number mixes two things together: where Pip tends to go, and what it finds there. Plain T D would have to unlearn and relearn, walk by walk.

successor:3.t: Two questions. So keep the two apart. Question one: from here, where will I go? That depends only on the maze and Pip’s habit. Question two: what does each cell pay? That is the part that changed. Like knowing your town’s streets: whether today you want the bakery or the pool, the streets you would walk are the same. Only the errand changes.

successor:4.t: Counting future visits. Answer question one by counting. Walk 1 from the start: Pip steps into cell 11, then 6, and so on, reaching the cheese on step 7. Score each cell it steps into: 1 for the next step, 0.9 for the step after, 0.81 after that, one more 0.9 per step. That is the same discounting as for rewards. The cheese cell gets 0.9 multiplied 6 times: 0.53. Ending cells count too; after them the walk is over.

successor:5.t: Pip’s map from the start. One walk is luck. Average such scores over all possible walks from the start, and you get Pip’s map of where it will go: 1.12 for the cell above the start (more than 1: Pip can step in more than once), 0.43 for the cheese cell, 0.03 for the cat’s. This map is called the successor representation (Peter Dayan, 1993). The start itself gets 0.17, from walks that wander back to it; counting begins with the next step, to match “reward on arrival”. Computed here with the rulebook, as a check.

successor:6.t: Value from the map. Now question two. What each cell pays when Pip steps onto it: cheese plus 1, cat minus 1, every other cell 0. This works because the pay depends only on the cell Pip lands in. Multiply each cell’s visits by its pay, and add up. From the start: 0.43 times 1 plus 0.03 times ( minus 1) equals 0.40. That is exactly the start’s value under this habit, the number the sweeps found in the earlier reels.

successor:7.t: Learning the map by T D. Without the rulebook, Pip learns the map the T D way, one row per open cell: 16 times 18 numbers instead of T D’s 16. After each step, the whole row of the cell just left moves toward 1 for the landing cell plus 0.9 times the landing cell’s row; nothing is added if the walk ended. It is the T D rule with a 1 for “I arrived here” in place of the reward. Walk 1, step 1: Pip lands in cell 11, whose row is still all 0, so the start’s entry for cell 11 moves a fifth of the way to 1: 0.2.

successor:8.t: 200 walks later. After the same 200 walks, Pip’s learned start row: 1.23 above the start, 0.41 at the cheese, 0.07 at the cat; close to the rulebook’s map on the usual route, rougher elsewhere. Multiply by the pays, and every cell matches the T D reel’s notebook exactly: 0.34 at the start. Why? Same walks, same alpha, and the map update is linear, so multiplying it by the pays gives the T D update term by term. With fixed rewards the map buys nothing; it pays off when rewards change.

successor:9.t: The swap. Now the cheese and the cat trade places. Pip keeps its map: the habit and the walls did not change. It only rewrites the pays: plus 1 for the old cat cell, minus 1 for the old cheese cell, and multiplies again. Instantly, with no new walk: the start reads minus 0.34, the cell left of the old cheese minus 0.98. Here the pays simply traded places, so every value flips its sign; the next example is less tidy.

successor:10.t: Relearning, the slow way. Plain T D has only its old notebook. Let it walk 200 more times after the swap. Gold: how far its numbers are, on average, from the true new values under the old habit. Dashed teal: the instant re-weighted values, 0.26 off. T D starts 0.96 off; its start value turns negative only after walk 34; after 200 walks it is 0.29 off. Both share the noise of a fixed alpha; the map got there at once.

successor:11.t: Any new reward. Rewards can change anywhere, not only at the ending cells. Put the cheese and cat back, and add a crumb in cell 6, on Pip’s usual route: plus 0.5 every time Pip steps onto it, and the walk goes on. Same map, new pays: the start’s value jumps from 0.34 to 0.86 at once, because the map says Pip steps onto that cell often and early. The rulebook’s answer is 0.89.

successor:12.t: Your turn. Tap a cell to put a crumb there, worth plus 0.5 each time Pip steps onto it. Tap it again to take it away. Pip’s values come straight from its learned map times the new pays, with no new walks. Crumbs on the usual route lift many cells; crumbs in corners Pip rarely visits barely matter, because the map gives them few visits.

successor:13.t: The catch. The map belongs to the habit. After the swap, Pip’s arrows still march toward the old cheese corner, now the cat. A better habit would take other routes, and a new habit has a new map, which must be relearned, at least in part. To pick better moves without the rulebook, keep a map per move, like Q-values per move, and improve the habit as Q-learning does. The successor representation makes new rewards cheap, not new habits.

successor:14.t: Successor features. Big worlds have too many cells to map one by one. Successor features (André Barreto and colleagues, 2017) map future amounts of a few features, like food or water; a task gives each feature a weight, and value is map times weights. Keep several old habits’ maps. For a new task, each habit’s value comes instantly; at every spot, follow the habit that looks best there. This generalised policy improvement is at least as good as each old habit.

successor:15.t: A map in the brain?. The hippocampus holds place cells: neurons that fire when an animal is in a particular place. Kimberly Stachenfeld, Matthew Botvinick and Samuel Gershman (2017) proposed that they hold a predictive map like Pip’s: firing for where the animal is likely to go next, not just where it is. This fits some recordings, such as place fields that stretch backward along a habitual path. How far the idea goes is still debated.

successor:16.t: Recap. The successor representation splits value into a map of where Pip will go, discounted future visits to every cell under its habit, and what each cell pays. Value is visits times pay, added up. The map is learned by T D, with “I arrived here” in place of the reward. When rewards change, new values come instantly; when the habit changes, the map must be relearned.

contextual:0.t: Contextual Bandits. Same slot machines, but now you know who’s playing.

contextual:1.t: Open late. The cheese arcade now stays open from 10 in the morning until 10 at night. One new rule: the chances drift with the hour. Each pull happens in one of the 12 opening hours, 10:00 to 21:00. At 10:00 they are the ones from the earlier reels: A 30, B 55, C 70, D 15 percent. Through the day C fades and D wakes up. By 21:00: A 25, B 45, C 25, D 80 percent.

contextual:2.t: Who is best, and when. Here are the four chances through the day. Left to right: the hour. Upward: the chance of a crumb. Each line is one machine, moving in a straight line from morning to night. The dots mark the best machine each hour: C until 14:00, then B at 15:00, then D from 16:00. Pulling the best machine for every hour would drop a crumb on 63 percent of pulls.

contextual:3.t: One winner for everyone?. Each pull now happens at a random opening hour. A plain bandit ignores the clock and hunts for the single best machine on average: that is B, at 50 percent, with C and D close behind at 48 percent. Even if it found B perfectly, it would get a crumb on 50 percent of pulls, while the best-for-the-hour plan gets 63 percent. One winner for everyone leaves crumbs on the table.

contextual:4.t: Look at the clock first. Information you can see before choosing is called the context: here, the hour. It is like a state that your pulls cannot change. A contextual bandit sees the context, picks an arm, gets a reward, and learns which arm is best for each kind of situation. One thing stays simple: Pip’s pull doesn’t change what time the next pull happens. When actions shape future situations, you need full reinforcement learning.

contextual:5.t: A row for each part of the day. The simplest fix: keep separate tallies for each context. Split the day into two rows, 10:00 to 15:00 and 16:00 to 21:00, and run U C B in each row on its own, as if each were its own arcade. Each row starts from scratch: it first pulls every machine once, then follows estimate plus bonus, using only that row’s pulls.

contextual:6.t: Each row settles. After 1000 pulls in this visit, the morning row pulled C 297 times out of 480, and the evening row pulled D 380 times out of 520. Each row found its own winner. Within a row the hours still differ: at 15:00 B is best, but only by one percentage point over C, so lumping 15:00 in with the morning costs very little.

contextual:7.t: Keeping score. Regret now compares each pull with the best machine at that hour: at 10:00 a pull of D gives up 0.70 minus 0.15, at 21:00 it gives up nothing. Averaged over 2000 visits of 1000 pulls: the clock-blind U C B, in grey, ends at 158. Two rows of U C B, in gold: 85. A row player that already knew its best machine would lose under 1 crumb per 1000 pulls, so nearly all of that is the cost of learning.

contextual:8.t: Finer rows?. Why not one row per hour? Rows that fine are exactly right about their hour. But learning is the real cost here, and each of twelve rows sees only about one pull in twelve, starting from scratch. With twelve rows, regret after 1000 pulls is 125: worse than two rows. More rows means more to learn, with less data in each. Real contexts, like a visitor’s age, place and history, would need millions of rows.

contextual:9.t: Share what you learn: a line. Instead of rows, give each machine a straight line: chance equals start plus slope times lateness, where lateness runs from 0 at 10:00 to 1 at 21:00. Every pull of D, at any hour, helps place D’s line. Here are D’s 45 results from the first 100 pulls of one visit: a dot at the top for a crumb, at the bottom for nothing, placed at its hour. The line is the best fit through them.

contextual:10.t: Lin U C B: a line plus a bonus. To explore, add a bonus, as in U C B. The shaded band shows how unsure each line is. It depends on how many pulls the machine has had near each hour: narrow where results pile up, wide where they are few, like U C B’s bonus shrinking with n. Score equals line plus half the band’s width. This is Lin U C B (Li, Chu, Langford and Schapire, 2010). Lines start flat at 0, so an untried machine gets tried only thanks to its wide band.

contextual:11.t: Lines win. Lin U C B, in purple, ends at 24 after 1000 pulls, far below two rows (85) and twelve rows (125). Be fair to the rows, though: here the true chances really are straight lines, so the line model fits perfectly. When the real pattern is curved, a line can be wrong for some hours however much data it gets; then richer models, even neural networks, are used.

contextual:12.t: Your turn. Drag the hour: these are Lin U C B’s lines after 1000 pulls of one visit, with its scores and pick at that hour. A and B were pulled only 3 times each and dropped nothing, so their lines sit at 0; only their wide bands keep them in the running. Try 15:00. B is truly best there (50%), but Lin U C B picks D (45%): a miss of about 6 percentage points at that hour.

contextual:13.t: The fine print. A bandit only sees the result of the arm it pulled. With rows, if Pip never pulled A in the evening, it has no evening data on A at all. A line can guess from morning pulls, but only if a line is the right shape. The same gap bites later: records of old pulls only show what the old strategy chose, so testing a new strategy on them fairly needs special care.

contextual:14.t: Where it is used. In 2010, Lin U C B chose which news stories to show on the Yahoo! front page. In the authors’ tests, it earned about 12.5 percent more clicks than a bandit that ignored the context. Contextual bandits now help choose ads, recommendations and notification times, and are studied for personalised treatments in medicine. The context is whatever you know about the user and the moment.

contextual:15.t: Recap. A contextual bandit looks at the context before choosing, because the best arm can depend on the situation. Few contexts: keep a row of tallies for each and run a bandit per row. Many contexts: learn a model that shares data, like Lin U C B’s line plus bonus. Either way, the pull does not change the next context.

dt:0.t: Decision Transformer. What if R L were just predicting the next word?

dt:1.t: A box of old diaries. Pip finds a box of 40 diaries. Each records one walk by the Wanderer, the mouse from earlier reels who moves at random, bumping into walls. Pip may not walk itself; it can only learn from these pages, as in the offline R L reel. In this box, 2 walks reached the cheese, 8 met the cat, and the other 30 were stopped after 30 moves.

dt:2.t: Rules for this reel. Same maze, dry floor, but new scoring: every move costs 0.05, stepping onto the cheese pays plus 1 and onto the cat minus 1, and either ends the walk. Rewards are simply added up, with no discount: a Decision Transformer works with plain totals, so the total still wanted simply drops by each reward received. So shorter is better. The best possible walk takes 7 moves: 1 minus 7 times 0.05 equals 0.65. The best diary in the box scores only minus 0.10.

dt:3.t: Return-to-go. The key number is the return-to-go: the total still to come from this moment. Here is the box’s best diary: 22 moves, 7 of them bumps into walls or rocks. At the start it is minus 0.10, the walk’s whole total. Each move’s cost, once paid, is no longer to come, so the number creeps up by 0.05. On the last move the cheese’s reward arrives, and nothing is left: 0.

dt:4.t: A walk as a sentence. Write each step of a diary as three tokens, like three words: the return-to-go, the cell, the move. The return-to-go goes in as a plain number; the network turns each token into a list of numbers it can read. A whole walk becomes a sentence. Cells are numbered 1 to 20 as in the loop reel; the start is cell 16. A transformer, the kind of network behind chatbots, reads such sentences and learns to predict the next move token, the way a chatbot predicts the next word.

dt:5.t: Training is plain prediction. Training needs no values and no Bellman updates: the model just learns to predict the logged move from what came before. That is simple and stable: no values feeding on their own guesses, the loop that inflated numbers in the offline R L reel. Ours is a stand-in, not a network: a lookup. In this cell, find the diary steps whose return-to-go is closest to the total still wanted, and copy their most common move, up first on a tie. A real one also reads recent steps and generalises. Grey dots mark where the diaries went.

dt:6.t: Ask for 0.65. Now ask for the best possible total, 0.65. In cell 16 the closest return-to-go is 0.40, from a diary that came back to cell 16 late in its walk, so Pip copies up. After each move Pip subtracts the reward it got from the total still wanted, and looks again. Pip reaches the cheese in 7 moves: 0.65. That beats every diary in the box; the best scored minus 0.10.

dt:7.t: Pieces of different walks. How can it beat every diary? At each cell it copies a step from whichever diary fits the total still wanted, and those steps came from 2 different diaries, the only 2 in the box that reached the cheese. Pieces of different walks join into a better one: stitching. The Decision Transformer paper saw the same thing in a small test: trained only on random walks, asking for a high return gave short paths.

dt:8.t: Ask for less. The number is a dial. Ask for 0, and Pip reaches the cheese the long way, in 20 moves: 0.00. Ask for minus 1.5, and it wanders until it is stopped after 30 moves: minus 1.50. Nobody wants a bad walk, but it shows the model really listens to the total it is given.

dt:9.t: Asked versus got. Every request in steps of 0.05, from minus 1.5 to 1. Across: the total asked for. Up: the total Pip got. On the dashed diagonal Pip gets exactly what it asks. Below minus 0.5 it always wanders until stopped, minus 1.50. It never finds a quick trip to the cat, because no diary made one: the quickest of the 8 cat walks took 10 moves. From minus 0.5 up to 0.65 the dots sit on the diagonal. Above 0.65 they stay flat: asking for 1 still gives 0.65. No better walk exists here to copy.

dt:10.t: Only what is in the box. Another box, where no diary ever reached the cheese. Ask for 0.65 and Pip wanders until stopped: minus 1.50. No total, however high, can produce cheese steps that were never written down. A copier is limited by the pieces in its data. Value learning on that box reaches no cheese either: it heads for the cat in 5 moves, minus 1.25, the least bad ending it has seen.

dt:11.t: When pieces do not join. A third box has all the pieces of the 7-move route. Asked for 0.65, Pip still takes 9 moves: 0.55. In cell 11 the closest return-to-go came from a diary that went right, the long way. Value learning, from the offline R L reel, here a table over logged moves only, so nothing is invented, finds 0.65 here: a move’s value is its reward plus the best value seen where it lands, so good endings flow back through shared cells. The lookup joins pieces only when the countdown lines up.

dt:12.t: A hundred boxes. Now 100 boxes for each size: 5, 10, 20, 40 and 80 diaries. Across: diaries per box. Up: how many of the 100 boxes gave the 7-move walk. Grey: a single diary already was that walk. Blue: the lookup asked for 0.65. Green: value learning. Both join pieces far beyond any single diary. The lookup does it less reliably: with 40 diaries, 78 boxes against 85.

dt:13.t: Your turn. Drag the total to ask for, and Pip plays it from the start, in the first box. Tap the maze to switch to the third box, where the pieces do not line up. Watch where it lands below 0.65, and what happens when you ask for more than the maze allows.

dt:14.t: Where it came from. Lili Chen and colleagues introduced the Decision Transformer in 2021; the similar Trajectory Transformer appeared at the same time. On offline benchmarks of Atari games and simulated robots, it held its own against offline R L methods of that time. Later studies found stitching unreliable, as here, and that in worlds with chance it can copy moves that were merely lucky: on a wet floor, a slide that happened to land well carries a high return-to-go, so asking for a high total copies that move. Its appeal is that training is plain, stable prediction.

dt:15.t: Recap. A Decision Transformer treats R L as sequence prediction: write each logged step as return-to-go, state and action, and learn to predict the action. At play time, ask for a high return and subtract rewards as they arrive. It can join pieces of walks, but less reliably than value learning, and it cannot use pieces the data never had.

grpo:0.t: R L for L L M Reasoning (G R P O). Let the model try, let a checker grade it, repeat.

grpo:1.t: Bot’s homework. Bot, the answer machine from the R L H F reel, now helps Pip with sums, like 4 plus 7 times 3. These answers can be checked by a program: compute the true value, compare the final number. Right scores 1, wrong scores 0. No people comparing answers and no learned reward model to fool: just a cheap, exact check. This is a verifiable reward. A checker can still have loopholes; more on that later.

grpo:2.t: Four ways to answer. A real language model writes its working word by word. Bot is a stand-in: it picks one of four ways of answering, each with a chance, learned by copying examples. Guess a number. Work left to right, which goes wrong whenever times follows plus. Do times first, with an occasional slip. Or do times first and then check, which catches most slips.

grpo:3.t: How good is each way?. Only the simulation knows this. On 400 test sums, half like 3 plus 5 and half like 3 plus 5 times 2: guessing gets 0.18 right, left to right 0.50, times first 0.89, times first and check 0.97. Bot starts by guessing 0.30 of the time, left to right 0.40, times first 0.20, times first and check 0.10. With these chances it gets 0.53 of the test sums right. Bot never sees this table; it only sees the checker’s 1s and 0s.

grpo:4.t: A group of eight. Take one question, 7 plus 8 times 7. Bot answers it 8 times, a group, each time picking its way of answering by chance. The checker marks each one. 2 of the 8 are right. The small names show which way Bot used: both right answers did times first; a third times-first answer slipped to 64.

grpo:5.t: Grade on the curve. The group’s average score is 0.25. That is the yardstick, as in the baselines reel. Each answer’s advantage is its score minus the average: right answers get plus 0.75, wrong ones minus 0.25. G R P O, Group Relative Policy Optimization, also divides by the group’s spread, the standard deviation of the 8 scores, here 0.43: so plus 1.73 and minus 0.58. That puts every question on one scale, though a lone right answer in 8 would get plus 2.65. If all 8 scores are equal, the spread is 0 and every advantage is set to 0.

grpo:6.t: No critic needed. P P O usually trains a critic, a second network that predicts the expected score, to serve as the yardstick. For a language model the critic is about as big as the model itself. G R P O uses the group’s average instead. The price is several answers per question; the gain is one less big network to train and store.

grpo:7.t: One update. Now nudge the chances. As in the policy gradient reel, a chance is e to a preference, rescaled to add up to 1. Each answer adds advantage times (1 minus chance) to its own way’s preference and takes advantage times chance from the others, averaged over the group. Times first rises from 0.20 to 0.30, left to right falls from 0.40 to 0.33. A K L leash, beta (beta) equals 0.04, pulls toward the original Bot, as in the R L H F reel. Real G R P O also clips like P P O; with one pass per batch the clip never acts.

grpo:8.t: A training run. Each update: 8 questions, half easy on average, 8 answers each, so 64 answers. The chart shows test accuracy after each update; the bars, Bot’s chances. After 40 updates, accuracy rises from 0.53 to 0.95. Guessing and left to right fade to 0.01 and 0.02; times first and check grows to 0.87. Even times first drops to 0.11: its slips lose out to the checked answers in the same groups.

grpo:9.t: Silent groups. If all 8 answers are right, or all wrong, every advantage is 0: the group teaches nothing. Over updates 1 to 10, 11 percent of groups on easy sums were silent, and 2 percent on hard ones. Over updates 31 to 40, as Bot improves, that rises to 51 and 49 percent. Easy and hard are now equally silent: left to right, the one way that fails only on hard sums, has nearly vanished. Useful questions are ones Bot sometimes gets right and sometimes wrong.

grpo:10.t: Your turn. Drag the group size. Every update still uses 64 answers, so bigger groups mean fewer questions. The curve shows the chance that a group is not silent, for a question Bot gets right with chance p. The card gives the average of 20 training runs after 40 updates, so group 8 shows 0.93, not the single run’s 0.95. Tiny groups are often silent. Here group 16 does best, 0.95: a steadier yardstick outweighs having fewer questions.

grpo:11.t: It sharpens, it does not invent. Suppose Bot never checks its work: that chance starts at 0, and its share is spread over the other three ways. Then no group ever contains a check, and nothing can reward it. The same training reaches 0.87, against 0.95 with checking available. G R P O raises the ways Bot already sometimes uses. And a checker is only as honest as its rules: one that accepted any answer containing the right number could be gamed.

grpo:12.t: Where it is used. G R P O was introduced in DeepSeekMath (Shao and colleagues, 2024) to train a model on maths problems. DeepSeek R 1 (2025) used it with rule-based rewards: is the final answer right, is the format followed. During R1’s training its answers grew longer and more often contained checking and rethinking, habits the starting model already showed now and then. Many labs now train reasoning models in a similar way.

grpo:13.t: Recap. When answers can be checked by a program, the checker gives the reward. For each question, sample a group of answers and score them. Each answer’s advantage is its score against the group’s average, scaled by the spread: no critic needed. A K L leash keeps the model near where it started, and groups that are all right or all wrong teach nothing.

saferl:0.t: Safe  and  Constrained R L. Win the game, but never cross the line.

saferl:1.t: A room with a glass floor. A new room for Pip: 6 cells across, 4 up, no rocks, no cat. Start bottom left, cheese bottom right: plus 1 on the step onto it, which ends the walk; every other step pays 0; gamma (gamma) equals 0.9. In the middle of the floor are four glass panels. Stepping on them changes nothing in Pip’s reward. That is exactly the problem.

saferl:2.t: A second number: cost. We care about the glass: every step onto a panel risks breaking it. So we count it in a second signal, the cost: 1 for each step onto glass, 0 otherwise. Cost is kept separate from reward. Reward says how well Pip did; cost says how much harm it risked. Ideally the harm would stay low even while Pip is learning; we will see how far this method gets.

saferl:3.t: Two routes. The shortcut runs along the bottom: 5 steps, 2 of them on glass. The detour goes up and around: 9 steps, no glass. Counted from the start with the 0.9 discount, the shortcut’s cheese is worth 0.9 to the 4th, 0.66. The detour’s is 0.9 to the 8th, 0.43. Reward alone prefers the shortcut.

saferl:4.t: Pip ignores the glass. First Pip trains for 300 walks with Q-learning on reward alone, as in earlier reels, one move in five random. It learns the shortcut. Over walks 201 to 300 it stepped on glass 3.0 times per walk on average: the 2 of the shortcut, plus random moves that land on glass.

saferl:5.t: Why not a fixed penalty?. We could subtract a fixed penalty w for each glass step, counted plainly, without discount. The shortcut is then worth 0.66 minus 2 times w, the detour 0.43. Below w equals 0.11 the shortcut always wins, two glass steps every walk, not counting random moves; above it, the detour always wins, none. Only a w exactly at the tie could mix the routes, and finding that knife-edge value by hand needs all these numbers.

saferl:6.t: Say what you want. Constrained R L states the goal directly: get as much reward as possible, counted with the 0.9 discount as always, subject to the average cost per walk staying under a budget we choose. Our budget: at most 1 glass step per walk, on average. The shortcut costs at least 2, the detour almost nothing, so the best way to meet the budget is to take the shortcut only some of the time. Pip has to find that balance.

saferl:7.t: A price on glass. The trick is a price lambda (lambda) per glass step: Pip maximises reward minus lambda times cost. After each walk, lambda goes up by 0.01 times the overspend, glass steps minus budget, never below 0. Overspend and the price rises; underspend and it falls. In maths, lambda is a Lagrange multiplier: it turns a limit into a price. The 0.01 is a knob: larger reacts faster but swings more, smaller overspends longer.

saferl:8.t: Two notebooks. Pip keeps two numbers per move: reward to come, with the 0.9 discount, and glass steps to come, simply counted, because the budget counts plain glass steps. After each move, each is nudged as in Q-learning toward what this step gave plus the next number: 0.9 times it for reward, all of it for glass. “Next” means the move Pip would pick next by its score. The score is reward minus lambda times glass. So the glass number describes how Pip really plans to act, and a new price changes its choices at once.

saferl:9.t: Reading the chart. The chart starts at walk 301, when the price is switched on. Across: walks, up to 1000. Gold, on top: the price lambda. Rose, below: glass steps per walk, averaged over the last 25 walks. The dashed line is the budget, 1. Watch the two lines push against each other.

saferl:10.t: The price at work. At first Pip overspends, so the price climbs, peaking at 0.53 on walk 345. By then the detour wins and glass drops below budget, so the price drifts down until the shortcut wins again now and then. Over the last 300 walks the price averages 0.12. Pip goes along the bottom on 105 of them, about 2.3 glass steps each, and around on the rest, 0.3 each from random moves. Together: 1 per walk, right on budget.

saferl:11.t: The tipping point. Back at the cell where the routes split. “Right” promises 0.73 reward and 2 glass; “up” 0.48 and 0. The scores are equal at a price of 0.13. From the start it was 0.11: reward shrinks with distance, glass does not, so the tie depends on where you stand, and this cell is where the routes split. The price settles near there, 0.12 on average. Just below it Pip takes the shortcut, just above it the detour, so small swings mix the two routes.

saferl:12.t: Glass broken while learning. The budget holds on average, after the price has settled. Before that, Pip stepped on glass a lot: 754 times in the first 300 walks, 712 more in the next 700. Even on the detour, random moves still land on glass 0.3 times per walk. If one break is a disaster, averages are not enough. Safe exploration needs more: a shield, a hand-written rule that blocks a few known-dangerous moves while Pip learns the rest, or starting from a safe habit.

saferl:13.t: Your turn. Pick a budget, in glass steps per walk. The run is repeated: 300 free walks, then 700 walks with the price. Whenever the routes must be mixed, the price settles near the tipping point; what changes is how often Pip takes the shortcut. A budget below what even the detour costs cannot be met, and the price keeps climbing. A loose budget leaves the price near 0.

saferl:14.t: In the real world. Eitan Altman’s 1999 book set out constrained MDPs. In 2017, Joshua Achiam and colleagues proposed Constrained Policy Optimisation for deep R L, and in 2019 OpenAI released Safety Gym, simulated robots that must reach goals while avoiding hazards, where price-based methods like P P O-Lagrangian are standard baselines. The same idea suits robots with limits on force or energy. Real deployments add many more safeguards.

saferl:15.t: Limits to know. The constraint is about the average: single walks can still go over, and learning itself can break the limit, as we saw. Someone must choose the budget. And cost is written by people, just like reward. A badly specified cost can be gamed too, as the reward hacking reel showed.

saferl:16.t: Recap. Keep harm in its own signal, the cost, separate from reward. Constrained R L maximises reward while the average cost stays under a budget. A Lagrange multiplier is a price on cost that rises while you overspend and falls while you underspend; it settles at the tipping point between options.

her:0.t: Goal-Conditioned R L  and  H E R. Missed the target? Pretend you were aiming there all along.

her:1.t: Go to the flag. New job. The cheese and the cat leave the meadow. Instead, each walk a flag is planted at a random spot, the goal, and Pip should go there. Pip starts at a random spot at least 0.3 away. Same moves and wobble as before. Landing within 0.04 of the flag pays plus 1 and ends the walk; every other move pays 0. A walk is stopped after 30 moves; that is not an ending, so the last move’s target still adds 0.9 times a guess. gamma is still 0.9.

her:2.t: The goal is an input. A new flag every walk means one fixed set of Q-values cannot work: “up” is good for a flag above Pip and bad for one below. So the goal becomes part of what the network sees. Six inputs: where Pip is, where the flag is, and the gap between them, across and up. The network could work out the gap itself; handing it over makes this small network’s job easier. 16 hidden units, four Q-values out. One network for every goal: a goal-conditioned network.

her:3.t: Almost never there. At first Pip’s network knows nothing, so its moves are aimless. The flag’s circle is tiny, only 0.04 from its centre to its edge, so aimless walks almost never land in it. Here are the first walks of a training run, one after another. In the first 100 walks, Pip reached the flag 12 times in this run; averaged over four runs, 4.8 times. Rewards this rare are called sparse.

her:4.t: A memory full of zeros. Look inside Pip’s replay memory after 2000 moves: 2000 cards, and only 9 of them carry a reward of plus 1. Every other target is 0 plus 0.9 times a guess, and the guesses start near 0. So nearly every lesson just copies one guess from another, with no real reward behind it. The 9 successes are drowned out, and almost nothing tells the network which way leads to a flag.

her:5.t: Training on zeros. Four training runs, 10000 moves each. Every 500 moves, Pip is tested on 30 fixed start-and-flag pairs, following its largest Q-value. The chart counts the flags it reaches, out of 30. After 10000 moves the four runs reach 21, 2, 6, 0 flags. One run broke through late; the other three stayed low.

her:6.t: A miss, in hindsight. Here is one failed walk from training. The flag was at (0.51, 0.19); after 30 moves Pip was stopped at (0.18, 0.17), well outside the flag’s circle. Now ask a question in hindsight: what if the flag had been where Pip ended? Then the very same walk would have been a success. Nothing about the moves changes; only the goal written on the cards.

her:7.t: Store it twice. This is Hindsight Experience Replay, or H E R (Marcin Andrychowicz and colleagues, OpenAI, 2017). Each card of a failed walk is stored twice: with the real goal and reward 0, and with the goal set to where the walk ended. In the copy, every move landing within 0.04 of the new goal pays plus 1 and ends it: always the last move, plus any earlier one that came that close (here, none). The rest pay 0 but bootstrap from the plus 1, as in T D.

her:8.t: Why that is not cheating. The copied cards tell the truth: from those spots, those moves really did lead to that place. So Pip learns, for real, how to reach that spot. Early walks often end against the fence, so many hindsight goals sit there, gold below. That still helps: the network reads the gap to the goal, so practice on any goal teaches the skill the real flags need, shrinking the gap.

her:9.t: A memory with successes. With H E R, after 2000 moves: 3620 cards. Only failed walks are copied: 54 walks times 30 moves equals 1620 copies. 313 cards carry plus 1 (without H E R: 9). 285 are copies, about 5 per copied walk, because Pip often lingered near its end spot: 253 of them come from walks that ended pinned against the fence. Real successes stay rare at first, but the network now gets plenty of lessons that end in plus 1, and they teach it how to steer toward a goal.

her:10.t: The race. Now the race: four runs with H E R in teal, the same four runs without it in orange, same seeds, same number of updates. Each minibatch draws 32 cards at random from the whole memory, real cards and copies alike. Thin lines: single runs; thick: averages. After 10000 moves, with H E R the runs reach 28, 23, 27, 25 of 30 flags, 25.8 on average. Without it, 7.3.

her:11.t: Any flag. Here is the H E R network of run 1 after training, sent to six of the test flags in turn. It never trained on these exact pairs; it reads the gap and steers. It reaches 5 of these 6. Near a flag it sometimes overshoots: one move covers 0.15, while the flag’s circle reaches only 0.04 from its centre, so the last step has to land just right.

her:12.t: Your turn. Tap the meadow to plant a flag. Pip starts bottom left and follows the H E R network’s largest Q-value, no random moves. Try flags far away, near the edges, and close by. The network was never told about your flag; it only reads where it is.

her:13.t: Where it’s used. Andrychowicz and colleagues used H E R with D D P G, an off-policy learner for continuous moves, where an actor network proposes the move (see the D D P G reel), on a simulated robot arm: pushing a block, sliding a puck, picking up and placing an object, with reward only on success. Without H E R, plain D D P G failed to learn these tasks; with it, the arm learned all three. A policy trained in simulation for picking and placing also worked on a real robot arm. Feeding the goal in as an input goes back to Tom Schaul and colleagues, 2015.

her:14.t: Limits. H E R needs goals that are places you can reach, so that wherever a walk ends can be written down as a goal. For a goal like “win the game”, an accidental ending is rarely useful. It also needs an off-policy learner like D Q N or D D P G, since the copied cards were made while chasing another goal. Here each copy uses the walk’s final spot; the paper did even better relabelling each card with spots the same walk reached after that card’s move, its “future” strategy.

her:15.t: Recap. A goal-conditioned network gets the goal as input, so one network serves every goal. With a reward only at the goal, early walks almost never succeed, and the memory fills with zeros. Hindsight Experience Replay stores each failed walk again as a success for the spot it actually reached. The moves really got there, so the lessons are true, and they teach the network to steer.

rnd:0.t: R N D  and  Go-Explore. How agents finally cracked the hardest exploration game.

rnd:1.t: Back in the meadow. Remember the meadow from the function approximation reel? Pip’s position there is two numbers, x and y. Each move goes 0.15 in its direction, plus a little random wobble. Because of the wobble, Pip practically never stands on exactly the same spot twice. Keep that in mind: it is about to break the counting trick from the curiosity reel.

rnd:2.t: A long meadow. Pip’s new meadow is 4 long and 1 wide. Pip starts at the left. The cheese circle sits at the far right end: plus 1 on the move that lands inside it, and the walk ends. There is no cat. Each walk is cut off after 40 moves, and Pip is put back at the start. Even walking straight right, the cheese takes at least 25 moves.

rnd:3.t: Random wandering. First, a Pip that picks every move at random, for 30 walks. Each walk is drawn as its own trail of dots. The farthest it ever gets is x equals 1.16, not even halfway. It never reaches the cheese. Random steps cancel out, as they did in the maze.

rnd:4.t: Nothing to count. Those walks landed on 1200 spots. Only 13 were exact repeats, all in the two left corners, where the fence squeezes Pip. So a count bonus would pay the first-visit 0.1 almost everywhere, even a hair away from a spot Pip has crossed many times. Counting only works when places repeat. Here, "near" never counts as "the same".

rnd:5.t: What we want instead. We want a sense of familiarity that spreads to nearby spots: if Pip has been around here a lot, here should feel boring, even if this exact spot is new. Networks do exactly that kind of spreading. In the function approximation reel, a nudge at one spot also moved the guesses at nearby spots.

rnd:6.t: A random network. Burda and colleagues proposed a neat trick in 2018. Take a small network, fill its knobs with random numbers, and never train it. Feed it a spot, and out come 4 numbers that mean nothing at all. Call it the fixed random network. (Not the target network of the D Q N reels: that one is a copy of the Q-network.)
