The map shows its first number across the meadow: gold positive, rose negative. Meaningless, but smooth and fixed.

rnd:7.t: The copier. A second network, the copier, tries to give the same 4 numbers. But it only gets lessons at spots Pip actually visits: after each move, one small gradient step that shrinks its copying error at that spot. The copying error is the average squared difference between the copier’s 4 numbers and the fixed random network’s 4 numbers.

rnd:8.t: Error marks the new. We give the copier lessons at the random walker’s 1200 spots, three times over. Before: error about 0.08 on the left, 0.07 at x equals 3. After: 0.003 on the left, where Pip walked, and 0.047 at x equals 3, where it never went. Both maps use the same colour scale: orange marks big error. Where Pip has been, the copy is good; far away, poorer. So copying error works as a novelty bonus. That is Random Network Distillation, or R N D.

rnd:9.t: Familiar by accident. Look again at the copier before any lessons: a pale band runs along the middle, where Pip has never been. At x equals 2 its error there is 0.042, against 0.243 near the top fence. By chance, the untrained copier already roughly matches the random network there. Spreading cuts both ways: lessons on the left also lowered the error at x equals 3, from 0.07 to 0.047. Such accidents can mislead Pip a little, until lessons sort them out.

rnd:10.t: Why a random network?. Any fixed pattern would do; random knobs are just the easiest. It never changes and looks only at what Pip sees now, so lessons can learn it: the bars show a fresh copier’s error at x equals 2 falling. Next-view prediction must guess the future, and a random future, like the noisy TV, can never be guessed. R N D never predicts the future. But static that is new each time is still a new input: less fooled, not immune.

rnd:11.t: Pip peeks. Pip knows roughly where each move takes it, but not where the cheese is. Before each move it checks the copying error at the four landing spots and takes the biggest, except 1 move in 10 at random. Then the copier gets one lesson at the new spot. This toy Pip only explores and does not learn from the cheese. Real R N D adds the bonus to the game reward and trains a policy on the sum.

rnd:12.t: The R N D explorer. Same start, fresh copier. The map shows the copier’s error at the start of each walk. As places become familiar, the orange retreats, and Pip’s peeks lead it into fresher grass. In walk 1 it gets to x equals 2.06. It first lands in the cheese in walk 14. Note that the bonus knows nothing about cheese: Pip finds it only by going where it has not been.

rnd:13.t: A chart of reach. To compare fairly, we run 20 different seeds of 30 walks each. Across: the walk number. Up: the farthest x reached so far, averaged over the 20 runs. The dashed line is the near edge of the cheese circle. A line that climbs means Pip keeps pushing into new ground.

rnd:14.t: Novelty pushes outward. Averages over 20 runs, so they differ from the one run we watched. Gold, the random walker: it creeps to 1.58 after 30 walks. Teal, the R N D explorer: 1.8 in walk 1 and 3.85 by walk 30, at the far end. The bonus ignores the cheese, so hitting the circle, radius 0.12, is partly luck: R N D landed in it in 11 of 20 runs, the random walker in 0. A learning agent would then use that plus 1.

rnd:15.t: Montezuma’s Revenge. The famous hard case is an Atari game from 1984, Montezuma’s Revenge. An explorer climbs through a pyramid of rooms, 24 on the first level, with keys, doors, ladders and deadly falls. Points are rare, and each needs a long chain of exact moves. In 2015 the D Q N agent, which mastered many Atari games, scored 0 here. In 2018, R N D became the first method to beat the average human score without human demonstrations.

rnd:16.t: Forgetting the frontier. Even with a bonus, every walk starts back at the start. The R N D explorer reached x equals 2.06 in walk 1, but walk 2 began from scratch and got only to 1.71. Our meadow has no fatal moves, so R N D copes here. In a game where a few wrong moves end the try, a promising place may never be reached again. Ecoffet and colleagues turned this around with Go-Explore, first shown in 2019 and published in 2021: first return, then explore.

rnd:17.t: How Go-Explore works. Pip lumps spots into coarse cells, squares 0.25 on a side, and keeps an archive: one saved spot per cell, the one reached in the fewest moves. Yes, that is counting again: coarse cells make places repeat, at the price of choosing the cell size by hand. R N D needs no such choice. Each round: pick a cell, favouring ones Pip has landed in rarely. Restore its saved spot, like loading a saved game. Then take 40 random moves.

rnd:18.t: Go-Explore in the meadow. Round by round, the archive grows outward. Shaded squares are cells in the archive. In this run, Pip lands in the cheese in round 31, with 60 cells saved. Over 20 runs it found the cheese within 60 rounds in 20 of them, a median of 29 rounds. Its moves are random: remembering and returning do the work. A round has the moves of one walk but never pays for the trip back, and a real robot usually cannot restore a saved spot.

rnd:19.t: Your turn. Tap the meadow to give the copier 30 lessons around that spot. Watch the orange, its copying error, fade there and a little around it. Tap a few spots in a row to paint a familiar trail. Tap below the meadow to start over with an untaught copier.

rnd:20.t: Where it worked. R N D, from OpenAI in 2018, was the first to beat average human play on Montezuma’s Revenge without demonstrations. Go-Explore, from Uber AI Labs, scored far higher there and also did well on Pitfall, another very sparse game. Go-Explore explored by restoring saved game states, then trained a network policy by imitating its own best routes, so it could follow them even when the game behaves a little randomly.

rnd:21.t: Recap. When places never repeat, counting fails. R N D measures novelty as the error of a copier chasing a fixed random network: small where you have been, large elsewhere, and it spreads to nearby spots. Go-Explore keeps an archive of reached places, returns to one, and explores from there. Reward novelty, and remember the frontier.

curriculum:0.t: Curriculum Learning. Nobody learns calculus before counting. Neither should agents.

curriculum:1.t: A long way to the cheese. A bigger maze: 8 cells wide, 6 high, with two walls of rocks. The cheese is top right, Pip starts bottom left, and the shortest route takes 12 steps. No cat this time. The rules: plus 1 for the step onto the cheese, which ends the walk; gamma (gamma) is 0.9. If Pip has not found the cheese after 30 steps, the walk is stopped and pays nothing. Being stopped is not a real ending: the last update still uses the number where Pip landed.

curriculum:2.t: How Pip learns. Pip learns with Q-learning, as in its own reel: a number for every move in every cell, nudged after each step toward the reward plus 0.9 times the best number where Pip landed. It mostly takes the move with the biggest number; one move in five is random. All numbers start at 0. So until Pip first reaches the cheese, every nudge is 0 toward 0: it learns nothing and just wanders.

curriculum:3.t: Wandering in the dark. Walk 1, from the real start. With every number 0, each move is a random pick among four. After 30 steps Pip has not found the cheese: stopped, reward 0, and nothing learned. It goes on like that. In its first 50 walks, Pip never reached the cheese; the first time was walk 57.

curriculum:4.t: Rare rewards, slow learning. This strip shows Pip’s first 300 walks, one bar each: teal when the walk reached the cheese, pale when it was stopped. In the maze, gold shading shows each cell’s best number. Each success pushes the good news only about one move further back, so the next success is still mostly luck. Over all 300 walks Pip reached the cheese 22 times. Only from walk 288 on could it follow its best numbers from the start to the cheese.

curriculum:5.t: Start easy. A curriculum is a list of lessons, from easy to hard. Lesson 1: Pip starts only 3 steps from the cheese, for 20 walks. Lesson 2: 6 steps away, 20 walks. Lesson 3: 9 away, 20 walks. Then the real start, 12 away. Only the starting cell changes. The maze, the rules and the way Pip learns stay exactly the same.

curriculum:6.t: Lesson 1. Walk 1 of the curriculum, 3 steps from the cheese, with the same seed as before. Even at random, the cheese is close: Pip finds it in 9 steps, and the last move gets the first non-zero number. In lesson 1, 19 of its 20 walks reached the cheese. The gold shading shows each cell’s best number: a trail of good numbers grows back from the cheese.

curriculum:7.t: Each lesson builds on the last. Lesson 2 starts 6 steps away. Pip still wanders, but it only has to stumble into the gold trail; from there the big numbers lead it home. 20 of 20 walks reached the cheese, then 13 of 20 in lesson 3. Then the real start: in its next 40 walks Pip reached the cheese 36 times. From walk 65 on, its best numbers led from the real start to the cheese.

curriculum:8.t: The same strip, with lessons. The same kind of strip, for the curriculum run. The black ticks mark the ends of lessons 1, 2 and 3; after that, every walk starts at the real start. Teal from the very beginning: the reward is no longer rare. Without the curriculum, the same seed gave 22 cheese walks in 300; with it, 287.

curriculum:9.t: Fifty runs, same seeds. One seed could be luck, so we repeat with seeds 1 to 50. After every walk we test: from the real start, following its biggest numbers with no random moves, does Pip reach the cheese? The lines count the runs that pass; lesson walks count too. After 100 walks: 0 of 50 without, 50 with the curriculum; after 200, 4 against 50. Grey, another easy fix, starts each walk in a random cell: 19 after 100 walks, 47 after 200.

curriculum:10.t: Why it works. Learning needs rewards. On the hard task, rewards were so rare that most walks taught nothing. Easy lessons pay off almost every time, and what Pip learns there is exactly what it needs later: the end of the route. Compare reward shaping: shaping changes the rewards to give hints. A curriculum keeps the rewards and changes the tasks.

curriculum:11.t: Order matters. A badly paced curriculum is slower. Too big a jump: 60 walks 3 steps away, then straight to the real start. After 100 walks, 35 runs pass, against 50; all 50 pass from walk 146, against 69 with the gradual lessons. Too slow: 120 walks on lesson 1 before moving on. No run can pass before it meets the real start, so the fair measure is when all 50 pass: from walk 172. Those extra walks went on a skill Pip already had.

curriculum:12.t: Your turn. Drag the number of walks per lesson: the three lessons, 3, 6 and 9 steps away, each get that many walks before the real start. 0 means no curriculum. All 50 runs are redone; the rose line is always no curriculum. Too few walks per lesson and the trail is not ready; too many and walks are wasted.

curriculum:13.t: Automatic curricula. Writing lessons by hand takes knowledge and trial and error. Instead, a teacher program can pick the next lesson itself, for example start cells where Pip currently succeeds about half the time: not hopeless, not boring. It can judge that from Pip’s recent walks from each start, without extra tests. Self-play, from the multi-agent reel, is a curriculum too: the opponent gets harder exactly as fast as the learner improves.

curriculum:14.t: Where it is used. In 2009, Yoshua Bengio and colleagues named it curriculum learning for machine learning, inspired by how people are taught. In 2017, Carlos Florensa and colleagues trained simulated robots by starting them near the goal and moving the start farther away, as in this reel. OpenAI’s Rubik’s cube hand, in 2019, widened its randomised simulation as it got better, which OpenAI called automatic domain randomisation: an automatic curriculum.

curriculum:15.t: Recap. When rewards are rare, an agent learns almost nothing: it must stumble on success before any learning starts. A curriculum starts with easy versions of the task and makes them harder step by step. Easy lessons pay often and build skills the hard task needs. Order and pace matter: too big a jump or too slow both waste practice. A teacher can choose the lessons automatically.

metarl:0.t: Meta-R L: Learning to Learn. Train on many tasks so a new one takes minutes, not months.

metarl:1.t: A family of mazes. A new game for Pip: one room, five cups along the top. The cheese hides under one of them. Pip can’t see under a cup; it finds out only by stepping onto that cell. Stepping onto the cheese pays plus 1 and ends the walk. A walk is stopped after 30 steps. gamma (gamma) 0.9. Each new maze, the cheese moves to a random cup, and stays there for that maze’s 10 walks.

metarl:2.t: Starting from scratch. Plain Q-learning, as in the Q-learning reel, treats every maze as brand new: numbers start at 0, one move in five random, alpha (alpha) 0.2. The chart: across, walks 1 to 10 on one new maze; up, the steps each took, averaged over 300 new mazes. 30 means the walk was stopped. From scratch: 27.0 steps on walk 1, still 20.6 on walk 10. The shortest walk averages 5.2.

metarl:3.t: Learning to learn. But these mazes are all alike: the cheese is always under a cup on the top row. A learner that has seen many of them could know that, and search smartly. Meta-R L trains on many related tasks so that a new one takes only a few tries. Two loops: an inner loop that adapts to one maze within its 10 walks, and an outer loop, across thousands of mazes, that improves how the inner loop adapts.

metarl:4.t: The task is hidden. Which cup hides the cheese is part of the state, and Pip can’t see it, just like the corridor cells in the fog reel. So this is a P O M D P, and the same fixes apply. With memory, Pip can carry what it found from one walk to the next. That is exactly what an adapting learner needs.

metarl:5.t: Memory across walks. So give Pip a memory that survives between walks of the same maze: which cups it found empty, and where the cheese was. It is wiped only when a new maze begins. Pip’s policy now reads its cell plus its memory: 925 situations, 3,700 numbers. Fine for a table here; a real R L squared agent’s memory is far bigger, so it uses a network. Pip is never told where the cheese is; it has to find out, and remember.

metarl:6.t: Training on many mazes. The outer loop is just ordinary Q-learning on cell plus memory, across mazes; the inner loop is the memory filling up within one maze. It runs over 3,000 mazes with 10 walks each, one move in five random, alpha 0.2. That is 218,432 steps of experience. Every maze rewards the same thing, the cheese. But to collect it quickly in a new maze, the habit that pays is: search the cups, then remember. That is what the numbers come to encode.

metarl:7.t: A new maze. A maze Pip has never met, the cheese under cup 5. Walk 1: Pip heads for the cups and looks under them until it finds the cheese, in 10 steps. Its memory now holds the spot. Its order, nearest cup first, then left, then right, is one of the best, 6.8 steps on average without random moves; cup 5 is its worst case. Walk 2: straight there, 6 steps, the shortest. These walks show Pip’s own choices, with no random moves.

metarl:8.t: Where the learning lives. On new mazes we freeze Pip’s numbers: none of them changes, yet Pip adapts. The fast learning happens in its memory. The slow outer loop learned a fast inner learner. This is the idea of R L squared, written R L squared, from Duan and colleagues and from Wang and colleagues, both 2016. There a recurrent network had to learn what to remember, too. Our toy hands Pip its memory slots ready-made.

metarl:9.t: Another idea: a good start. A second family, mammal (Finn, Abbeel and Levine, 2017), keeps ordinary learning as the inner loop, and learns starting numbers from which a few learning steps fit any maze in the family. Our toy uses Reptile, a simpler cousin of mammal: copy the start, run Q-learning on one maze for 3 walks, then move the start a tenth of the way toward the result. Repeat for 3,000 mazes. Each move pulls the start toward one maze’s answer; averaged over thousands, it settles on what all mazes share.

metarl:10.t: What the start knows. Here is the learned start: in each cell, the move with the biggest starting number. Follow the arrows from any cell and you reach the top row, where they sweep right along the cups, and back from cup 5. The start can’t know which cup, since that changes every maze; it only knows where cups are. Without memory, it is one fixed set of numbers. On a new maze, ordinary Q-learning takes it from there.

metarl:11.t: Three learners, new mazes. Same 300 new mazes, all three still making one move in five at random. From scratch: 27.0 steps on walk 1. From the learned start: 10.8, and 8.7 by walk 3, as Q-learning adapts. With memory: 9.0 on walk 1, then about 6.6 per walk from walk 2 on. Random moves keep both above the shortest, 5.2. The good start stalls higher: each visit moves a number only a fifth of the way, so overriding its pull toward every cup takes many walks.

metarl:12.t: The catch. Meta-learning only helps on tasks like its training ones. A new family: the cheese on the left wall, in one of three cells at random, 3 to 5 steps from the start. By walk 10: from scratch 10.5 steps, learned start 13.7, memory learner 24.5. Our memory has slots only for cups, so it can’t even record this cheese; a real R L squared network might do better or worse. And the 218,432 training steps pay back only after about 1,200 new cup mazes.

metarl:13.t: Your turn. Slide to change how many mazes the memory learner trained on, from none to 3,000. The chart shows its steps per walk on the same new mazes, with the from-scratch line for comparison. How much outer-loop experience does it take before Pip has learned how to learn?

metarl:14.t: Where it matters. Meta-R L is studied for robots that must cope with a new load, a new surface or a damaged leg after a few tries, and for systems that must adapt quickly to a new user or opponent. Most results so far are in simulation, and on task families that are close together, like Pip’s cups.

metarl:15.t: Recap. Meta-R L trains on many related tasks so that a new one takes a few tries. The hidden task makes it a P O M D P. R L squared learns a fast learner that lives in memory: it searched the cups once, then remembered. mammal learns a good starting point for ordinary learning. Both help only on tasks like those they trained on.
